title: Packers-Bears Thursday Injury Report: Chicago Star Out Again
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – With Sunday’s rivalry showdown between the Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears looming, both teams’ offensive lines are coming together.
The question is who they’ll be blocking for.
For a second consecutive day, Bears running back Kyle Monangai did not practice on Thursday due to thumb and toe injuries. He carried the ball 30 times during last week’s pounding of the Jets, so another day of rest should do him some good.
For the Packers, running back Chris Brooks – the starter last week against Tampa Bay – did not practice for a second consecutive day due to an ankle injury.
“We’re going to give him another day, see where he’s at tomorrow and then, obviously, make a decision after that,” coach Matt LaFleur said before practice .
If Brooks is out, the Packers will ride with MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson and practice-squad back Pierre Strong.
Whoever is in the backfield, chances are they’ll be running behind what the Packers hope will be the No. 1 line for the rest of the season. During the media portion of practice, Kevin Zeitler was the right guard. He got repeated snaps in combo-blocking drills alongside starting center Sean Rhyan or starting right tackle Anthony Belton.
“He’s progressing good,” LaFleur said of Zeitler. “He’s getting a little bit more each and every day. Again, we’re trying to ramp him up to where he feels comfortable to go out there and play winning football.”
Along with Brooks, former starting left guard Aaron Banks (knee and toe) and former starting right guard Jacob Monk (quad) were the three players who did not practice.
Rookie center/guard Jager Burton, who did not play against Tampa Bay due to a groin injury, returned to practice on Thursday. He sat out Wednesday due to back spasms.
“I had a little tweak from lifting, but I’m feeling a lot better now,” he said. “It’s more of a day-to-day thing, but it’s just kind of weird with backs. It’s something you’ve got to protect a little bit.”
Receiver Savion Williams, who was designated for return from injured reserve this week following a preseason ankle injury, practiced for a second consecutive day as limited participation.
“It’s great,” quarterback Jordan Love said on Wednesday. “Say has missed a good amount of time right now, been on IR. He’s a key part to our offense. He’ll definitely be able to step in and make plays when he gets back and, obviously, it’s just about getting him back, ramping him up like you said, but he’s a key part of our offense. So, we’ll need him out there and it’s good to see him back.”
Burton’s progress to limited was the only change to Green Bay’s injury report.
The big development in Chicago came on the offensive line. After playing about 90 snaps against the Jets, left guard Joe Thuney, right guard Jonah Jackson and right tackle Darnell Wright did not practice on Wednesday. All three progressed to limited participation on Thursday.
Their presence will be huge, obviously, because they are the driving force behind the NFL’s top-ranked running game. Plus, starting left tackle Braxton Jones was placed on injured reserve on Saturday with a knee injury.
Also for Chicago, the team’s other top running back, D’Andre Swift, progressed to limited participation as he rebounds from hip and knee injuries.
Monangai is seventh in the NFL with 324 rushing yards and Swift is eighth with 311 rushing yards. The Packers have 232 rushing yards as a team.
Quarterback Tyson Bagent, who will start again in place of injured Caleb Williams (hamstring), downplayed the impact of the injuries.
“We're having a ton of meetings throughout the day,” he told reporters in Chicago. “Those guys will hit the field at some point this week. I’ve really just got to be a pro, get the base plan down and really nothing changes.
“Every week, you see big boys taking a couple days off here and there, especially when you get 90 plays. We wouldn't expect all 11 to be out there firing on all cylinders after a game like that. So, really just doing what we need to do right now. Recovery is at a premium in order to get everybody feeling fresh. I think that's more important than having guys beat up out there, going through half-effort reps on the practice field.”

title: Is Packers Coach Matt LaFleur on Thin Ice? Here Are Latest Hot-Seat Rankings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Is Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur on the hot seat?
A team that’s built to win a Super Bowl is about the ugliest 2-2 imaginable and facing a Week 5 showdown against the rival Chicago Bears, whose coach, Ben Johnson, would love to push LaFleur off the hot seat and into the boiling cauldron.
On the other hand, while the NFL is a bottom-line business, there needs to be some nuance to the conversation about LaFleur’s future.
“LaFleur’s roster right now is a nightmare,” noted Sports Illustrated’s Conor Orr, who put LaFleur at No. 4 in his latest hot-seat rankings .
LaFleur’s calling card is his creativity as an offensive play-designer and play-caller. The offense, however, ranks just 27th in points scored.
Is that LaFleur’s fault? Or is that the fault of a combination of misfortune, with season-ending injuries to receiver Jayden Reed and Zach Bako-Bewele, and poor roster construction by general manager Brian Gutekunst, who was guilty of overrating the talent on the offensive line?
On paper, running back Josh Jacobs, tight end Tucker Kraft and receivers Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Jayden Reed would be a formidable quintet.
But Jacobs is, essentially, serving an indefinite suspension, Kraft is coming off a torn ACL and Reed is out following a neck injury. Those five players didn’t play a single snap together last season and they won’t this season.
Without Jacobs and with that had been a subpar offensive line, the running game has been terrible.
NFL rushing leaders pic.twitter.com/WWuESV5ffs
The defense, meanwhile, is starting the season without its best player, Micah Parsons, and just lost arguably its second-best player, Edgerrin Cooper, to a torn Achilles.
“Green Bay has something like 30 percent of its total salary cap either on injured reserve or the commissioner exempt list,” Orr noted.
Then again, the Packers hold the dubious NFL leads for penalty yards, dropped passes and fumbles. LaFleur isn’t guilty of false starts and drops, but those continued mistakes reflect poorly on the coach and his staff.
Discipline-Related Penalties 1. PHI, LV & IND 1 ... 30. LAR & GB 8 32. SEA 32 Penalties included: Unnecessary Roughness, Unsportsmanlike Conduct, Taunting, ... (see footnote for full list) pic.twitter.com/LhnPPpgEYP
“Green Bay had a string of high-improbability losses last season and already saw a divisional game against the Vikings turn violently on the heels of a strange fourth-down decision,” Orr concluded as part of a much more extensive and thoughtful breakdown.
“But LaFleur has also been making tuna salad out of a dreadful situation in 2026. Jordan Love’s hit total went way down on Sunday, and the Packers’ rushing game looked like it improved marginally. He deserves credit for that.”
LaFleur is No. 5 in Fox Sports’ hot-seat rankings , with Ralph Vacchiano placing him between the Eagles’ Nick Sirianni and the Chargers’ Jim Harbaugh.
The contract extension that LaFleur was given after last season’s flameout could be his saving grace this time around, with Vacchiano wondering if the team’s board of directors would be willing to eat the remainder of a contract that is believed to be worth in the neighborhood of $15 million per year.
“However,” he continued, “the Packers also can’t ignore what’s happening to his team. They are regressing offensively even though they have an outstanding young quarterback in Jordan Love and an array of good receivers. And the defense has taken a huge step back after the loss of DC Jeff Hafley.”
Those last two points aren’t exactly accurate. Watson and Golden aren’t exactly an “array” of receivers, and the defense hasn’t taken a “huge step back” under new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon.
Regardless, Vacchiano is correct that the Packers “are at risk of being buried in a very dangerous division.” That’s part of what makes this such a huge game for the Packers.
At CBS , LaFleur ranks only ninth and the hot seat is actually “cool.” Bryan DeArdo also pointed to the contract, though it’s important to note the Packers would be off the hook (at least partially) if LaFleur were to land on his feet in the next coaching cycle.
“Because of his contract, the only way LeFleur's job would actually be in jeopardy at season's end is if the Packers have an epic collapse and there are rumblings that he's lost the locker room,” DeArdo wrote (while misspelling LaFleur’s name).
In the prediction markets, LaFleur’s seat has cooled considerably since the night of the blowout loss to the Falcons. At Kalshi , for instance, his odds to be “out before March” were as high as 90 percent. It was at 20 percent on Thursday morning but bounced up to 28 percent while this story was being written.
This, obviously, is a huge game for the Packers. They are 2-2, with their two wins coming against teams with a combined 1-7 record. With a win, they’d be in second place in the division and right in the thick of everything that they set out to accomplish this season. With a loss, they’d be in last place in the division and in deep trouble.
LaFleur, for his part, is keeping the messaging as normal as possible this week. It’s not about him. It’s not about Ben Johnson. It’s about winning this game.
“I do think, it’s an NFC North opponent and they’re the defending champion,” he said on Wednesday. “So, there’s always an added importance in divisional games. And they’re one of the premier teams in the National Football League. I think our guys will be ready to roll, but it’s more important that we focus on the day to day, making sure our process is right and making sure our preparation’s on point.”

title: Packers Thursday Update From Practice: A Strong Possibility
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers running back Chris Brooks missed a second consecutive practice on Thursday with the ankle injury sustained last week at Tampa Bay.
“We’re going to give him another day, see where he’s at tomorrow and then, obviously, make a decision after that,” coach Matt LaFleur said before practice, the second of the week before Sunday’s huge rivalry showdown against the Chicago Bears.
Brooks was one of three players who didn’t practice on Thursday.
If Brooks isn’t able to play this week, the Packers almost certainly would add Pierre Strong from the practice squad. While the Packers have an empty spot on their 53-man roster, they probably would elevate him rather than promote him.
With 15 carries for 58 yards (3.9 average), Strong was one of the team’s more productive running backs during the preseason but lost out on his bid to make the 53-man roster after the team traded for Kaleb Johnson.
“I feel like God puts everybody through a test. So, I'm hungry,” he said after the final preseason game. “I'm always going to be hungry. Practice squad, 53-man roster. I'm still hungry, but I'm very hungry now. So, I want to get back to where I've been.”
The Packers have the worst rushing attack in the NFL this season and are on pace for the worst rushing attack in NFL history .
Could Strong help? A fourth-round pick by the Patriots in 2022, he totaled 499 rushing yards and averaged 5.0 yards per carry with New England in 2022 and Cleveland in 2023 and 2024. He added 26 receptions, averaged 23.8 yards per kickoff return and even contributed 17 tackles.
Jager Burton is back after dealing with back spasms yesterday. Three players aren’t practicing: Chris Brooks, Jacob Monk and Aaron Banks. Here’s a little of QB1. pic.twitter.com/MainZbIEsT
Four players did not practice for the Packers on Wednesday. Along with Brooks, the others were Aaron Banks (knee/toe), who was supposed to be the starting left guard, Jacob Monk (quad), who had been the starting right guard, and rookie interior lineman Jager Burton (back).
Banks and Monk didn’t practice on Thursday, either, though they were doing rehab work on the field. Burton, who didn’t play at Tampa Bay after being listed as questionable with a groin injury last week, was dealing with back spasms on Wednesday but returned on Thursday.
Right tackle Anthony Belton, who was limited participation on Wednesday with a knee injury, practiced again on Thursday. LaFleur said he didn’t have any concerns about his availability for Sunday.
The team doesn’t do any 11-on-11 drills in front of reporters. During the opening segment of the media viewing period, there is a five-man line working with quarterback Jordan Love on cadence and adjustments.
Kevin Zeitler for the second consecutive day was the right guard.
“He’s progressing good,” LaFleur said. “He’s getting a little bit more each and every day. Again, we’re trying to ramp him up to where he feels comfortable to go out there and play winning football.”
The Packers’ new No. 1 line of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Laken Tomlinson, center Sean Rhyan, Zeitler and right tackle Anthony Belton could make its debut on Sunday.
“I’m real excited, just based off last game, just how much better that felt coming out of it,” Rhyan said. “I think the whole unit wants to feel that way. And we played pretty well, but I think that we can play even better.
“And that’s real exciting because if we’re playing really well, then the whole team is going to play well and I know we as O-line take pride in that, so f*** it, we’re excited. We’re going to keep getting better, they’re going to throw the best five out there, and we’re going to keep going.”

title: With Bad Run Game, Packers Should Trade for One More Veteran to Fill Hole
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers’ big-ticket left guard, Aaron Banks, is injured. Because of ineffective play from the backups, they signed 34-year-old Laken Tomlinson. Because of ineffective play from young right guard Jacob Monk, they signed 36-year-old Kevin Zeitler.
With Luke Musgrave injured, they signed 31-year-old tight end Jonnu Smith. To strengthen their defense after offseason attrition, they signed 31-year-old tackle Javon Hargrave and traded for 30-year-old linebacker Zaire Franklin.
Suddenly, the youngest-in-the-league Packers have hit middle age.
So, with general manager Brian Gutekunst setting aside youth for seasoning, maybe there’s one more oldie-but-goodie roster move to be made.
Trading for Cardinals running back James Conner.
It’s a possibility we’ve mentioned a few times, both before and after Josh Jacobs was arrested.
Conner, 31, is on injured reserve following a foot injury that sidelined him for most of last season. He was limited to individual drills during training camp but was placed on IR for the start of the season. He is expected to be ready to go in a few weeks, at which point maybe there will be some clarity on Jacobs’ future.
At 6-foot-1 and 233 pounds, Conner fits the big-guy mold the Packers have typically preferred. Jacobs is one of the best dirty-work runners in the NFL. Block a play for 2 yards, Jacobs is going to fight for 2 or 3 more.
Conner is that same style of player. In 2024, Jacobs during his blockbuster debut season in Green Bay ranked eighth out of 46 backs who had at least 100 rushing attempts with 3.45 yards after contact per carry, according to Pro Football Focus. Conner was 13th with 3.30. He was 14th in rushing attempts but fourth with 62 forced missed tackles.
“Conner, he’s a beast,” Packers coach Matt LaFleur said before the 2024 matchup against Arizona. “He’s a big, physical back that is more elusive than he leads on just in terms of (being) a bigger guy.”
Conner is a proven workhorse. In 2023, he rushed for a career-high 1,040 yards even while being limited to 13 games. In 2024, he topped that with 1,094 yards in 16 games.
Jacobs is an adept receiver. So is Conner. Drafted in 2017, Conner from 2018 through 2024 averaged 40.1 receptions per season. He caught a career-high 55 passes in 2018 and averaged a career-high 10.1 yards per catch in 2021. In 2024, he caught 47 passes for 414 yards (8.8 average) and one touchdown.
When healthy and assuming he’s still got some spring in his step, Conner would be leaps-and-bounds better than Chris Brooks, MarShawn Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson.
Brooks is an incredibly valuable role player but doesn’t bring a lot of juice as a runner. Lloyd, the 2024 third-round pick, has some juice but hasn’t shown the speed to turn the corner, as he would prefer to do, or the power to gain yards after contact. Johnson has power but lacks the acceleration.
Moreover, Lloyd and Johnson fumbled last week against Tampa Bay, with LaFleur clearly exasperated after the game. Conner fumbled four times out of 283 touches in 2024 but had zero in 235 touches in 2023.
Just like Tomlinson brought stability and performance to the line in his debut against Tampa Bay, Conner could do the same thing for a rushing attack that ranks last in the NFL with 58.0 yards per game and is on pace to finish with the fewest rushing yards since the 1970 merger , when teams played only 14-game seasons.
Again, working under the assumption he comes back in something close to vintage form and hasn’t been tackled by Father Time, Conner’s size, power and proven production would give the Packers the balance they’ve been lacking all year. That, in turn, would do two things for the offense.
One, it would be in better down-and-distance situations. Green Bay is last in the NFL in third-down conversions due in large part to its average third-down play requiring 8.1 yards. That’s the fourth-longest distance required, with three teams averaging 8.2.
Two, it would have a real play-action threat. Love’s play-action passer ratings were 113.7 in 2023, 104.4 in 2024 and 100.3 in 2025. This year, it’s a whopping 132.8, but LaFleur hasn’t leaned on it much because he hasn’t been able to lean on his running game at all.
Josh Jacobs was one of the Packers’ team leaders. He was voted a captain in 2024 and 2025 and probably would have again if not for the off-the-field incident that has meant what’s essentially a paid, indefinite suspension.
“You want positive energy around you whether you’re talking (to people) or not,” Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur told reporters recently . “You know when you walk in a room or walk into someone’s house and you can just feel that the energy’s right? That’s what you feel – at least me, and I know the offense and the team, when you walk by him or when he’s in the room. He doesn’t have to say much to get his point across.”
Yes, age is a number that can’t be ignored with a running back, though three 30-something backs – Baltimore’s Derrick Henry, Minnesota’s Aaron Jones and San Francisco’s Christian McCaffrey – all have more than 340 combined rushing-receiving yards. Among running backs, they are in the top 14 in the league.
With first-round pick Jeremiyah Love and free-agent Tyler Allgeier atop the depth chart and their season going nowhere fast, the Cardinals might be interested in trading one of their more popular players. With Jacobs’ status in limbo, the Packers might be interested.
The financial price wouldn’t be exorbitant; Conner’s base salary is $2.355 million; the Packers would only have to pay a prorated portion of that. There also are per-game roster bonuses. The price to make the trade would be low, too, considering that Conner is 31 and coming off an injury that limited him to three games last season.
To be sure, the Packers will need some sort of assurance that Conner is healthy and can be a factor, whether that’s the Cardinals getting Conner some game reps once he’s healthy or simply an honest conversation between the coaching brothers.
“I always go back to return to play, return to performance, and both those guys are smart enough to know that they want to be back when they can actually perform at the level that they're capable of,” Mike LaFleur said of Conner and tight end Tip Reiman.
By the time Conner is ready, the Packers might have some certainty on the status of Jacobs and the ability of the others to provide a real, honest-to-goodness running threat. Those timelines, and the trade deadline being Nov. 10, could be in a convenient alignment.
The Packers for the better part of two decades had shown almost zero interest in 30-something players. It’s different this year, with general manager Brian Gutekkusnt frantically trying to maximize the Jordan Love-Micah Parsons window.
Thus, for a team that hasn’t just bent from its usual roster-building philosophy but run from it with its veteran-centric additions, a healthy Conner would make a lot of sense in perhaps providing the running game the Packers have lacked through four games.

title: Packers Sign Elite Size-Speed Linebacker Prospect to Practice Squad
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers are signing rookie linebacker Jack Dingle to the practice squad following a Wednesday workout, according to a source.
Dingle will take the place of Kristian Welch on the practice squad; Welch is taking the place of Edgerrin Cooper on the 53-man roster. A corresponding roster move will have to be made.
Dingle went undrafted this year but there’s plenty to like from a skill-set perspective. Before this year’s draft, he measured 6-foot-4 18 and 232 pounds. He posted elite testing numbers, including a 4.57 in the 40 and a 20-yard shuttle of 4.17 seconds.
His Relative Athletic Score was 9.82. That means he’s in the 98th percentile among linebacker prospects over the last four decades.
Jack Dingle is a LB prospect in the 2026 draft class. He scored a 9.82 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 65 out of 3460 LB from 1987 to 2026. https://t.co/FvjagUF5bb pic.twitter.com/gGoxszCYea
The Packers worked out a bunch of linebackers this week to fill Welch’s spot on the practice squad. They included Penn State’s Curtis Jacobs, Florida State’s Cam Riley, Michigan’s Josh Ross and Georgia’s Channing Tindall on Wednesday and LSU’s Deion Jones and Mississippi’s Chris Paul on Tuesday.
By far the most accomplished was Jones, a second-round pick by Atlanta in 2016 with 91 career games. He played in 17 games for the Buccaneers last season. Tindall was a third-round pick by the Dolphins in 2022 who appeared in 51 games with zero starts during his career. Paul was a fifth-round pick by the Seahawks in 2025 who has not played in a game.
Ultimately, the Packers zeroed in on Dingle, who was selected to the famed Freaks List by The Athletic’s Bruce Feldman.
As a senior at Cincinnati, he had 60 tackles, including four tackles for losses. In four seasons, he tallied 164 tackles, with four sacks, 9.5 TFLs and two passes defensed.
In The Beast , The Athletic’s Dane Brugler called him a potential core special-teams player.
“Dingle passes the eye test with his tall, athletic build, and NFL scouts praise his “old-school” style, both on the field and as a worker behind the scenes. His instincts aren’t quite fully developed, but he can unlock and go once he diagnoses the play. He attacks with pop, which helps him disengage from blockers. Stiffness through his core and lower half hinders him at times, both as a tackler and in coverage.”
Dingle went undrafted and signed with the Cincinnati Bengals but failed to make their roster.
“I'm an undrafted player. I have to be the best communicator on the field,” he said while with the Bengals. “I've got to get the playbook as fast as I can so I have every detail to prove myself out there. Just take it one step at a time.”
The ticket for any undrafted player to make it in the NFL will be special teams. That’s how Welch has carved out a long NFL career.
“That’s the No. 1 thing,” he said at the Bengals’ local pro day in April. “Get on a team and start learning special teams right away. That’s very important to these coaches. I’ve talked to a lot of current NFL players and they say, ‘Learn that kick-step on punt man. If you make the punt team, you’ll make the team.’”
His father, Nate Dingle, was a linebacker who played a combined 17 games for the Eagles, Jaguars and Rams in the 1990s.
“He says he was a beast, that’s what he tells us, but we don’t really know,” Jack said . “He was definitely a hard worker; that’s who I learn from a lot.”
He wasn’t exactly a natural because he was late to mature physically.
“I told his mother his sophomore year of high school, if you would have seen him, I said he wasn’t going to play at Trinity,” his dad said. “He was this gangly, small, thin, maybe 5-10 kid that was uncoordinated. His brother used to make fun of him.”
Obviously, Dingle won’t be a reason why the Packers persevere without Cooper. It will be up to the new linebacker tandem of Zaire Franklin and Isaiah McDuffie to pick up the slack left by the budding star’s torn Achilles.
“Obviously, J.G. is going to put us in good position, but I got a lot of faith in Hopp and Duff,” Franklin said on Wednesday. “Both of those guys have played a lot of ball, made a lot of plays on Sunday – made plays against Chicago before. I think those guys will be ready to play.
“We’re close and I think we have a talented linebacker room since I’ve been here. Obviously, it was headlined by Coop who’s an amazing player, but I think those guys will do a good job of stepping in and making plays, as well.”

title: As Part of Comeback, Packers TE Tucker Kraft Needs His Stinger Back
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – When Tucker Kraft talked to reporters in June, he was brimming with confidence that he’d be just as good this season as he was last season despite coming off a torn ACL.
“I’m not really buying into the people come back off an injury and aren’t the same,” Kraft said at the time. “People com(ing) back off their injury, if you’re not coming back off your injury the same, then what are you doing? What were you doing your entire rehab?”
When Kraft was injured during a midseason game against Carolina, he was on top of the tight end world – or not far from it.
When Kraft said what he said, he raised the bar to perhaps an impossibly high level. After all, Kraft was coming back from a torn ACL, not a sprained ankle or groin injury. It’s a serious injury. The return-to-play standard might be nine or 10 months. The returning-to-a-player’s standard – an elite standard, in the case of Kraft – almost always takes longer.
So, it’s no knock on Kraft that he has 15 catches for 148 yards and one touchdown through four games this season after catching seven passes for 143 yards and two touchdowns against Pittsburgh in his last full game of last season.
Reminded of what he said in June, is Kraft better now than he was last year?
“Statistically, obviously not,” he said after practice on Wednesday, the first of the week before facing the Bears on Sunday. “But I feel like the game is constantly slowing down for me.”
He spoke at length about his mental acumen. When he motions across the formation, “I can see my triangle of humans and I can make the call for our side.” In the passing game, he is “feeling more savvy” with his coverage recognition.
Then Kraft provided an interesting thought, courtesy of his own family.
“Statistically, it might not look like I’m playing better,” he continued. “Some could even say that I might’ve lost my stinger. My brothers were telling me that. They said, ‘You look like you kind of lost your edge out there.’
“They said it to me last week. I tried to go out in Tampa and be a meanie but it was too damn hot; I couldn’t breathe out there. This week, try to get back to my roots, the kind of sh** I was on my first and second year when I was playing to the echo of the whistle and being hard on the defense.”
He joked that opposing players have been coming up to him during games and congratulating him on his contract extension.
“They asked me if I was out there just being friendly,” he said of his brothers. “I’m like, ‘Well, kind of.’ It’s nice at the end of a play when a guy’s not talking crap to you but he’s dapping me up and saying, ‘Congrats on your contract’ or something like that. I’m going to have to flip the script now.”
There are reasons for Kraft’s slow start. The combination of a porous offensive line, a blitz-happy opponent and the deafening noise in Minnesota limited his chances against the Vikings. Against the Jets, he also had to help cover up for the line.
“I hate to look back, but you go back to Minnesota, and we’re second-and-12 for like a third of the game. So, I’m chipping and running to the flat,” Kraft said. “And then you’ve got the second game, away in the rain, we have a game of turnovers and still quarterback’s ending up on the ground, so not another opportunity for me to have 130 yards, eight receptions, two touchdowns.
“But there’s more to come. This is Week 5. So, we’re excited to keep this ball rolling.”
Tucker Kraft had a good YAC game against Tampa Bay. pic.twitter.com/9JsOC2x8nJ
Last week against Tampa Bay, there were signs of that ball rolling and vintage Kraft emerging. Yes, he dropped what should have been an easy touchdown. But he also turned two short catches into explosive gains with his renowned run-after-catch skills. On his first catch against the Buccaneers, he broke two tackles.
“Yeah, I’m still waiting for the big one, that vintage feeling you’re talking about,” Kraft said. “I’m still waiting on that, but I’ve learned now, really, especially with how my career started here, it’s all about just doing the most with each and every opportunity you get. So, I’m going to continue to attack that. The football is coming to me. What am I doing with the ball?”
Kraft is capable of doing great things with the ball in his hands. Against the Steelers last year, he had 128 yards after the catch. It was the most YAC by a tight end since 2018. Perhaps Kraft was guilty in June of raising the bar too high, only to be clocked by the reality of overcoming his injury and the team’s assorted problems.
As coach Matt LaFleur said this week, it’s important to practice; Kraft missed the offseason practices and the start of training camp and didn’t play in the preseason as he worked his way back from a major injury.
“I know we want instant gratification, and the expectation is whatever you saw that that’s what it’s going to be,” LaFleur said. “But I think for many of these guys, not just us, but around the league, guys that come off major injuries, it just takes them some time. They got to get back to playing.”
However, maybe he’s getting closer to becoming that elite version of Kraft again. In the first three games, he forced one missed tackle and had 50 yards after the catch on nine receptions. Against the Bucs, he forced two missed tackles and had 42 yards after the catch.
Of 33 tight ends who have been targeted 10 times, his 6.1 YAC per catch ranks a solid ninth, so it’s not as if he’s been bad. If he can get past his early-season drops and the offensive line allows him to be a bigger factor in the passing game, the production will return to his lofty expectations.
“Yeah, absolutely,” Kraft said of rounding into form. “And the goal is always to ascend. If you’re not getting better, you’re getting worse. So, my goal is to walk in this building every day with the right mindset. See the film, see our run/pass pictures, and really just apply it with all the reps that I’ve had throughout my time here since 2023.
“So, yeah, I’m just trying to continue to evolve, get some more of those breakout on the field plays. That all starts with catching the ball.”

title: Packers-Bears Wednesday Injury Report: Seven Chicago Starters Didn’t Practice
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – For the first time in a long time, the injury drama might be with the Green Bay Packers’ opponent this week.
The Chicago Bears listed 12 players on their initial injury report of the week following Wednesday’s practice. Seven players did not practice – and they’re all starters. That includes quarterback Caleb Williams, who will miss a third consecutive game with an injured hamstring.
Four players didn’t practice for the Packers . That list includes the starting guards – or, more accurately, the former starting guards – Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and Jacob Monk (thigh). Also not practicing were running back Chris Brooks, who suffered an ankle injury last week against Tampa Bay, and rookie offensive lineman Jager Burton.
Burton was on the injury report with a groin injury last week. He was active for the game but didn’t play. Now, he’s listed on the injury report with a back injury.
Receiver Savion Williams was designated for return from injured reserve, where he had been since suffering a sprained ankle during camp, and defensive tackle Anthony Campbell, who missed the last two games with a sprained ankle.
“We’ll see,” coach Matt LaFleur said of Williams’ status for this week. “He’s kind of been ramping up in terms of just with our strength coaches, with our athletic trainers. We’ll just see how he handles the week.”
Also, cornerback Brandon Cisse, who missed the last handful of plays against Tampa Bay with a neck injury, was full participation.
Brandon Cisse missed the end of Sunday’s game. pic.twitter.com/VtljmzoIYV
“Everything’s good,” he said.
He said Chicago had an “unbelievable” offense, which is led by coach Ben Johnson.
“I think they got a really good receiving corps,” Cisse said. “Obviously, really talented. Got to be able to play both [run and pass] because they got guys who can – if you're trying to play the run so much, they can play-action you – and they got a great head coach who’s an offensive head coach.
“Understand that they try to create matchups, so you got to make sure that you're tackling in the run game, but got to be definitely aware in the pass game because he (Johnson) throws a lot of things at you. He’s very smart. So got to make sure your eyes are in the right place, ready to make plays.”
The Bears are entering the week with a lot of injury problems. However, of the seven players who didn’t practice, six are on the offensive side of the ball. That unit was on the field for an astounding 89 plays against the Jets, so there might be a bit of wear and tear to get past.
The list includes running backs Kyle Monangai and D’Andre Swift, who form one of the top tandems in the NFL. Both players have more than 300 rushing yards for the NFL’s top-ranked rushing offense. That’s more than the Packers have as a team.
“Thumb's not an issue, but he did have 30 carries and he feels like he had 30 carries,” Johnson said of Monangai.
Three of their top blockers didn’t practice, either, with right tackle Darnell Wright and guards Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson on the sideline. With starting left tackle Braxton Jones on injured reserve, the Bears’ imposing front wall might not be at its best for this rivalry showdown.
“We had a long discussion there with our guys and we're trying to do the best we can to balance it out,” Johnson told reporters in Chicago before practice. “Like I said before, we are still in improvement mode.
“We're just starting the second quarter of the season. It's all about how do we improve as a team and, so it's not like we can go full-fledged walkthrough – we don't believe in that – and yet it'll be a little bit different practice here today to make sure that we're smart about the number of reps that we got on Sunday.”
Also for Chicago, starting nickel Kyler Gordon was full participation as he comes back from injured reserve. He was full participation.
Two other players coming off injured reserve, linebacker Noah Sewell (Achilles) and defensive tackle Shemar Turner (knee), were limited.
“We’ll let this thing play out,” Johnson said when asked if Gordon could return for this game. “That’s been the thought throughout – let’s utilize the time that we have and we’re given, and we’ll make a decision at the end of the week if one of those three are ready to go. We’ll see how it works out. We’ve got a lot of things in flux with the roster and who’s going to be active here this week. We’ll make those decisions as we go.”

Limited participation: RT Anthony Belton (knee), DT Anthony Campbell (ankle), edge Lukas Van Ness (shoulder), WR Savion Williams (ankle), DT Devonte Wyatt (ankle).
Full participation: CB Brandon Cisse (neck).
Note: Williams has been designated for return from injured reserve and is within his 21-day practice window.

title: Packers Wednesday Update From Practice: Help’s On the Way as Bears Week Begins
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers are getting a boost on offense with the return of receiver Savion Williams.
A third-round pick last year, Williams was having a good training camp until he suffered an ankle injury. He opened the season on injured reserve with a designated-for-return status.
Speaking before Wednesday’s practice, coach Matt LaFleur hinted that Williams could be a factor sooner than later – perhaps even as soon as Sunday’s home game against the Chicago Bears.
“We’ll see,” LaFleur said. “He’s kind of been ramping up in terms of just with our strength coaches, with our athletic trainers. We’ll just see how he handles the week.”
It’s worth noting the team has an open spot on the 53-man roster if he handles the week well and is ready to play against Chicago.
A glorious Wednesday with Lambeau the backdrop. pic.twitter.com/uhiyG1vZz2
It’s a good thing the Packers signed three linemen last week. That’s because Aaron Banks, who should be the starting left guard but was inactive the last two games, remains out with toe and knee injuries, and Jacob Monk, who started the first three games at right guard but was inactive at Tampa Bay, is out with a toe injury.
Plus, rookie guard/center Jager Burton, who started at left guard in Week 3, didn’t practice because of a groin injury. He was active for Sunday’s game but didn’t play.
It might mean nothing at all, but Kevin Zeitler was with the No. 1 unit at right guard for the start of practice at right guard. Last week, Donovan Jennings was at right guard during the brief media viewing window but Travis Glover got the start. Zeitler, however, was signed with the intention for him to start.
“Kevin’s still kind of a work in progress as far as the guy hasn’t been doing stuff for a while,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday. “He had one day in pads last week and he didn’t take any team reps because he didn’t really know what was happening yet.
“We’ll just evaluate that as we go. I anticipate him helping us out at some point in the near future, but I don’t want to say he’s going to play this week. He might, but we’ve kind of got to evaluate that as we go.”
The fourth player who didn’t practice was running back Chris Brooks, who suffered an ankle injury against Tampa Bay. The roster move made on Tuesday hinted that Brooks might be questionable, at best, for Sunday.
Brandon Cisse missed the end of Sunday’s game. pic.twitter.com/VtljmzoIYV
On the bright side, starting cornerback Brandon Cisse, who missed the end of the Tampa Bay game with a neck injury, and defensive tackle Anthony Campbell, who missed the last two games with an ankle injury, returned to practice.
Williams had a quiet rookie season as a third-round pick but had a couple of really big days at training camp this summer.
“First off, I think he’s caught the ball really well this training camp. Caught the ball with great hands, body control, staying on his feet,” passing game coordinator Jason Vrable said during training camp. “So, I think that was a big thing coming to college. I kept talking to him about being more comfortable with the catch point. I think he’s taken big strides there, and then ultimately, I think it’s been the playbook for him.
“Just from coming to college, to here to our system, which I’d say he was a little bit raw in some of maybe the routes we’re asking to run and what we’re asking to do down the field were a little bit newer to him compared to his role in college. But he’s done a really good job with the playbook. When you know the plays and you’re confident at the catch point, just building trust with Jordan – and I think as you see, Jordan’s giving him some opps in those practices.”
Like Matthew Golden but to an even greater extent, Williams was buried on the depth chart as a rookie. He caught all 10 targets for 78 yards and one touchdown and carried the ball 11 times for 37 yards.
At 222 pounds, he looks a bit like a running back, and that’s largely how he was used. He had a huge 33-yard catch on third down against the Giants to help rescue the Packers. Otherwise, his other nine catches came on passes he caught a combined 20 yards behind the line of scrimmage.
The Packers parted ways with Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks this offseason, opening the door for Williams to get more opportunities. Now, with Jayden Reed out for the season, Williams has a chance to be a critical factor.
He showed some flashes during training camp. One of the highlights of Family Night, for instance, with a jump-ball touchdown catch.
“Savion, his measurables are off the charts in terms of his size, speed, and strength,” LaFleur said afterward. “And then he’s just a young player that’s still learning and he’s got a long way to go, but I think he’s showcased a lot of great traits and that’s why we drafted him and that’s why we loved him coming out.”
The Packers need all the help they can get in the passing game. Christian Watson has 20 catches for 331 yards and Matthew Golden has 18 catches for 274 yards. The other receivers, Skyy Moore, Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant, have combined for 10 catches for 67 yards with a long gain of 12 yards.
“Say, he’s big, he’s strong,” Melton said during training camp. “But the good thing about Say that I love about him is his poise and getting to know him. Knowing Say, when he’s going out there and he’s joyful, he’s great. In training camp, there’s days when you’re up and down, but Say, I grew so close to him and the way he plays the game is really good.
“He could be a great player. He knows that. We know that and he’s shown that a lot. He’s going to keep working. He’s a big guy and he’s going to do great.”

title: Three Stats That Show Why Packers Could Be In Big Trouble Against Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – For the Green Bay Packers, this will be their big opportunity.
On Sunday, the sputtering Packers will face the rival Chicago Bears. The game will be played at Lambeau Field, where the Packers beat the Bears last season. And the Bears will be playing with backup quarterback Tyson Bagent as Caleb Williams will miss a third consecutive game with a hamstring injury.
A victory could be a season-changing achievement for the Packers. Imagine, after a difficult first quarter of the season , they would be 3-2 and in second place in the NFC North.
It won’t be easy. The Packers will have to overcome these statistical mismatches.
Only one game separates the teams in the NFC North standings, but the tale of the statistical tape shows a different reality.
The Bears have outscored their opponents by 47 points, or 11.8 points per game. That’s the third-biggest point differential in the league. They are plus-six in net touchdowns, trailing only San Francisco in the NFC.
The Packers have been outscored by 32 points, or 8.0 points per game. That’s the fourth-biggest negative point differential in the league. They are minus-five in net touchdowns, better than only Arizona in the NFC.
Both teams beat the Jets. Green Bay scored the final 13 points and won in overtime 20-17 at New York in Week 2. The Bears with Tyson Bagent at quarterback won 23-12 at home last week. The stats from the games show the difference in the teams.
Yards gained on offense: Green Bay, 199; Chicago, 492.
Yards allowed on defense: Green Bay, 285; Chicago, 157.
Net passing yards allowed: Green Bay, 218; Chicago, 98.
Rushing offense: Green Bay, 63; Chicago, 232.
Third-down offense: Green Bay, 1-for-9; Chicago, 7-for-15.
Third-down defense: Green Bay, 8-for-19; Chicago, 0-for-7.
Time of possession: Green Bay, 26:57; Chicago, 42:45.
The numbers show teams that are on a completely different trajectory.
After the game on Sunday, coach Matt LaFleur seemed annoyed even in victory. On Monday, LaFleur said, “What makes you say I was annoyed?”
When told it was his focus on the negative things, LaFleur replied: “I think there was a lot of things to build upon.”
But then, without missing a beat, he went right back to the negative.
“The one thing that I’d tell you is when you have opportunities, you have to capitalize on them, especially in this league. It’s so competitive and, certainly, the penalties are inexcusable. Putting the ball on the ground is inexcusable, especially when you have an opportunity to make a game a two-score game.
“That’s stuff that we have to absolutely clean up. I told the guys that whoever holds that ball, you hold it for everybody in the organization. Every player, their families, we’re all dependent on that. You can drill it, you can do ball-security drills all you want, but you have to have the mindset and you’ve got to have good fundamentals when you do it, as well. But we can’t be doing stuff like that.”
He’s right, obviously. The Packers can’t beat a good team until they stop beating themselves.
The Bears are first in the NFL in rushing with 196.3 yards per game. The Falcons, who routed the Packers at Lambeau a couple weeks ago, are second with 181.0 rushing yards per game. The Bears also are fourth with 4.94 yards per carry.
The Packers are last in the NFL with 58.0 rushing yards per game and 31st with 3.18 yards per carry. That puts them on a 17-game pace of 986 rushing yards. The lowest number since the 1970 merger was the 1970 Boston Patriots, who rushed for 1,040 yards in a 14-game season. The lowest 16-game total was the 2000 Chargers with 1,062 rushing yards.
MarShawn Lloyd leads the Packers with 81 rushing yards, or a season pace of 344 yards. That would be the lowest team-leading total since Michael Haddix’s 311 yards in 1990.
“I think – and he’ll probably tell you that, too – that there’s more out there,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday of Lloyd. “The one run that I saw that got me excited was a third-and-1. We ran an inside zone to the right, he bounced it left, made a guy miss and just had a really nice play. That’s kind of what I’m expecting to see from him, so that was good to see him just create a play like that. It was really good.”
Here's, “The one run that I saw that got me excited,” Packers OC Adam Stenavich said yesterday. It's MarShawn Lloyd on third-and-1 turning a TFL into a first down. pic.twitter.com/PiByEF55MI
An occasional run with vision and acceleration provides some hope but what the Packers need is production. Much better production. Much more consistent production.
The Packers have 232 rushing yards. The Bears have almost 3.5 times that number with 785. Their dynamic duo of Kyle Monangai (324 rushing yards) and D’Andre Swift (311) are two of the 17 individuals with more rushing yards than the Packers have as a team.
NFL rushing leaders pic.twitter.com/WWuESV5ffs
“For most of the day, it felt like we were moving the line of scrimmage,” Bears tight end Cole Kmet said after the Jets game. “When we’re doing that, we’re pretty tough to beat. … I know everyone loves the flashy plays. But, at the end of the day, it’s about how physical you are up front. That’s what we pride ourselves on.”
The rushing numbers play into what’s next.
A picture is worth a thousand words. So is this third-down graphic.
3rd Down Conversion Rates through Week 4 Offense: #1 SF, ..., #32 GB Defense: #1 CHI, ..., #32 DET pic.twitter.com/u6ImD7sAny
The Packers are last in the NFL in third-down offense. By a wide margin. They’ve converted 26.1 percent of their third-down opportunities; Seattle is next at 31.1 percent. Rather incredibly, even with better offensive line play, Green Bay was actually worse last week against Tampa Bay (2-of-10, 20.0 percent) than it had been all season.
The Packers’ conversion rate would be the 12th lowest since the NFL began keeping that data in 1972.
The Bears are second in the league in third-down defense, according to the official league stats. Opponents are converting only 23.7 percent of the time, just behind Minnesota’s 22.6 percent. As noted above, they pitched a third-down shutout against the Jets.
Looking at the defenses, the Packers have allowed 29 third-down conversions while the Bears have allowed only nine, even though opponents are facing similar down-and-distances.

title: Texans' Poor 0-4 Start Isn't Fooling Titans' Cam Ward, Robert Saleh
full_text:
The Houston Texans have their second AFC South game of the year on tap for this weekend as they'll be traveling to Nashville for a date with the Tennessee Titans .
And it's a massive game for both sides. Each side has suffered from four straight losses to open the new year, is hungry to flip the script this weekend, and avoid extending that streak to build some momentum in their race to climb up the division standings, and the AFC as a whole.
So one of these 0-4 teams is leaving this weekend with a win. And it seems like, even with such a gloomy record, the Titans certainly won't be overlooking the talent this Texans roster will bring to the table for Week 5 .
It's clear those in the Titans' building have been talking up what the Texans will be bringing to the table throughout this week––because there are a select few who haven't been shy to express how Houston's talent goes beyond what their record on the season says.
Titans quarterback Cam Ward was among those in Tennessee to applaud the type of talent the Texans have, as he would call them one of the best 0-4 teams in the NFL while previewing the Week 5 matchup on Wednesday.
"Every division game is a rivalry. That's one thing we want to do, is own the South," Ward said this week. "We've got a great opportunity versus them, and they gonna be excited. They look at us the the same exact way as we look at them: we're both 0-4 teams. We're both searching for a win this year. And it could really get us going the right direction."
"But it's going to be an exciting game. They're one of the best 0-4 teams out there in the NFL, and they're going to have their hands full when they come play us as well."
Yet it's not just Ward who's keeping all hands on deck for the challenge the Texans will bring this weekend. Titans head coach Robert Saleh was even more complimentary about Houston's roster, touting them as maybe "the greatest 0-4 team in the history of football."
"Might be the greatest 0-4 team in the history of football," Saleh said of the Texans. "Their defense is, obviously, one of the top-five units in all of football. They've lost four games to four really, really good football teams... They've been in a lot of really, really tight games. I think they've all come down to the last second, with the exception of maybe Cincinnati."
"But, overall, well coached. A lot of respect for DeMeco and his staff. Playmakers all over the place on defense. Nico Collins is there. C.J. Stroud plays at a high level. They're putting up a lot of points and yards on offense. And it's going to be a tremendous challenge."
Of course, all of that praise from a divisional opponent is certainly nice for the Texans to hear heading into their matchup after facing a bundle of criticism through the past several weeks. But at the end of the day, talk is cheap.
A loss against Tennessee might just end up being the dagger for any dream of a 2025-esque comeback for Houston. So DeMeco Ryans and his crew are going to have to ensure they have all of their operations tightened up to land their first win of the year against a divisional opponent they've frequently taken care of in recent memory.
Houston has won six of their last seven games against Tennessee dating back to 2022. Time will tell if they can add to that win total this weekend and prove those in the Titans' building right that this is indeed one of the best 0-4 teams in the league.

title: What Texans' Will Anderson Jr. Said About DeMeco Ryans Calling Plays
full_text:
The Houston Texans' defense will be making some changes heading into their Week 5 game against the Tennessee Titans .
Rather than Texans' defensive coordinator Matt Burke continuing to be the team's lead defensive play-caller, head coach DeMeco Ryans announced on Wednesday that he could be reclaiming the role as defensive play-caller this weekend against Tennessee.
The move effectively places Ryans back in the same role that he was in when he first arrived in Houston back in 2023. He had been the Texans' defensive play-caller for two years, and had relative success in the process, though decided to make a pivot in those operations last season.
After the Texans' 0-3 start in 2025, it was Burke who would take those duties over from Ryans en route to their 12-win season. And now, the two will be reverting back to their previous ways in hopes they can spark a similar change from their even-worse 0-4 start.
It's a move that many have suggested could be a possibility for the Texans to try out in hopes of getting their defense back on track from the up-and-down start they've had to the season.
Ryans noted upon his announcement that being the play-caller is no slight on Burke's abilities, yet allowed for the communication process to be a bit more streamlined on that side of the ball–– which has seemingly been an issue through four games of the season.
But how do the players on the Texans' defense feel about the shift?
In Will Anderson's mind, Ryans brings a different style of coaching: one that's more direct, but also allows for a bit of grace.
"I think what DeMeco brings–– that style of coaching where he's going to call you out. He's going to make sure that you know exactly what you're going to do, what you need to do and what you didn't do," Anderson said.
"I think he gives grace, but he's also going to hold people accountable. He's going to come in the meeting because he played this game, and he knows, like, 'Hey, man, you ain't repping our style right here."
So from Anderson's perspective, it feels like a positive change. The Texans' can get a more direct style of coaching, more direct communication, and hope to lead to better results on the defensive end.
Through four games this season, the Texans have allowed the 26th-most points scored and the 20th-most yards in the NFL on top of their brutal 0-4 start .
For a defense that many expected to be at the top of the league in terms of effectiveness, something had to change. And now, Ryans will be the one leading the ship defensively, and hope to turn things around in the process.
"I think it comes a little differently when it comes from DeMeco," Anderson continued. "When DeMeco's up there, you sit up a little bit more. You're more on your P's and Q's. Nothing against Burke. Burke's done a good job, but when the head coach is up there, it's kind of different."
"We have a ton of respect for him. He's going to get a lot of guys going with the energy that he brings. So, I'm excited for that."
Getting the right play-caller for this defense would be a big step for this Texans' defense to get back on track. That process becomes even easier when you've got the buy-in of one of the best defenders in the NFL . So perhaps this is the week where Houston flips the script for their first win of the new year.

title: Texans Sign Former Titans WR to Roster Just Before Week 5 Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans have added a depth piece to their wide receiver room just a few days ahead of their Week 5 matchup against the Tennessee Titans ––doing so by adding a pass-catcher who played in Tennessee a little less than two months ago.
According to an announcement from the Texans, the team has signed wide receiver Bryce Oliver to the 53-man roster.
Oliver is actually a recent part of the Texans' practice squad as well, considering he was in the facility for a two-week stretch in September . Houston added him as a part of the practice squad following his release from the Titans on cutdown day, yet the Texans would also release him on September 30th.
Fast forward to right ahead of Week 5, and the Texans seemingly wanted to bring Oliver back onboard, thus offering another layer of depth at the position, and even someone who was a part of the opposition for the past couple of years.
Oliver, 26, is a 6-foot-1, 214-pound wideout in his third year pro, and was a pretty regular piece of the Titans' receiver room for two years from 2024 to 2025.
An undrafted product out of Youngstown State, Oliver has played in 13 games throughout his NFL career thus far, all of those coming in Tennessee.
He's played in over 200 combined offensive and special teams snaps from his two years stationed there, and has hauled in seven receptions on 10 targets for 103 yards. He's also recorded three kick returns for 113 yards in 2024.
So he's not exactly the most experienced pass-catcher at the NFL level just yet. Most of his offensive production stems from his college days at Youngstown State. However, the Texans saw some value in him to bring him back aboard to their main roster, and clearly have a role in mind for him.
Oliver's signing now makes for the Texans' second practice squad reunion of the week, considering the front office opted to bring back quarterback Mark Gronkowski on Wednesday, thus giving this depth chart a third signal caller to lean on.
Heading into the Texans' Week 5 game against Tennessee, they had five wide receivers on their active roster before bringing in Oliver. Now, that total rises to six, and feels like a sign that the former Titans wideout will be primarily commanding special teams duties.
The Texans already have a solid dose of receivers on the roster due for their respective reps on the offensive side: Nico Collins, Xavier Hutchinson, Jaylin Noel, and Kayshon Boutte easily rise above him, and maybe even Jared Wayne.
There's also Tank Dell, who's presence on the team simply can't be ignored at this point in the season . He's officially seen his 21-day return window activated from injured reserve, hinting at Houston's wide receiver room will likely have another target to roster here in the coming weeks.
So for Oliver to make an impact, that gravity will have to come from outside of the offensive side of the ball and onto the special teams side. Or, he'll simply have to be moved up the depth chart in the event of any injury above him, which has yet to be reported within the wide receiver room as of Wednesday's injury report.
His first opportunity to do so will also come against the team he started his career with in Tennessee on Sunday at 12 PM MT, if he is indeed activated for game day.

title: DeMeco Ryans Knows Texans' Offense Needs to Fix This Key Weakness
full_text:
The Houston Texans' offense certainly showcased some signs of life this past weekend against the Dallas Cowboys, even in a 30-34 losing effort .
But one area of the Texans' offense that continues to be lackluster is how they've performed in the run game.
Outside of David Montgomery's three-touchdown performance in Week 1 against the Buffalo Bills, the Texans' production on the ground has been largely uninspiring, and a large piece of what's held their offensive ceiling back.
The team as a whole has ranked bottom three in the league for both total rushing yards (316) and yards per carry (3.5), and has lacked really any level of consistency or explosiveness that this team was really looking for heading into the year.
It was a topic of the Texans' offense that head coach DeMeco Ryans made sure to address heading into Week 5's matchup against the Tennessee Titans.
And for Ryans, their flaws in the run-game haven't been attributed to either of David Montgomery and Woody Marks in the backfield–– he's actually looking for the offensive line to step up on their end.
"For us to improve in the running game, we have to sustain our blocks better," Ryans said on Wednesday. "We start in the right way. We're attacking with the right hand placement. But what I'm imploring our guys is, how are you going to strain? How are you going to stay attached to your block and finish? That'll be the key this week."
Ryans certainly hasn't seen everything go awry on the offensive line this season. In fact, he made sure to highlight how the Texans' front has performed in pass protection over the last few years along with his run-blocking critiques.
However, not being able to hold up in the run game has been a key piece of what's killed the Texans' offensive ceiling to start the year off. So Ryans knows it's something he and his staff have to get right.
"The mentality is there, and we just have to go out and finish in the run game on Sunday," Ryans said. "I think everybody's seen our pass protection has been much better over the past couple years. We've done a great job of protecting it. C.J. is throwing the ball well. We just have to clean up some things in the running game."
Perhaps it'll take some offensive line maneuvering upfront to get that run-blocking up to par. Maybe the Texans will need to emphasize heavier personnel more and allow their tight ends to get on the field for longer stretches to help out their run-blocking.
Regardless, expect the Texans' production and efficiency on the ground to be a key emphasis this coaching staff looks to get right before Week 5 in Tennessee . Because another uninspiring day on the ground is far from what this team needs now at an 0-4 record.

full_text:
The Houston Texans got back to the practice field on Wednesday, heading into their Week 5 matchup against the Tennessee Titans — meaning we were also able to get a look at the injury report for both sides a few days away from this weekend's kickoff.
And for both sides, there were certainly a few noteworthy names who were either limited in practice, or didn't participate at all.
Let's break down what the state of injuries are for both the Texans and Titans after their first practice of the new week:
DE Will Anderson Jr.: DNP (ankle) OT Trent Brown: DNP (rest) LB Jamal Hill: DNP (knee) LB Azeez Al-Shaair: LIMITED (groin) WR Nico Collins: LIMITED (rest) DE Jadeveon Clowney: LIMITED (knee) WR Tank Dell: LIMITED (knee) DE Logan Hall: LIMITED (knee) DT Kayden McDonald: LIMITED (ankle) OT Braden Smith: LIMITED (foot) OT Nate Thomas: FULL (illness) S M.J. Stewart: FULL (knee) LB Wade Woodaz: FULL (thumb)
For the Texans. it's a much lengthier injury report than we've been accustomed to so far this season–– 10 players were deemed either limited or DNPs due to injury or simply rest.
The biggest name listed on the Texans' injury report by far is their All-Pro edge rusher Will Anderson, who was deemed a DNP with a new ankle issue that hasn't appeared on any other injury report to date.
And that's certainly at least a little bit eye-catching for the Texans, especially when noting it's not exactly a "rest" day for Anderson, and instead has him listed with an actual injury designation.
You'd have to expect Anderson to do everything he can to get on the field this Sunday for Week 5 for a pivotal game in Houston's season. But in any event, the Texans are without their best pass-rusher; it's a huge loss for their pass-rush and overall defense, likely leaving Jadeveon Clowney as the next man up to claim his snaps.
The Texans also saw depth linebacker Jamal Hill end up as a non-participant in practice with a knee issue, while offensive tackle Trent Brown was sidelined due to rest. Everyone else who was active, however, was at least a limited participant––and within those names were a few ideal pending reinforcements.
For one, Azeez Al-Shaair was able to be a limited participant in practice after missing Week 4's game against the Dallas Cowboys with a groin injury. That's a great sign that the Texans' starting middle linebacker, green-dot signal caller, and defensive captain can be back in the mix leading the charge in this front seven after a brief absence.
But Houston also saw a trio of recent injured reserve returnees make their way back to practice for the first time since training camp that deserve attention as well: rookie defensive tackle Kayden McDonald, veteran offensive tackle Braden Smith, and of course, wide receiver Tank Dell .
How those three progress over the course of the remaining practices will be key in determining whether or not they'll be ready to go for Sunday. Seeing them back in practice in some capacity, though, is a great sign to be had.

Also, names to keep an eye on: running back Tony Pollard and safety Amani Hooker, who each missed out on Wednesday themselves. Considering Hooker just suffered a concussion last weekend against the Baltimore Ravens, there's a good chance he won't be able to go, but Pollard's status might have a bit more optimism.

title: Texans Sign Undrafted QB to 53-Man Roster Heading Into Week 5
full_text:
The Houston Texans are making an addition to their quarterback room heading into their Week 5 game against the Tennessee Titans.
And it's actually a signal-caller they had in the building this season already, considering he was on the practice squad for two weeks.
According to the Texans' transaction log, the team is signing quarterback Mark Gronowski to the 53-man roster.
Gronowski was signed to the Texans' practice squad right before Week 1 against the Buffalo Bills last month, which came right after he was waived from the Miami Dolphins' roster, where he initially signed as a UDFA out of Iowa.
He'd spend two weeks with the Texans on the practice squad, was released after the events of Week 2, but in a short amount of time, now finds his way back to Houston in an even bigger capacity from where he left off last month.
Ironically, Gronowski’s college career before hitting the NFL as a UDFA rookie this season is a lot of what the Texans could benefit from this year: winning.
Gronowski is the all-time NCAA leader across all levels for total quarterback wins in a career. He won a 58 games between his time at both South Dakota State and Iowa, and has some pretty solid numbers in the process.
Gronowski had a college career completion percentage of 63.7% with over 12,000 total yards, 103 touchdowns, and 27 interceptions. He's also gained some noteworthy numbers on the ground, as he has over 500 carries for 2,312 yards and 53 rushing touchdowns.
That dual-threat ability is really what makes Gronowski shine. It was enough for the Texans to give him a spot on the practice squad to start the season, and now just about a month later, he now becomes QB3 on the 53-man roster behind C.J. Stroud and Davis Mills .
The Texans walked into this season with the expectation of having a select three quarterbacks on their roster: that was C.J. Stroud, Davis Mills, and Graham Mertz.
However, it wouldn't take long into the new year for those plans to change within the quarterback room. Graham Mertz suffered a torn ACL in the Texans' first preseason game vs. the LA Chargers, was ruled out for the season, and thus slimmed this quarterback room to two names heading into Week 1.
That two-man setup within a quarterback room that the Texans had for the first four weeks of the season isn't exactly uncommon in the NFL. But having that emergency third quarterback on the roster who can be called up in case of injury is always a nice layer of security to have.
So that's what the Texans are getting here: a third quarterback in Gronowski who will likely be inactive on most gamedays, work behind Stroud and Mills in practice as he had been in Weeks 1 and 2, and likely only get a chance to get on the field if an injury arises to either of the pair ahead of him on the depth chart.
Nonetheless, any player getting the call-up to a 53-man NFL roster is certainly a step in the right direction for their stock moving forward. So Gronowski undoubtedly walks into Week 5 as the biggest winner of anyone in this move.

title: Texans' Defense Could Solve Its Problems With This One Change
full_text:
The Houston Texans' defense––through the first four games of the 2026 season––has been a massive step below where they stood when wrapping up their previous campaign; a year in which many considered this group as the best defense in the NFL next to the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.
And now in part because of those defensive woes, which were most recently displayed in Week 4 against the Dallas Cowboys , the Texans now sit at a brutal 0-4 record.
So moving forward, seeing some type of change for this side of the ball could be recommended. Not a massive panic move, but something to flip the script defensively from what this team has seen through the last four weeks.
The easiest way for the Texans to try and flip the switch in a short amount of time? That might just be by giving head coach DeMeco Ryans primary defensive play-calling duties; a role he hasn't had since the start of the 2025 season when he handed that spot to defensive coordinator Matt Burke.
This isn't a spot that Ryans hasn't been in before. The Texans' fourth-year head coach, with a defensive-minded background, started his tenure in Houston controlling the defensive operations, while handing the offensive duties to then-Bobby Slowik, and now, Nick Caley .
But the Texans' coaching setup changed last year after Houston sunk to 0-3. Ryans handed over his defensive role to Burke, who would instead take more of a CEO role, and that led to the team finishing with a 12-5 record.
Naturally, the Texans entered this season with the same plan. Burke runs the defense, while Ryans oversees the whole project. But that's only led to Houston falling to an even deeper hole than they were in this time last year.
So at this point, why not make a similar change this time around, only to put Ryans in charge of the defense?
There is some good reason for the Texans to consider this, rather than simply making changes for the sake of doing so, because Ryans knows how to coach a defense.
Ryans led the Texans to a pair of top-half finishes through both 2023 and 2024 and a couple of playoff appearances when he was running the ship defensively.
He's also unlocked some of Houston's top talents on that side of the ball into what we know them as today, whether that be Kamari Lassiter and Jalen Pitre in their rookie seasons , coaching up Azeez Al-Shaair in his first season with the Texans, or helping Will Anderson Jr. en route to a Defensive Rookie of the Year award in 2023.
The numbers will tell you that Burke's defense from last season certainly produced better than Ryans' over his first two years in Houston. But over that stretch, this defensive unit has gotten better individually, built more chemistry collectively, and might set up for an easier task for Ryans to take on.
When Ryans was asked about the possibility of taking those duties after the Texans' Week 4 loss, he didn't exactly shoot the idea down. So perhaps it's something that's already being considered behind closed doors heading into this weekend against the Tennessee Titans.
Texans HC DeMeco Ryans was asked about the possibility of taking over defensive play calling duties from Matt Burke. #Texans #Sarge pic.twitter.com/LyJL5Ee4rP
The two key aspects that Ryans needs to get right? Limiting explosives and tuning up Houston's pass coverage. Houston's run defense has remained stout, pressure on opposing quarterbacks has remained mostly consistent, yet it's those two glaring holes in defending the pass that have left Houston's defense back at the drawing board like they are now.
This team certainly has the talent on that side of the ball to get it right, but might need a new mind leading the way for this group to really key in on their same successes seen from 2025. Maybe Ryans can be just that.

title: 4 Texans Players Who Need a Big Week 5 vs. Titans Amid 0-4 Start
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into Week 5 desperate to cling onto their first win of the 2026 season––having lost their initial four games of the year as a few players on both sides of the ball have been a bit underwhelming for one way or another.
Which means, as Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans arrives for the Texans, those struggling players will have to pick up their slack to help change the narrative and get a win on their record books.
Let's take a look at four players in the Texans' lineup who need a big Week 5 against the Titans this weekend, and might just help Houston get over the hump for their first win:
The Texans' run game really just hasn't found any sense of life since their first outing against the Buffalo Bills, where David Montgomery hauled in three touchdowns with nearly 80 all-purpose yards throughout the day.
In the games that Montgomery has played since that three-touchdown debut, he's logged a total of 27 carries for 67 yards, coming out to less than 2.5 yards per carry throughout. That lack of efficiency and explosiveness has really put a damper on the ceiling of this ground game, and has even led to Woody Marks claiming close to 50% of the snaps in the backfield.
The Texans need a big game from Montgomery against a lackluster Titans team to back up their investment of a fourth-round pick and Juice Scruggs given up for him earlier this offseason. Because right now, it feels as if Houston would like to have that one back .
Another name on the Texans' offense who had a strong start to the year, yet has been a bit disappointing in recent weeks is tight end Dalton Schultz. In Week 2 against the Cincinnati Bengals, Schultz put together an impressive 12 catches for 140 yards without Nico Collins that inspired confidence in what the rest of his season could look like .
But the Texans haven't exactly involved Schultz, or any of their other tight ends on the roster, much at all through the past two games––really in a bit of a head-scratching decision from Houston's coaching staff.
From a broader perspective, the Texans could certainly benefit from giving more opportunities to more than just one of their tight ends. Yet, seeing a pass-catching threat like Schultz start clicking again would be a positive step forward for this offense.
We now have had two of the Texans' first four games on the calendar where cornerback Kamari Lassiter has had some of his most overwhelming games as an NFL pro.
In his first game against Buffalo, Lassiter allowed Josh Allen to have a perfect passer rating when he was targeted. Last week against the Dallas Cowboys, he allowed 136 yards and eight receptions on the 11 plays he was targeted on––a lot of which allowed for star wideout CeeDee Lamb to have a career day.
For this Texans secondary to be at its best, Lassiter has to hold his own as the high-end complement to Derek Stingley on a way more consistent basis. Whether it be an individual fix or for the coaching staff to address, Houston's defense has to find better success in the passing game if they want any hopes of climbing back to .500.
The addition of Reed Blankenship into the Texans' secondary this offseason was done with the intent of getting a bit more consistency, talent, and another leader within their safety unit after the position had suffered from a ton of turnover throughout the course of 2025.
However, Blankenship's placement in this Texans defense seems as if it's led to more problems created than problems solved.
He did secure Houston's first interception of the year in Week 3 against the Indianapolis Colts, yet has allowed at least a 109.0 passer rating when targeting, and hasn't seen his zone-heavy fit mesh with the rest of this secondary that excels in man-to-man.
Blankenship showing that his presence really can be valued in this lineup will be big for his stock moving forward. Because if there are any similar secondary struggles from what's been seen over the past few weeks, the coaching staff might just make a change to plug newly-healthy veteran M.J. Stewart into that strong safety spot instead.
