title: Jaguars' Injury Report Gets Longer Before Eagles Clash, But What Are the Real Concerns?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' injury report is getting quite long.
The Jaguars started to see defensive back injuries creep up over the last week, which culminated in safeties Eric Murray and Caleb Ransaw leaving Sunday's win over the Cincinnati Bengals after injuries had hit the cornerback room.
Now, the injury report has gotten extensive as the Jaguars prepare for Week 5 against the Philadelphia Eagles . Here is the first injury report of Week 5, and what it means for the Jaguars moving forward.
The Jaguars had one player listed as a non-participant in Wednesday's practice in Murray (concussion), while the list of limited Jaguars was quite long: offensive tackle Cole Van Lanen (knee), cornerbacks Montaric Brown (hamstring), Jarrian Jones (foot), Jyalon Jones (hamstring), and Jourdan Lewis (hamstring). In addition, the Jaguars also had offensive tackle Anton Harrison (elbow), defensive tackle Davon Hamilton (foot), and defensive end Josh Hines-Allen (groin) listed as limited.
The Jaguars had two players as full participants after they had previously been limited throughout the season in running back LeQuint Allen (hip) and wide receiver Jakobi Meyers (thumb). It must also be remembered that the Jaguars placed Ransaw on injured reserve on Tuesday, with Liam Coen declining to say on Wednesday whether it was a season-ending injury ,
As for which of these injuries look to be the most concerning, the secondary has to be the first group to note. The Jaguars will be without Ransaw for at least a month, if not longer, and Murray missing Wednesday's practice could mean the Jaguars have to gear up either Rayuan Lane or third-round rookie Jalen Huskey to step into the lineup.
Lane, who made the game-ending tackle on fourth-down against the Bengals last week, is a second-year Day 3 pick who has not started a game. Huskey, the No. 100 pick in April's draft, has not yet made his official NFL debut after being a healthy scratch for the first four games.
"Huskey, I think you look at the amount of reps that he got at the Carolina joint, at the Saints joint, Tampa joint, he's been in competitive situations, played a ton throughout the preseason. I think he's been coming along," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Wednesday.
"I like his play energy. He's got his hands on the ball in multiple of those joints and made some downhill, physical plays. We'll have to look at it throughout the week and hopefully we lock him in to be able to give us communication, stability back there. That's the key point and put those guys in a position to be successful. I'm excited about him getting a potential op.”
Then there is the cornerback room. The Jaguars did not have Montaric Brown available against the Bengals last week, and now the Jaguars have three other cornerbacks added to the injury list, including two with dreaded hamstring designations. As things stand today, the only healthy cornerbacks on the Jaguars' active roster are Travis Hunter and Alijah Huzzie, who they signed off the Houston Texans' practice squad on Tuesday.
Added to that injury list is Jones, who the Jaguars signed as cornerback and special teams depth on Tuesday. The Jaguars very well could need Jones to step up on special teams due to the injury to Ransaw and the chance of Lane being elevated to a starter role on defense.
"Obviously, continuing to add depth and competition there. Jaylon Jones has been a really good special teams player around this league for the last few years. I think he had like [12] tackles last year on special teams," Coen said.
"Continuing to try to add players that are diverse, that fit your culture, that are going to be able to help us, whether, if they have a hat on game day, not just maybe in one phase, on special teams and being able to give you quality snaps throughout the course of the week at different positions, whether it's at corner, nickel, safety, and I think the two guys that we added have some of that flexibility. “
As for the other injures: Van Lanen has been limited in practices all season and, as usual, should be good to go on Sunday. Hamilton has also been limited in practice over the last few weeks but has still managed to play. The Harrison and Hines-Allen injuries are new, but Hines-Allen did not give any indications from the locker room on Wednesday that this would be a game he would be missing.

title: 3 Most Important Things Jaguars' Liam Coen Said About Week 5's Eagles Matchup
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are off to a 3-1 start in 2026, but now is no time for them to start looking behind them. That is, of course, because they have another big matchup on the way in Week 5.
The Jaguars are set to travel overseas to play the 2-2 Philadelphia Eagles in London on Sunday, giving the Jaguars a challenge that will change their preparation, environment, and much more.
“We got to have mental toughness to prepare ourselves throughout this week, and also have a professionalism to us that understands that this is a business trip. We're going out there to play football games, and it's something you have to do," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Wednesday.
"Anytime you get outside of your normal rhythm, routine and environment, something is going to happen to you. Something will tweak. It's natural for every human being and so, what I challenge them with is to identify what it is for you that can occur when you step out of your environment and routine, and to think about it and to get ahead of it."
So, what were the most important things Coen had to say about the Jaguars' Week 5 matchup on Wednesday? We break it down below.
The Jaguars will not be facing All-Time great right tackle Lane Johnson on Sunday following Johnson's retirement on Tuesday . That means the Jaguars will be facing either rookie right tackle Markel Bell or former Jaguars offensive tackle Fred Johnson, who the Jaguars traded back to the Eagles last season. The Jaguars should naturally have an advantage against whoever the Jaguars put at right tackle, though Coen noted Wednesday that he does not expect many changes for the Eagles.
“Not much. I think it changes in terms of you're losing a really good player, right? If you look at over the course of the years, injuries, some of the times they've had guys, sometimes they haven't, " Coen said. "I think that they have confidence in the guys being able to step up and play. So, from a game plan standpoint, it doesn't change much.”
Johnson was still having a terrific season for the Eagles, which makes his retirement a true loss for Philadelphia. So while the Eagles obviously have built-in contingency plans for the tackle position, the simple fact is that the Eagles have now lost Johnson, Cam Jurgens, and Jeff Stoutland over the last year. The Eagles are going to be hurting at the offensive line spot.
Travis Hunter had one of the best highlights of the early NFL season in Week 4. He intercepted Joe Burrow on a play that would end up being negated due to a roughing the passer penalty, and he made Bengals wide receiver Tee Higgins look absolutely ridiculous on a juke as he transitioned from cornerback to ball-carrier. The nifty move has led plenty of people to wonder if that makes any impact on Coen and his desire to get Hunter more snaps on offense, but Coen made sure to clear that up Wednesday.
Travis Hunter snatched Tee Higgins' ankles 😭 pic.twitter.com/AFCDe8csjZ
"I thought it was a really good play," Coen said. "No, we know we’re going to get him. That was really cool. It was. It was really cool.... It's good to see. But what you guys want more of, and I get it, but look at the last two weeks, what he's been able to do while we stay firm on the plan. And so, will it come? Absolutely.”
Coen is essentially saying to trust the Jaguars' process when it comes to Hunter and his usage. It has paid off with impact plays from Hunter at cornerback over the last two weeks, with Hunter playing a massive role in each of the Jaguars' last two wins. Coen and the Jaguars' process has clearly worked with Hunter to start 2026, so there is no real reason for them to shift directions, even if the Hunter play was, well, unreal.
Coen is one of the best play-callers in football, and he will be in quite the chess match with someone else who can make the same claim. Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio is one of the best coordinators of his generation, and the impact he has made on the rest of the NFL with his scheme and mindset is clear when you look across the league, including in Jacksonville. Most defensive coordinators are playing catchup when it comes to facing Coen, but that does not seem to be the case this week.
"I think that's what makes him so challenging is that he's going to have those touchés a little bit, right? Where you're like, I thought I had him there or that looked like they schemed him up and then they play a totally different coverage that they had played maybe in that situation for the previous three to four weeks. That's what I've always really appreciated about him," Coen said. "I remember 2018 Chicago-Rams, that was really the first time we had seen the 6-1 stuff and playing everything from top down and making us earn every single play. Every single blade of grass was earned, wasn't giving up the big plays, and obviously, Coach Belichick [North Carolina Head Coach Bill Belichick] gets a lot of credit for that Super Bowl. It really started with him at Chicago that year in 2018.”
Fangio has had quite a bit of success against Trevor Lawrence in their matchups, but he has never faced Coen and Lawrence as a duo. The Jaguars have one of the best offenses in the entire NFL, but Fangio is one of the few coordinators who has the ability to keep pace with them. Coen will need to be on his A-Game as a play-caller.

title: Good, Not So Good From Jaguars' First Month of Season: Trevor Lawrence, Brian Thomas Jr., and More
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars made it through the first month of the NFL season mostly unscathed.
Jacksonville is sitting at 3-1 after the first four games of the season, are alone at the top of the AFC South, and have gotten off to an early three-game lead over the Houston Texans. Alll things considered, the Jaguars have been among the NFL's best teams.
But what ultimately were the highs and lows of the first season and how the Jaguars got to where they are? We break down The Good and Not So Good of the first month below.
The Jaguars have certainly seen Trevor Lawrence take a step. He ranks top-eight in both EPA/Play and success rate amongst quarterbacks despite playing in an aggressive offense that doesn't often utilize checkdowns or screens like other quarterbacks who play in the AFC. According to NextGenStats, Lawrence has thrown downfield (10+ air yards) at the highest rate in the NFL this season (43.3%), completing 60.0% of such attempts (5th-highest) for 470 yards (12th-most) and six touchdowns (T-2nd-most). Lawrence is the engine that drives the offense, and I think his accuracy and decision-making are the best they have ever been in his career. Lawrence got hot at the end of last season, and he has only gotten better since.
Travis Hunter's progress at the cornerback position has been nothing short of remarkable. After serving as part of the rotation for the first two weeks of the season, Hunter has been one of the best cornerbacks in football over the last two weeks and he has completely changed the Jaguars' secondary with the way he gets his hands on the football at such a high rate. The Jaguars have stuck to their guns by keeping Hunter mostly at the cornerback position instead of using him at wide receiver, and it has led to Hunter becoming a game-changer for the Jaguars' defense. Hunter has developed even quicker on defense than anticipated.
The Jaguars drafted Nate Boerkircher at No. 56 overall with hopes of him allowing the Jaguars to expand the position's role in the offense, and that has happened without a hitch. The Jaguars have played 12 and 13 personnel at higher rates than they did a year ago, and the selection of Boerkircher is the biggest reason why. The Jaguars have been more explosive out of 11 personnel, but the fact that they can actually turn to other formations when needed, depending on the matchup, is a very good sign.
The Jaguars had one of the NFL's most middling running games a year ago, and Liam Coen went out of his way this offseason to say fixing it was a priority. They Jaguars did that by adding an effecient power back in Chris Rodriguez Jr. and adding strong run blockers in the draft in Boerkircher, Emmanuel Pregnon, and Josh Cameron, but perhaps the biggest reason the running game has taken off is because of Bhayshul Tuten. According to NextGenStats, Tuten has reached 15+ mph on 19 of his 60 rushes this season, the most of any player. Nearly half of Tuten's rushing yards (49.9%) have come after a missed tackle this season, the highest share of any player (min. 25 rushes).
The Jaguars' run defense has once again been elite. The only team that found some semi-success against the Jaguars on the ground were the Denver Broncos in Week 2; otherwise, the Jaguars have been able to suffocate running games and force offenses to air the ball out. That strategy has led to several turnovers for the Jaguars, and it is clear that their strong run defense from a year ago was not simply a one-year jump. The run defense is amongst the best in the entire NFL, if not the very best overall -- and it comes down to how they play.
After a stellar offseason program and the best training camp of his career, things just not have panned out for Brian Thomas Jr. this season. Through four games, Thomas has nine catches for 105 yards and a touchdown, averaging just over 25 yards per game. Thomas is tied at No. 61 amongst all NFL receivers in catches, sharing production with names like Pop Douglas, Laquon Treadwell, Kayshon Boutte, and Isaac TeSlaa. Thomas is an important part of the Jaguars' offense due to his speed element, but he simply has not seen the ball thrown his direction very often.
It is tough to say things look good for Caleb Ransaw after Sunday's knee injury in the first quarter. After not appearing in any games as a rookie due to his training camp foot injury, Ransaw made it healthy through training camp this year and then played 59 snaps in the first 13 quarters of the season before his injury against the Bengals last week. Ransaw was placed on injured reserve on Tuesday as a result, and head coach Liam Coen declined to answer whether it would be a season-ending injury for the second-year safety. If it is indeed a long-term injury, then Ransaw could have just 59 real snaps in his first two seasons. That is not ideal considering the importance Ransaw played to their safety depth behind Antonio Johnson and Eric Murray.
The Jaguars' offensive line was facing plenty of changes entering the 2026 season, with Anton Harrison moving to left tackle, Ezra Cleveland moving to right guard, and a rookie starting at guard with Emmanuel Pregnon. That does earn them some grace, but it is perhaps worrisome that the line's two worst games by far, especially in pass-protection, came against the two best defensive lines they played. The line has had some good performances vs. the Cleveland Browns and New England Patriots, but their tough days in protection against talented pass-rushers from the Denver Broncos and Cincinnati Bengals is a potential red flag.

title: Week 5 NFL Power Rankings Roundup: Jaguars Keep Climbing Toward AFC's Elite
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are stacking wins, and they are continuing to rise in the power rankings as a result.
After last week's impressive 22-7 win over the Cincinnati Bengals , the Jaguars have plenty of shine to them moving forward. When checking out this week's power rankings roundup, it is clear the Jaguars are quickly becoming one of the AFC's favorites.
The Jaguars are only behind the Seahawks in these power rankings, which is hard to deny after the success the Seahawks got against the Jaguars in 2025. The Seahawks have been terrific once again to start the 2026 season despite an odd loss to the Washington Commanders in Week 3, and the Jaguars can confidently say there are not many teams better.
A reminder that the Jaguars were ranked No. 17 at the start of the season for ESPN. What a swing and a miss, with the Jaguars now looking like one of the true powers of the AFC. Liam Coen is pushing all of the right buttons for the Jaguars on both sides of the ball, and they have earned their big rise in these rankings.
The Jaguars should be No. 4 on here. The Minnesota Vikings, to me, have zero possible explanation for being ranked above the Jaguars. They have one of the worst offenses in the entire NFL, and it is worth a debate as to whether their defense is any better than Jacksonville's considering the difference in quality of quarterbacks faced.
The Chicago Bears keep beating bad teams, which has earned them a spot over the Jaguars here. They get some credit for Caleb Williams being out, but not enough to rank them over the Jaguars right now.
The Bills over the Jaguars after their performance against the New England Patriots in Week 4 seems .... odd.
The Buffalo Bills are one spot behind the Jaguars, which could say it all when it comes to the Jaguars' spot in the AFC pecking order. The Baltimore Ravens are ahead of the Jaguars, which will be sorted out later this season.
The expected teams are in front of the Jaguars here: the Seattle Seahawks, Kansas City Chiefs, and San Francisco 49ers. Those are the only teams I think you can semi-justify when it comes to putting them above the Jaguars after the first month.
Only the Chiefs and 49ers, who are both undefeated, are ahead of the Jaguars in these rankings. Those are tough to argue against, even though it is worth considering the Jaguars beat both of them a year ago -- including a win over the San Francisco 49ers on the road. The Jaguars are in a proper spot in these rankings.
In short, the Jaguars are starting to get the respect they deserve. No power ranking has the Jaguars below No. 6, and they are ranked in the top-3 more than once. The Jaguars have proved their mettle through the first month of the season, with impressive wins against the Cleveland Browns, New England Patriots, and the Cincinnati Bengals. Now, it appears people have caught up.
With that said, do not expect the Jaguars to hone in on any additional respect, or any perceived lack of it, over the course of the next few weeks. The Jaguars used it as a rallying cry a year ago, but it certainly appears the Jaguars have accepted that they are simply a good team with very little to prove to anyone.
“I don't think we really care about the credit. We're going to go into each week, and if you don't look at us as an imposing defense, then we're going to impose our will on you," Jaguars safety Antonio Johnson said Monday.
"If you don't respect us, then we're going to make you respect us. I know personally, in the rooms that I've talked to the players, we don't care about the respect. You don't respect us, cool. We're going to make you respect us, so we're not even tripping about that.”

title: How the Jaguars' Defense Should Attack the Eagles With Lane Johnson Retiring
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are set to face an undermanned Philadelphia Eagles team on Sunday, and there is reason to believe they can take advantage of it.
The Eagles have faced several injury questions ahead of the two sides facing off in Week 5 in London, but the biggest blow came on Tuesday with All-Pro right tackle Lane Johnson officially announcing his retirement after a 14-year career.
With Johnson no longer a factor for Anthony Campanile and the Jaguars' defense, how should Jacksonville attack the Eagles' offense on Sunday? We take a look below.
With Johnson officially not playing against the Jaguars, the Eagles will most likely turn to rookie offensive lineman Markel Bell as their new right tackle. Bell is a hulking lineman with plenty of talent and athletic traits, but he did struggles last week against the Los Angeles Rams. According to Pro Football Focus, Bell led the Eagles with six pressures allowed in a blown loss to the Rams that saw the Eagles' offense struggle.
The #Eagles offensive line Markel Bell -- 6 pressures allowed, 18.8% pressure rate Cam Jurgens -- 5 pressures allowed, 12.5% pressure rate Drew Kendall -- 3 pressures allowed, 9.4% pressure rate
Bell is not a lost cause, of course, since he still showed good things as a run-blocker and because he had not received first-team reps in the lead-up to Sunday's game. But it does mean that the Jaguars have potentially found a weak spot in the Eagles' normally strong offensive line, which might also be without Cam Jurgens this week.
The Jaguars, of course, are coming off a strong game in terms of their pass-rush. They collected two sacks and 11 quarterback hits against the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 4 that saw Arik Armstead have a stellar outing, in addition to others like Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen. The trio combined for 15 pressures against the Bengals, and they could be picking up some much-needed momentum entering the Eagles week.
Hines-Allen and Walker are the Jaguars' two best pass-rushers by quite a bit, and the Jaguars have never been afraid to let both get reps against right tackles. Walker faces off against opposing right tackles more than Hines-Allen does, but this could be a week where the Jaguars are better off flipping that ratio to give Hines-Allen the most advantageous matchup possible.
Bell was a mark for the Eagles' offense last week, and the Jaguars need to ensure that they take advantage in the same manner. Johnson has held the right tackle spot down for a long time for the Eagles, and it will take longer than one week in London for the Eagles to truly fill his spot and move on.
The Jaguars have been better at getting after the passer this year when they rush four and do not blitz. That should be the strategy they take into Sunday: rush four and put the best pass-rushers on Bell, whle dropping the other seven defenders back in coverage to disrupt Jalen Hurts. This is a winning formula when executed against most teams, but the Eagles seem especially prone to it.
The Jaguars have all of the momentum entering Week 5 . With Johnson now out of the picture, they must take the appropriate steps to ensure they can keep that momentum going.

title: The Chiefs' Pass Rush Has Room to Improve, But It's Probably Been Better Than You Think
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs haven't recorded a sack in three games. At face value, that's an alarming statistic that paints a grim picture of the team's pass rush. After a longer look, there are plenty of reasons to be optimistic that the team's defensive line will be able to put it all together after the bye week.
Using this week off to take a longer look at a few key position groups that will determine where the Chiefs go in the next act of the season, Kansas City's D-line has some work to do, but they have been better than their box score indicates.
First, find the Chiefs in this chart of key pass rush stats. (There's a lot of information for all 32 teams, so we'll break down the important parts next.) Surface-level, what do you see?
Key pass rush stats: pic.twitter.com/uq0LEa6pEK
There's a whole lot of green (which is good) throughout the Chiefs' row, with two dark purple (bad) cells. Why?
In that chart, the Chiefs are No. 6 in the NFL in pressure rate, No. 8 in quick pressure rate, No. 13 in non-blitz pressure rate and No. 8 in average time to pressure. Those are the numbers of a top-10 pass rush unit! Then, the purple boxes.
The Chiefs are No. 31 in sack rate (2.5%) and dead last, No. 32, in pressure-to-sack ratio (5.7%). The KC D-line is creating pressure at a top-10 rate, but they've been one of the worst-finishing teams on those opportunities. Ultimately, I think that paints a relatively positive picture of the pass rush, and it certainly beats the alternative.
Those numbers are supported by other individual stats, like the fact that George Karlaftis was credited with a whopping seven quarterback hits against Kirk Cousins by Pro Football Focus ( a performance supported by a longer look at the film ), giving him a total of 12 quarterback hits this season , despite getting zero sacks out of those hits.
Most QB hits this season, via @PFF George Karlaftis - 12 Greg Rousseau - 12 Dallas Turner - 9 Cameron Thomas - 9 Maxx Crosby - 9 Resulting Sacks Greg Rousseau - 6 Dallas Turner - 6 Maxx Crosby - 3 Cameron Thomas - 2 George Karlaftis - 0 pic.twitter.com/CdsAVfNdmt
Regarding the other defensive ends, rookie second-round pick R Mason Thomas has also flashed far beyond his one sack would suggest , while former first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah (lined up over the center in the clip below) has had some of his best reps as a pro throughout the start of this season.
The way R Mason Thomas can accelerate towards the QB is just nuts. pic.twitter.com/ZsjpPTFvY6
Even second-year third-round pick Ashton Gillotte's season benefits from a deep dive into more advanced metrics, as Gillotte's "DIPRA" (defensive impact per rush attempt) is 10th-best in the league through four weeks.
The defensive tackles, particularly superstar veteran Chris Jones and first-round rookie Peter Woods, haven't had a series of game-wrecking moments so far this season, but Woods has shown tremendous physical tools , and Jones has been on the injury report with a calf issue to begin the year. I'm still very optimistic about Woods, and I'll wait a few more weeks before I'm willing to worry about Jones in his age-32 season.
Defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga has been a positive force against the run, and second-year lineman Omarr Norman-Lott is still on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list due to his ongoing recovery from last season's torn ACL.
Yes, the Chiefs' pass rush still needs to turn pressures and hits into sacks, but they appear to have the players to get to the quarterback; that's a much better problem than the issues they had last season.

title: How Does the Chiefs' Wide Receiver Room Stack Up at the Bye?
full_text:
On Sunday in Las Vegas, the Kansas City Chiefs' offense felt like it was hitting its stride, particularly in the deep passing game. Explosive plays had returned both on the ground and through the air, giving the Chiefs multiple ways to burn opposing defenses. Then, on one of those deep completions, wide receiver Tyquan Thornton suffered a serious ankle injury, ending Thornton's two-touchdown, 111-yard day on a somber, season-threatening note.
For now, the Chiefs will at least be without Thornton for the foreseeable future , while Rashee Rice also exited the Raiders game with a tweaked hamstring. Even if the Chiefs do complete the much-speculated reunion with Tyreek Hill , he reportedly wouldn't be ready to return to the field until November . So, how will the offense adjust in the meantime?
Every *catchable* target for Worthy through 4 weeks. *Two route-pass location miscues not included, plus final pass vs LV + Best in open space & on the move (crossers and crossers) - 15/19 balls were caught against the body, double underhand - Rarely working back to the ball pic.twitter.com/d5x7D51rCf
Even as fan sentiment regarding third-year first-round wide receiver Xavier Worthy has shifted from excitement to frustration, the 23-year-old speedster is still the Chiefs' best chance to create explosive plays from the wide receiver position .
Yes, he's had his struggles with the deep ball. No, he hasn't yet found a way to turn his record-breaking speed into consistent NFL production. Yes, he still has a skillset that doesn't exist elsewhere on the roster (or many places throughout the NFL).
Worthy has already consistently been the Chiefs' most-used wide receiver by snap count (now at 80% of the offensive reps through four games), and the Chiefs' coaching staff has the benefit of an extra week to review Worthy's strengths and weaknesses while retooling the receiver room. For better or for worse, Worthy is even more important to the Chiefs now than he was before the season began.
Cyrus Allen target on third down.. like the idea of using him on possible M2M reps. Go get the DE’s hands down on a quick pass tho. pic.twitter.com/3Jbg3cqvkC
Elsewhere, Kansas City has no choice but to bring at least one of their most recent wide receiver draft picks into the fold. Second-year fourth-round pick Jalen Royals has played 60 offensive snaps through four games, with 38 of those reps coming in Vegas. Royals didn't take an offensive snap in Week 1 and has just three catches on the season, but he has been the team's No. 4 receiver so far.
Rookie fifth-round pick Cyrus Allen was the recipient of a massive amount of training camp hype , but he's taken only 10 snaps so far in the regular season —fewer offensive reps than defensive tackle/occasional fullback Khyiris Tonga.
Even with Allen's preseason hype, it always made more sense for him to be a late-season climber after he becomes more familiar with the offense and as the coaches and quarterback develop more trust in him. Now, however, the once-long runway could be shortening. If the Chiefs truly believe in Allen's skillset, the Chiefs' thinning receiver room needs playmakers wherever they can be found.

title: Will the Chiefs' Offensive Line Stabilize After the Bye Week?
full_text:
In some instances, an early Week 5 bye could be an unwelcome arrival for an NFL team, particularly for an undefeated squad with the type of momentum that only comes with four consecutive wins. For the 4-0 Kansas City Chiefs, however, it might be exactly the right time for the sake of their uncertain offensive line.
While we use this bye week to evaluate a few key position groups for the current No. 1 seed in the AFC, you may not expect too much concern for the only unbeaten team in the conference.
Still, offensive line uncertainty has been one of the defining storylines of the Chiefs' strong start. How will the group come together after the bye week? That's the team's biggest issue to solve before they host the Los Angeles Chargers on October 18.
Starting left tackle Josh Simmons has missed the first four games of the season with a bulging disc, an injury the team only publicly defined on September 30 . Starting left guard Kingsley Suamataia was benched for the Chiefs' Week 4 showdown against the Las Vegas Raiders, reportedly due to a " coaching decision ."
Undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson has held up at left tackle in Simmons' absence, while veteran backup Mike Caliendo got the left guard reps in Las Vegas. Right tackle Jaylon Moore has had his ups and downs, leaving an interesting question for the Chiefs to answer— Benson or Moore at right tackle? —when Simmons returns.
Even All-Pro center Creed Humphrey has had some issues to begin the year, tossing some bad snaps and starting the year on pace to have career-low grades from Pro Football Focus .
To be fair, across an array of offensive line metrics , evaluation of the Chiefs' performance varies —a frequent phenomenon due to the variety of often-subjective ways O-lines are evaluated . Still, with such uncertainty at left tackle, it's seemed apparent that the unit has not yet fully gelled to be as solid as the sum of its parts.
Pass block grade of offensive linemen in true pass sets only Mahomes/Trevor good What happened to the Broncos' OL?? pic.twitter.com/DQCqy3lTpE
The Chiefs bolstered their depth on the O-line just before roster cutdowns, trading for veteran lineman Joshua Ezeudu from the New York Giants and undrafted rookie tackle Diego Pounds from the Baltimore Ravens.
Ezeudu has taken five offensive snaps for the Chiefs, while Pounds has been inactive through the Chiefs' first four games. Pounds remains an intriguing developmental tackle prospect, but his future on the field appears to be some time away. Ezeudu is on a one-year deal and provides short-term versatility at guard or tackle, though either Benson or Moore would clearly be the team's backup swing tackle when Simmons returns.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Assessing the Landscape at Bye Week
full_text:
Somehow, we're simultaneously about a month through the 2026 NFL season already but still have several months to go before we truly find out who some teams are. Don't get it twisted — multiple pretenders have already managed to stand out, but the cream of the crop won't be made obvious for quite some time.
Sitting at 4-0 on the year, the Kansas City Chiefs' hope is for them to be categorized as the latter once the postseason rolls around. That'll take continued impact from general manager Brett Veach's rookie and sophomore classes, which have presented both positive and negative value to this point.
At the bye week, let's break down the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each 53-man roster member in tiers. Be sure to return to this series each week to see who's moving and shaking.
Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott isn't included due to him currently being on the physically unable to perform list .
There's no derailing the Nohl Williams hype train, even after an afternoon and evening in which the second-year cornerback got flagged for a pair of costly penalties . He remains a promising young building block in the secondary, forming a two-man show with rookie Mansoor Delane that could terrorize opposing offenses for years to come.
Second-round pick R Mason Thomas has bounced back from some rough moments in the last couple of weeks, flashing rare bend and quickness as a pass rusher on the outside. According to Pro Football Focus , he set a new career high with five Week 4 pressures. Late first-rounder Peter Woods may have just turned in his worst performance to date, although the interior lineman was also reportedly banged up at some point in the contest.
The real X-factor here might be Day 3 running back Emmett Johnson. While he earned a respectable 16 offensive snaps on Sunday, he only got one touch. Perhaps if Kenneth Walker III's workload dwindles a bit coming out of the bye, the Nebraska product will get his time to shine .
With left tackle Josh Simmons still working his way through a back injury , the Kahlil Benson roller coaster keeps on running in Kansas City. His level of play has undoubtedly slipped, but he was surprisingly fine in Week 4 considering he had a fill-in next to him at left guard and, per TruMedia , the Chiefs trailed only the Houston Texans in throws relative to the sticks on average.
An ankle dislocation for wideout Tyquan Thornton might just earn sophomore Jalen Royals some more snaps, but only if an external acquisition isn't made and the coaching staff deems the former Utah State standout worthy of the reps. Another member of the 2025 NFL Draft class, defensive end Ashton Gillotte has received more than a 40% workload share in three consecutive weeks and had a season-high three quarterback hurries in his last performance.
Bryson Eason , as promised, finds himself getting bumped up after being activated for the second week in a row. He could just as easily come back down given the restrictions capping him at three practice squad elevations per season. For now, he's worth keeping an eye on.
The only people who truly know when Simmons is coming back seem to be Simmons himself and those within the building at 1 Arrowhead Drive. Heck, there may not even be a solidified plan. Kansas City certainly hasn't done itself many favors with how it's handled the injury situation to one of its more polarizing youngsters, but all it'd take is a post-bye return for just about everyone to probably sweep that under the rug.
Late-round draft selection Cyrus Allen was the flavor of the summer in Chiefs circles; the Thornton injury will bring that buzz back around for the fall. Elsewhere on offense, tight end Jake Briningstool is still an occasional sighting on the field. Running back Brashard Smith is a special-teamer through and through . Barring injury, cornerback Jadon Canady is stuck in the same boat.
This is where things get a little interesting. Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa isn't in the huddle much on defense, but could forcing a fumble on special teams be the launching pad he needs for an increased overall role? Undrafted free agent Xavier Nwankpa helped seal the deal against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 4 by picking off a pass on his only defensive snap. It doesn't get much more efficient than that.
Nothing much to see here, truthfully. Both tackle Diego Pounds and defensive end Jack Pyburn have made routine appearances on the game-day inactives list in recent weeks. Seventh-round quarterback Garrett Nussmeier always carries an outside shot to get on the field, although it'd take a catastrophic stretch of injuries to both Patrick Mahomes and Justin Fields for that to happen as the emergency third signal-caller.

title: Kenneth Walker Has Been Incredible, But Emmett Johnson's Time May Be Coming Soon
full_text:
Through the first four games of the 2026 NFL season, Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker has been one of the best players in all of football and is firmly on track to be in the Offensive Player of the Year conversation in his first campaign with the Chiefs.
The only downside of Walker's 2026 so far? He's taken a whopping 99 touches through four games, putting him on pace for 420 touches this season. During his four years with the Seattle Seahawks, Walker recorded 255, 248, 199 and 252 regular season touches, respectively. It's still a compliment to note that Walker has been too dominant to take off the field, but with a long-term view of the Chiefs' season, another back will need to spell Walker at some point.
During the Chiefs' bye week, we'll be taking a closer look at a few key position groups to see how they've stacked up to preseason expectations and where they could improve after the bye. However, for the Chiefs' running backs, "improvement" seems almost impossible.
Walker has been darn near perfect through four games, and his impact on the Chiefs' offense has been remarkably evident. From his ability to be the "easy button" for Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes to his home run-hitting ability out of the backfield , Walker has exceeded even the most optimistic offseason expectations. Now, can the Chiefs keep Walker fresh enough to stay that consistent late into the year?
Outside of Kansas City, rookie fifth-round pick Emmett Johnson may be flying under the radar. He has 16 carries for 56 yards and five catches for 74—not quite enough to be added in most fantasy football leagues. However, Johnson's highlights have been about as impressive as anyone's.
Emmett Johnson has some MOVES 😮‍💨 (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/yEWu90SL7G
Even while currently standing in Walker's shadow, I'm confident that Johnson would have been the best running back in KC's 2025 backfield, and probably by a large margin.
Emmett Johnson is 1 of 5 RBs with 10+ missed tackles forced (MTFs) The 4 other RBs have 40+ touches each. Emmett Johnson has 10 MTFs on just 14 touches. Absurd.
Through four games, Walker has taken 75% of the Chiefs' offensive snaps (196) while Johnson has taken 26% (69). That's the 13th-most offensive snaps on the team for Johnson, and his role should only grow from there.
As long as Johnson is trusted by the coaching staff—and if he wasn't, I don't think the team would have parted ways with Emari Demercado during roster cuts—his workload should increase during the Chiefs' midseason grind as the team tries to spare Walker from a few hits while trying to keep him in top form for a postseason run similar to what he did for the Seahawks en route to his Super Bowl MVP award in February.
Even without significant statistical output so far, Johnson is dynamic enough that Walker can leave the field without allowing opposing defenses to let their guard down on the running game.
The only potential "negative" for the Chiefs' running back room so far would come in the evaluation of second-year seventh-round pick Brashard Smith. (Even then, "negative" is probably too strong.) Smith has taken only six offensive snaps this season, catching one pass but taking zero carries.
The optimistic case for Smith is that he's firmly behind one superstar back and one extremely promising rookie. On the other hand, Smith saw the field sparingly last season, recording just 44 carries (with 26 coming in the team's two games against the Las Vegas Raiders) in 2025. Smith's speed is still a unique enough trait that he should be worth keeping an eye on as the season unfolds, but he's more of a special teamer and injury insurance until further notice.

title: Three Things Andy Reid and the Chiefs Need to Correct Going Into the Bye
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are one of two NFL teams on bye this week, giving Andy Reid's group some additional rest after its strong 4-0 start. KC could certainly use the break after its grueling rivalry win over the Raiders this past Sunday.
While the Chiefs don't have a blemish on their record yet, there's always room for improvement. Certain aspects on both sides of the ball could be cleaned up as the squad gears up for a 13-week stretch without another break. Let's take a look at three things Kansas City needs to improve upon during the bye.
The biggest storyline for the Chiefs offense this year has been Kenneth Walker III , who's been better than anyone could have imagined in his first year donning the red and gold. He leads the league in rushing yards early on and is a serious candidate for AFC Offensive Player of the Year.
However, another encouraging factor is how Patrick Mahomes looks in his return from ACL surgery. He looks every bit like the Hall of Fame signal-caller he was before his rocky 2025 campaign. Mahomes will really get put to the test over the next few weeks as Kansas City's wide receiving corps battles injuries. Breakout candidate Tyquan Thornton ended his career day versus the Raiders in heartbreaking fashion , dislocating his ankle and potentially missing the remainder of the regular season. Earlier in the contest, WR1 Rashee Rice also exited with a hamstring strain that could sideline him for some time.
Thornton was one of Kansas City's two downfield threats, which means Xavier Worthy will have to step up in his absence. The third-year wideout has been shaky thus far but recorded a season-high 71 yards last game, including a 41-yard catch that could have gone for a touchdown had Mahomes not slightly underthrown the ball.
⏰⏰ @XavierWorthy https://t.co/bBmZo8b23u
Regardless of whether Rice's hamstring is long-term, Kansas City's deep passing attack will face a major challenge without Thornton in the mix. Walker's emergence on the ground could help open things up downfield with Eric Bieniemy's increased usage of play action.
I want to preface this by saying the pass rush came alive in the second half against Vegas. The defensive front finally started to generate pressure after halftime, which ultimately contributed to Kansas City's late stops. With that being said, the defensive line needs to see tangible results sooner rather than later. The Chiefs have yet to log a sack since the opening victory over Denver, going more than 190 minutes without getting to the opposing quarterback.
Despite having the immobile Kirk Cousins wrapped up multiple times this past weekend, the pass rush still failed to capitalize on its opportunities. George Karlaftis was the star of the show as he finished with 11 quarterback pressures, tied for the most in a game all year, yet even his fourth-quarter sack was wiped away by a penalty.
Simply put, KC needs more from pass rushers like Chris Jones, Felix Anudike-Uzomah, and rookie R Mason Thomas. Finishing with a goose egg in the sack column every week isn't a sustainable formula for success.
As if the Chiefs needed any more drama along the offensive line this year with Josh Simmons' bulging disc in his back, another issue surfaced on the left side of the trenches before Sunday's victory. Kingsley Suamataia was unexpectedly benched at left guard for Mike Caliendo due to a "coaching decision" which Coach Reid refused to clarify in his postgame presser.
Andy Reid addressing the benching of Kingsley Suamataia.  “That is between Kingsley and I.”
Entering the bye, there are now two spots on Mahomes' blind side that are completely uncertain heading into Week 6. That's obviously not ideal for your superstar quarterback who underwent a grueling rehab process this offseason.
Mahomes took a lot of rough hits from the Raiders' front four, and Chiefs fans surely don't want to envision another scenario where something goes awry with his lower body. Things won't get any easier when Kansas City faces a dominant edge-rusher duo in Khalil Mack and Tuli Tuipulotu next weekend. There have to be corrections made in the film room during this extended rest period. And obviously, having one of Simmons and/or Suamataia back on the field wouldn't hurt.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: Would a Tyreek Hill Reunion Be Good or Bad for the 2026 Chiefs?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are undefeated heading into their early Week 5 bye, but the team has issues to solve on both sides of the ball, particularly after the loss of Tyquan Thornton .
How will the Chiefs manage the wide receiver position? That's where we'll begin in this week's Chiefs On SI mailbag , where we take your questions from @chiefs_kcsn on Twitter/X and @jbbrisco.com on Bluesky .
Would a Tyreek Hill reunion help or hurt this team? We all know how long it takes new WRs to learn the system. - @dandykstra.bsky.social
Unsurprisingly, most of this week's questions revolved around the possibility of a reunion between the Chiefs and wide receiver Tyreek Hill.
I say this as someone who was lukewarm on the idea of a Hill reunion this offseason: I don't see the downside at this point.
Even if Thornton returns late in the year , the Chiefs need more speed at receiver right now. Perhaps Rashee Rice is able to return from his hamstring injury after the bye, but Rice would be leading a receiver room with Xavier Worthy and a pair of unknowns. Second-year receiver Jalen Royals has played 60 offensive snaps through four games, while rookie Cyrus Allen has played 10. Special teamer Nikko Remigio hasn't taken an offensive snap yet this season.
The point about "new" wide receivers is another vote in Hill's favor. Sure, it's been years since he was last in Kansas City, but he'd return as a player familiar with Andy Reid's offense and Patrick Mahomes' passes. I think he would have a much shorter ramp-up period than most of the other receiver names being tossed around as potential trade targets.
Tyquan Thornton is the first WR Mahomes has had deep ball chemistry with since 2021. How big of an issue is it if Worthy suddenly has to be the deep ball guy again? I'm concerned Kenneth Walker will now get more and more attention week after week (plus wear/tear), and we could have a diminished ability to make teams pay for it. - @oscarbobo.bsky.social
The closing worry in this question does give me a bit of concern. Kenneth Walker's outrageous impact on the offense is multiplied by the way it should force defenses to respect Kansas City's run game, while the rejuvenated explosive passing game can keep defenses from devoting all of their attention to Walker. The explosive plays must continue for the Chiefs, and that's one reason I think the Hill reunion makes so much sense.
Worthy was always on track to have a large role in this offense, but I do think the Thornton injury is the official end of any possibility that Worthy will be phased into a significantly smaller role. However the Chiefs try to utilize him now, Worthy will need to have his best year yet for the Chiefs' offense to remain as explosive as it's been through the first four weeks.
What is most to blame for the lack of a pass rush? Drafting? Chris Jones (age/contract)? Young guys still learning? - @lmackshry5
I think there are a few good answers to this question, and none of them should be particularly alarming just yet.
This defense was always going to have its fair share of growing pains this season; Peter Woods and R Mason Thomas have played roughly half of the team's defensive snaps in the first four games of their young careers. Thomas has stood out in a hugely positive way with his explosion off the edge, but I do think it's fair to acknowledge that he will continue to grow as the season goes on.
Chris Jones has been a bit underwhelming to start the year, but he's been demanding plenty of attention from opposing offenses while remaining on the injury report with a calf ailment. I'm holding off on a significant judgment on Jones until later in the year—perhaps the bye week also arrives at a good time for him.
No sacks in three weeks is certainly not ideal, but I think the pass rush has been a bit better than their box score indicates. I still expect growth from the unit later in the season, but if it stagnates at this level, it would put even more pressure on the Chiefs' secondary down the stretch.
What are the biggest impediments to a perfect season as of this moment? - @hokius.fromthehawkseye.com
Football. Football itself is the biggest impediment. I haven't even seriously considered the possibility that the Chiefs (or 49ers or Vikings) will go undefeated this season. I don't think the Colts are particularly good, and the Chiefs squeaked by them in overtime in a primetime game at Arrowhead.
Kansas City will go to the Seahawks and Broncos in Weeks 7 and 8, then later go on the road for the Bills, Rams and Bengals before hosting the Patriots and 49ers in late November through December. The highest mark of regular season success the Chiefs should be shooting for is the No. 1 seed in the AFC. The sport is too inherently wild and parity-filled for me to imagine anyone going 17-0 anytime soon.
How many games does a Chiefs team made up of 53 Khyiris Tonga clones win? Is there a player on the Chiefs you could clone that would win more? - @SirHunkzAlot
This is an incredible question, and one that I've actually considered before. Khyiris Tonga is a fun nominee, but I think speed is too important in this exercise. Even at age 37, six or seven Travis Kelces could probably block long enough for quarterback-Kelce to find pass-catching-Kelce down the field. Kenneth Walker might be the best answer, but we've now seen rookie Emmett Johnson make plays on offense and on special teams; either of those running backs could create some havoc... but I'm not sure any of those iterations are winning any games against a proper 53-man squad.

title: Chiefs Stock Report: Three Players Rising and Falling After Week 4
full_text:
After four weeks of play, the Kansas City Chiefs' perfect record remains intact. At 4-0 on the year, this looks much more like the Chiefs teams of 2018-2024 than whatever the 2025 disaster of a group was.
It isn't just luck, either. While some things have certainly broken in favor of head coach Andy Reid's crew, there's been plenty of adversity along the way as well. Week 4's contest against the Las Vegas Raiders was a prime example of that, as Kansas City never had complete control of things until the final whistle but emerged with a triumph anyway .
In the process, several players stood out with their play for both positive and negative reasons.
Let's dive into the good and bad from Week 4's Chiefs victory against Las Vegas and single out three players whose stock is trending up, as well as three who could use a better showing after the bye.
The following players found a way to improve over their prior-week performances and are on the up and up heading into a new week.
Third-year wide receiver Xavier Worthy has found his name in this recurring story multiple times, but this is the first instance of him going upstream. The former first-round pick had by far his most impactful game of the season on Sunday, hauling in four passes on seven targets for 70 yards.
Worthy's highlight of the day came in two situations he hasn't made the most of this year: a vertical pass on a late down. Facing a third-and-10 in Las Vegas territory, quarterback Patrick Mahomes uncorked a deep ball to his talented wideout that he managed to come down with, setting up a score on the drive.
XAVIER WORTHY BLURRR pic.twitter.com/6pwiGI9eag
With Rashee Rice rehabbing a hamstring issue during the bye and Tyquan Thornton set to miss most or all of the regular season following an ugly ankle injury, it's Worthy receiver room for the time being. That isn't inherently a great thing for Kansas City, although it's undoubtedly nice if you're the team to see the 23-year-old capitalize on his chances.
In a similar bucket as Worthy, defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah may never live up to the billing that came with his draft slot. With that said, he can still carve out a productive role in the NFL, which is exactly what he's doing early in year No. 4 with the club.
The former Kansas State standout made numerous plays in the second half of Week 4, including a pair of third-down disruptions of Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins and a nice run stop. A nice surprise from this campaign is that Anudike-Uzomah is rotating inside a bit and rushing as more of a tackle than an end, which gives the opposition an off-speed pitch to deal with.
Pro Football Focus credits the 24-year-old with eight pressures on the year. If he can average a pair of impactful plays and have them be on late downs, that'd make him a reliable piece both now and into January when and if the Chiefs are still playing.
Speaking of PFF , the outlet gave fellow defensive end George Karlaftis a staggering 11 pressures for his Sunday performance. It's this writer's opinion that the number is inflated and closer to a half-dozen, but either way, there's no denying that "Furious George" lived up to his nickname against a bitter division rival.
Karlaftis got home to Cousins six times. Even if a player doesn't come away with a sack for the afternoon or evening, that's still an impressive number. Technically Karlaftis did have a sack, although it got nullified by a holding flag on cornerback L'Jarius Sneed. Elsewhere, he was a menace in run support and also combined with linebacker Drue Tranquill for a fourth-down disturbance that forced a field goal.
Sensing a theme? Production on third and fourth down cuts deeper than early-down splash plays, and Kansas City had plenty of the former in Week 4. Karlaftis played a huge role in that.
These players are far from doomed but would benefit from better days at the office in the second "half" of the season.
Admittedly, the Chiefs do deserve some slack for their lack of elite offensive line play. The front is doing a nice job paving the way for running back Kenneth Walker III, so it isn't like the entire operation is failing. Additionally, left tackle Josh Simmons still isn't in the lineup due to his back injury. To top it all off, left guard Kingsley Suamataia was unexpectedly benched for Week 4 .
Still, the line has seen better days than this past Sunday.
According to TruMedia , Las Vegas' 39.4% pressure rate ranked 12th leaguewide for the week of play. Not only that, but defensive coordinator Rob Leonard brought five rushers on just 12.1% of dropbacks, good for the fifth-lowest mark. The left-side line duo of Kahlil Benson and Mike Caliendo underwhelmed, and that's without even considering a botched snap by center Creed Humphrey (who's otherwise been amazing in 2026, to be fair).
Perhaps the returns of Simmons and Suamataia can lead to improvement.
I won't spend too much time here, because it's otherwise been a great season for second-year man Nohl Williams. In many regards, even Sunday considered, he's living up to the hype and delivering quality play as the boundary corner the Chiefs desperately needed after losing both Jaylen Watson (free agency) and Trent McDuffie (trade).
That said, Williams might need to dial back the physicality depending on who's in charge of the referee crew each week. He was flagged twice versus the Raiders once for unnecessary roughness on a hard hit and elsewhere for defensive holding on a third-and-8 that could've gotten Kansas City off the field.
The aggressiveness shouldn't be coached out of Williams in a larger sample; it's part of what makes him intriguing. It came back to bite him in Week 4, though.
The Chiefs didn't necessarily break the bank for safety Alohi Gilman this offseason, and it's a good thing they didn't — at least at the bye week. He has yet to prove to be a ball-hawking force or much of a plus player in the secondary. Heck, the return of Chamarri Conner for his first game back at safety in quite some time saw him make more positive plays.
Gilman jumped off the screen only a couple of times, and one of them was when wide receiver Tre Tucker essentially brought him along for the ride on a 14-yard completion. Gilman surrendered a trio of receptions in coverage to go with a 143.8 passer rating and didn't factor into run defense in a major way despite logging 17 snaps in the box.
He'll have to improve to totally justify the club's signing of him to replace Bryan Cook.

title: The Chiefs' Offense Has Done the Hard Part; Now It's Time to Learn From Last Year
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are undefeated and have the second-highest-scoring offense in the AFC after four weeks, but they still have plenty of work to do.
At first blush, Chiefs fans may balk at that sentiment. Kenneth Walker is setting early-season records while Patrick Mahomes looks to be playing his best football in recent years. What has the offense failed to do in the first quarter of the year?
Ask Mahomes. After Sunday's win over the Las Vegas Raiders, Mahomes was asked how he felt about the current state of the offense, and he provided an interesting angle on where the unit stands right now.
"We're close," Mahomes said. "We have the explosiveness part, and now it's about just stringing drives together, being able to do both. We've done it in spurts where we've had some long drives in certain points of games, but being more consistent about that, not having as many three-and-outs, I think that'd be important for us, but if we can continue to have the explosive plays, that covers up a lot, and now we've got to add that consistency to it as well."
Now, take Mahomes' analysis and think back to the 2024 and 2025 Chiefs offenses. Those teams, relying on Kareem Hunt and Isiah Pacheco on the ground and Travis Kelce and a cast of others through the air, operated on fine margins, lacking in explosiveness but executing at a high enough level in got-to-have-it moments to go 15-2 in '24 before the wheels fell off in '25.
These relatively simple stats only tell part of the story, but just to jog your memory: Mahomes' yards per attempt stats in 2023-25 brought the lowest Y/A numbers of his career as a starter (6.9, 6.8, 7.0). This year, he's averaging 8.1 yards per attempt through four games.
On the ground across those same three seasons, the Chiefs averaged rushing yards per attempt of 4.3, 4.0, and 4.2, and those numbers were buoyed by Mahomes' efficient scrambling, while his top two running backs failed to average more than 3.9 yards per carry in the last two seasons. So far, the 2026 Chiefs are averaging an absurd 5.5 yards per carry in 2026 thanks to Walker's outrageous 6.2 average.
To Mahomes' point on Sunday—and presumably, to his delight—the Chiefs' offense has created explosive plays through the running game in a way that puts last season's rushing attack to shame.
Rushing plays of 20+ yards: Chiefs in 2025: 3 in 17 games (last in NFL) Chiefs in 2026: 6 in four games (most in NFL)
Define "explosive plays" however you'd like—the Chiefs have been creating them, both on the ground and through the air.
The Chiefs have an NFL-best 4 plays of 50+ yards through four games. They had 2 all of last year.
The Chiefs have had no problem creating big plays this season after remaining in desperate need of more explosion throughout their doomed 2025 campaign. This year's Chiefs offense has figured out the hard part. They have the players who can keep them explosive (even though the loss of Tyquan Thornton will loom large ). Bringing consistency should, comparatively, be the easy part.
With Mahomes, Walker, Kelce and Rashee Rice, the Chiefs have the tools to remain steady on a down-to-down basis. The return of left tackle Josh Simmons and left guard Kingsley Suamataia would go a long way to stabilizing the offensive line, which should provide Mahomes an opportunity to take his layups while patiently waiting for his chance to hunt for the next big play. Similar logic would apply for Walker and the running game: better O-line play would help KC through their recent short-yardage struggles, while Walker's home run ability isn't going anywhere.
Head coach Andy Reid and offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy will also need to evaluate their role in this search for consistency, but they've engineered plenty of steady offensive units over the years with lesser talent and much less explosiveness. As long as the big plays remain a core part of the Chiefs' offensive identity, the next act of Kansas City's season could be even more exceptional.

title: Could Tyquan Thornton Return to the Chiefs This Season? It’s Complicated
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs experienced both ends of the spectrum regarding wide receiver Tyquan Thornton in Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders . The fifth-year man delivered a career-best performance, but he also sustained a serious injury in the process.
Thornton suffered a dislocated ankle late in Sunday's 30-27 triumph against Las Vegas, ending his night and leaving many to wonder whether his season was also over. Less than 24 hours after the contest, there's some more clarity on a potential return timeline.
Per Ian Rapoport of ESPN and NFL Network , the door is open for Thornton to perhaps come back in a matter of months.
"After extensive tests today, Tyquan Thornton is expected back within 12 to 16 weeks, sources say," Rapoport's tweet began. "He'll have surgery within the week and there is a real chance at a late-season or playoff return."
After extensive tests today, Tyquan Thornton is expected back within 12 to 16 weeks, sources say. He’ll have surgery within the week and there is a real chance at a late-season or playoff return. https://t.co/AgiJI94AzJ
Given the gruesome nature of Thornton's injury, it's hard to view this as anything but a good thing for both him and the Chiefs. Avoiding major breaks and, seemingly, the extreme end for ligament damage may have kept his current campaign alive.
Should the former New England Patriots second-round pick make rapid progress in his recovery and get back at the 12-week mark, he might be able to play in a regular-season game or two. If his absence extends to 16 weeks or a bit longer, he'd be flirting with a postseason return and be up to the mercy of Kansas City's path through the AFC playoffs.
With all of that said, Thornton has to first make numerous steps before getting back on the field. Having a successful surgery during the Chiefs' bye week is the first hurdle, then checking off the appropriate boxes in rehab follows suit. Who knows what he'll look like athletically coming off the injury or what the state of the KC wideout room will be in late December or early-to-mid January.
For a team that's also without Rashee Rice temporarily and has rumors swirling that a Tyreek Hill reunion might be in the cards, it's nice to have some hope that Thornton could rejoin his teammates in due time. He's already up to 11 receptions for 219 yards and a pair of touchdowns in the first year of a two-season contract he signed during the offseason.
Fast-forwarding quite a while, the Chiefs round off the regular season with a Week 16 outing against the San Francisco 49ers before going to Los Angeles to tango with the Chargers. Week 18 sees them close out the regular season versus the very Raiders team they just played.
With the team at 4-0, many folks in Kansas City circles are already banking on a postseason run occurring. Maybe Thornton can be a part of that plan on the field if things go right.

title: Justin Herbert is in Trouble: Non-Chargers Fans Wouldn’t Be Able to Name 1 Starting OL
full_text:
Pray for Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert. Cross the fingers. Whatever. Just send the guy some good luck and vibes.
The Chargers enter Week 5 with an injury report 18 players long . One of those is starting star offensive tackle Joe Alt, who is out at least one week with a new injury. The other starting tackle? Rashawn Slater was spotted on crutches after a loss one week ago.
Just fire up the trade candidates talk already, really.
So, for those keeping count, the Chargers are about to roll out an offensive line that could include four rookies in Week 5 against the Denver Broncos.
Good luck even figuring out who goes where on the Chargers offensive line at this point.
On paper, it could look something like this:
There are other slight adjustments the Chargers can make to this in the name of “versatility” or whatever, but the point stands: Things are bleak.
Two things that won’t change? Jake Slaughter and Cole Strange. Slaughter is the center they drafted to play guard who trained there before going back to center after Tyler Biadasz got hurt. Odds are they won’t change that now.
Then there’s Strange, who has been a colossal bust of a signing and currently ranks 70th out of 74 guards at PFF.
Another thing that won’t change? Jim Harbaugh’s apparent confidence in his rookie linemen, as captured by Kris Rhim of ESPN: "I saw a confident demeanor, one that was ready to accept the challenge. Brought some memories back, being a player, what that felt like when I was put in that position and the feeling of stepping up to the challenge."
And look, maybe the Chargers will find out they have something with draft picks like Burke, Taylor and Harkey. That would be ideal. But the immediate outlook is a disaster and, frankly, the Chargers have managed to fail more than ever before in protecting and supporting Herbert.
Overall, Sunday feels like a massive red flag for Herbert and the Chargers, with health a concern as much as 0-5 at this point.

title: Chargers Week 5 Mailbag: Hypothetical Path Forward, Seats Getting Warm, Future Focus
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-4 and their roster has been brutalized by injuries. The Chargers personnel have been hot and cold with their performances and how they are grading out on gameday. They host the Denver Broncos at home in week five as they look for their first win and look to find any hope moving forward.
Fans and the media have clearly started the process of looking forward for the Chargers with the odds stacked against them for the remainder of the 2026. Trade scenarios are already being floated for Chargers star players and seats may be getting warm on the Chargers' sideline. This week's mailbag focuses on some of those forward looking hypothetical scenarios.
From JH^3 (@777onlinegamer on X): Two part question looking to the future. 1) Assuming the Chargers miss the playoffs and Jim Harbaugh is back but current struggles continue, what's the best path forward?
If the Chargers season continues on its downward spiral there will be massive questions to answer. The manner in which the season continues and wraps up will be the biggest factor in how the organization moves forward. The Chargers special teams unit is currently dead last in the NFL in terms of EPA per play and a change at special teams coordinator would be an easy and expected scapegoat-style change.
Chris O'Leary's defense has largely been the only reason the Chargers have been relatively competitive in the past two weeks and seem to be trending in the right direction. The offense is the question mark. The Chargers made a sizeable investment in Mike McDaniel but something is obviously off.
If the struggles lead to the Chargers and Mike McDaniel going their separate ways, the first call should be to former Chargers offensive line coach and run game coordinator Frank Smith. Smith served as Mike McDaniel's non-play-calling offensive coordinator in Miami the past three seasons and is currently the assistant head coach for the 4-0 Minnesota Vikings.
Smith would make sense because the offense would not necessarily have to change but someone familiar to the Chargers, Justin Herbert and who is getting a top of the line look at running a team side-by-side with Kevin O'Connell could be the perfect blend the Chargers offense would need without tearing it down to the studs. The largest contracts and investments that the Chargers have in the offense would be hard to move on from until after the 2027 season, so a teardown after 2026 seems unlikely.
I also believe, the with the current struggles of the roster, Joe Hortiz's seat could get very warm by season's end. The Chargers ownership usually gives a long runway to general managers but the offensive line woes that has plagued this team during the entirety of his tenure may be unforgiveable.
If the Chargers choose to move in a different direction, it has to be someone with an analytics background and a proactive philosophy to contract negotiations. The 49ers and Eagles are the teams that immediately come to mind. For continuity, 49ers assistant general manager Brian Hampton is the name I would have at the top of my list. He comes with a background in analytics, something that the current front office has seemingly gutted and actually worked with Jim Harbaugh during his time in San Francisco focusing on salary cap and contract negotiations.
Second part of the question from JH^3 2) Who do we target in the draft and free agency in 2027?
This is a broad and early topic but I will give two areas of focus. The Chargers have to look to upgrade their offensive line, they simply can't afford to narrow their focus to find scheme fits who could work if the world aligns perfectly in order to get value from the interior of their offensive line. Perennial all-pro guard Quenton Nelson is an unrestricted free agent next offseason and the Chargers should back up the Brinks truck even if the contract does not yield surplus value, they have to do something to change the interior.
The draft has a handful of promising interior guard prospects that could be available on the second day of the draft or they could target former teammate of Justin Herbert, Cowboys guard TJ Bass and let him battle it out with whoever is left standing from Branson Taylor and Jake Slaughter.
The Chargers need a difference-making wide receiver. Luckily, the 2027 draft class has at least five outside downfield threats that could be projected to go in the first round, possibly more. Depending on where the Chargers end up picking a wide receiver or potentially a cornerback would make a ton of sense in the first round based on needs and how the draft class is shaping up.
From Chargers Lead (@ChargersLead on X): Which of the three (Hortiz, Harbaugh, McDaniel) is most to blame? What do you think the likelihood of seeing an in-season firing is?
This may be a cliche answer but in terms of the Chargers struggles, the general manager, head coach and offensive coordinator all share in the blame significantly. Mike McDaniel has been a successful play caller and play designer but something went dramatically wrong in the initial install and implementation of the offense.
Jim Harbaugh instituted a new and lighter offseason training program designed to get the team to the season healthy. This lighter training camp may have set the offense back weeks and they coaching staff may have missed the opportunity to identify true weaknesses until it was too late.
Joe Hortiz uses the Baltimore Ravens philosophical approach to guards and focuses on gaining surplus value on interior offensive line contracts. Unfortunately this approach and drafting only one option, Branson Taylor, to potentially develop in the sixth round of the 2025 draft left the cupboard bare in terms of in-house options to fill roles. This approach has yielded disastrous results.
Justin Herbert is yet again one of the most pressured and hit quarterbacks in the NFL. Now, the Chargers are staring at a reality in which they will be starting three or four rookies against the Denver Broncos in week five.
In terms of an in-season coaching change, if the Chargers still do not have a win by the trade deadline, it has to be an unfortunate reality. But, it is worth noting, Chargers ownership does not want to make mid-season moves, it took the team flat out giving up on national television against the Raiders on Thursday Night Football for a change to be made in-season.

title: A Realistic Scenario and Path for the Los Angeles Chargers to Save Their Season
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have started their season 0-4 and have looked lost on offense as they try to find their identity. New offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel has been grappling with the team's struggles with the many moving parts of his offense. The 1992 Chargers started 0-4 and made the playoffs that season, the 2026 Chargers will look to follow the same path.
Los Angeles entered the season with Super Bowl aspirations and playoff expectations, to say the season has been a shocking disappointment thus far is a deep understatement. The Chargers defense has been performing well and showing up on game day, specifically in the past two weeks. The offense finally showed signs of life and fight in the second half of their week four loss to the Seattle Seahawks.
The Chargers enter week five at a crossroads. They could have easily folded against the Seahawks when Sam Darnold and Seattle's offense marched down the field to open the second half and go up 27-6. Instead, Justin Herbert and the Chargers, aided by penalties from Seattle, fought and clawed their way back into the game. The run game started landing heavy punches and Herbert seemed to lean on scrambling to make plays.
Chargers fans have seen what happens when the team is out of breath and gives up. It led to the dismissal of the previous coaching staff and general manager following a loss on Thursday night football to the Las Vegas Raiders. LA welcomes the Denver Broncos to SoFi Stadium in week five and with their massive list of injuries they will have a choice to make, come out swinging with everything they have like their season depends on it, or fold.
If Justin Herbert and the makeshift offensive line manage to take down the Denver Broncos and show they are not ready to lie down and die just yet, there is a realistic path forward for them to save their season and even potentially make the playoffs. Obviously, time is not on their side but lets take a look at the landscape across the AFC.
The Chargers find themselves in a tough spot but entering week five, there are five teams remaining in the NFL that are winless, four of them are in the AFC. The Chargers have three of the winless teams on their upcoming schedule and additionally will face the New York Jets who have only one win on the season.
Los Angeles has lost to three good teams so far to start this season but what once looked like a schedule of doom, has now become more manageable if they can figure out their offense. The Chargers face the Broncos in week five and the Chiefs in week six before their bye in week seven. The bye couldn't come at a better time given their injuries but it is also an opportunity to regroup before the final stretch of ten games.
In the Chargers final ten games they will face the currently winless Texans, Buccaneers and Dolphins. The Jets and Patriots are both struggling with their own issues as well as being AFC opponents. If Los Angeles can get their first win of the 2026 season against Denver, who are struggling on offense themselves, it could be the beginning of a turnaround for Los Angeles.
The Broncos are taking a more collaborative play-calling approach this week with HC Sean Payton having an increased role in the process and OC Davis Webb continuing with a significant game-planning and game-day role, per sources. Denver is looking to spark its offense ahead of… pic.twitter.com/6y2jHZTaYn
The Week 5 battle will truly be a battle of who can manage their injuries the best. The Broncos will be without wide receiver Pat Bryant as well as top cornerback Pat Surtain II and most likely number two cornerback Riley Moss will be out as well.
We asked @AdamSchefter for an injury update on Pat Surtain, Riley Moss, and Pat Bryant. "I don't expect any of them to play this week. My guess is we'll see certainly Surtain [on IR], quite possibly Bryant, and I would guess not Riley Moss." #BroncosCountry pic.twitter.com/qCgkJuS4oS
Assuming the Chargers can snag their first win against the Broncos in week five and in theory take care of four out five of the perceived winnable games down the road, they would be searching for five more wins on the season.
The Chargers face the Chiefs two times as well as the Broncos and Raiders down the road. They will also face off against the Rams, Ravens and 49ers. Of those eight matchups, can Los Angeles sneak five wins to get to 10-7 on the season? It is possible if they manage to get back on track.
