title: Chargers Week 5 Injury Report: Latest Updates, Practice Status and Replacement Options
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers limped back to LA after dropping their fourth straight to the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field in Week 4. The Chargers were already banged up heading into the game against Seattle but it got significantly worse by the end of the game.
The Chargers are the subject of several sports jokes and sayings. The term "Chargering" is now common knowledge among NFL media as a term used to describe the Chargers magical ability to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory. Now it seems that the Chargers curse is becoming more widely known and accepted.
The Chargers curse refers more to the high volume of injuries at key positions the Chargers seem to face on a consistent basis. The 2025 season became a train wreck on the offensive line when the Chargers lost both of their top tackles for the season and had a revolving door at the positions the entire season.
This offseason, newly signed center Tyler Biadasz suffered a season-ending knee injury during training camp. Entering Week 4, the Chargers were already down to their fifth option at left guard and ended up losing both tackles Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt on top of left guard Trevor Penning to injury. The final offensive line that finished out the game consisted of four rookies and the original starting right guard Cole Strange. Curse or no curse, the results are devastating.
The Chargers may be getting some reinforcements this week before they face off against the Broncos. The team opened the practice window for offensive lineman Branson Taylor and fullback/tight end Scott Matlock, both of whom started the season on injured reserve. If Taylor is healthy, he should be rushed to the starting lineup with guard Kayode Awosika still not practicing, guard Trevor Penning in concussion protocol and both Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt already ruled out.
wednesday's injury report for week 5 vs DEN pic.twitter.com/1xgJcHuFUy
One of the more positive developments is that tight end Charlie Kolar returned to practice in a limited fashion after undergoing forearm surgery after an injury suffered in Week 2. If Kolar is able to play, his blocking will greatly help the gameplan for a pair of inexperienced tackles, presumably Branson Taylor and rookie Travis Burke.
The Chargers skill position groups on both sides of the ball will be tested this week with three out of four of the top wide receivers and cornerbacks carrying an injury designation to start the week. With an inexperienced offensive line and receiving options banged up, establishing the run will be critical for the Chargers if they are going to have a chance Sunday.
Due to the significant injuries, the Chargers may use multiple practice squad elevations to fill out the game day roster. It will be worth noting who is able to log full practices as the week continues.

title: Ranking Chargers Trade Candidates If LA Starts Fire Sale
full_text:
The NFL is a league where the roster churning never stops, even during the season when teams are taking form and showing off the efforts of the offseason. While this has a positive connotation, the Chargers' 2026 season is indicative of the Bolts' 2026 offseason, an offseason filled with half measures and unrighted confidence.
With this, the Chargers are 0-4 and seemingly ready to move on from valuable assets in hopes of creating a brighter future for a team that was seemingly ready to make a run in 2026. Who are some of the players the Chargers can move on from and get trade value?
Khalil Mack is the most obvious player on the Chargers who should be traded to another team before the 2026 NFL trade deadline. A team that is in a position to compete and possibly make a run to the Super Bowl. Mack has been in the league since 2014 and has never won a playoff game.
He is by all means an NFL legend, and he deserves--in what is likely his last season in the NFL--to have a chance to make it far in the postseason. He is still playing at a high level, even at age 35. It would be hard to see Mack wearing another uniform in 2026 , but for the Chargers, it makes no sense to keep him around during a failed season. Get your trade value and do right by one of your all-time great defenders.
Current Contract Left: 1-year, $18 million
Estimated Trade Value: 2027 Third Round Selection + 2028 Sixth Round Selection
Denzel Perryman , like Mack, is one of the Chargers' great leaders and long-time defenders. He is not expected to play much longer in the NFL as he is a 34-year-old thumping linebacker who is already not known for his premier sideline-to-sideline abilities.
Perryman can bring a much-needed thumping presence and leadership to a defense that is in need of such a skill set. Even with Perryman being the Chargers'  "oldest" draft pick, it makes no sense to keep him around one last year, especially with other LBs on the roster, like Marlowe Wax, who can take on the role.
Current Contract Left: 1-year, $2.3 million
Estimated Trade Value: 2027 Seventh Round Pick / Late Round Pick Swap
Trey Pipkins III is currently on injured reserve and will be needed as soon as he returns from injury, considering the Chargers are expected to play their Week 5 game against a strong Denver Broncos defense with an offensive line that can consist of 3 rookies, a second-year Day 3 offensive tackle and one of the worst guards in the NFL.
Even with the need for Pipkins III, he brings obvious trade value to any team that needs offensive linemen. He has guard/tackle versatility while being a strong leader with a little bit of playoff experience.
Current Contract Left: 2-years, $10.15 million
Estimated Trade Value: 2027 Fifth Round Pick
Derwin James Jr. is the heart and soul of the Chargers' defense. He has been this since his arrival in 2018 as the Bolts' first-round pick. James Jr. has been a constant hellraiser for opposing offenses, striking fear into QBs and receivers alike.
That said, he is now 30 years old and is likely looking for a team that can actually make a playoff run and sees a real Super Bowl future. Trading James Jr. seems very unlikely given his brand-new contract extension, but weirder things have happened in the NFL.
Current Contract Left: 4-years, $100.2 million
Estimated Trade Value: 2027 Second Round Selection + 2028 Fifth Round Selection
Quentin Johnston is the player that seemingly every Chargers fan wants to trade away to another team, given his expectation as a first-round pick never really panning out, coupled with the constant drop issues and lack of explosive games.
Johnston has been very quiet in the 2026 NFL season, doing so after signing his fifth-year option, giving him one more season after 2026 with the team. Even with that, a team that wants to take a chance on a 6'4 athletic receiver can call the Chargers and make an offer to send him to whichever team is interested. This trade would allow the Bolts to play some of their younger receivers while giving the headache of Johnston to another franchise.
Current Contract Left: 2-years, 22.51 million
Estimated Trade Value: 2027 Fifth Round Selection

title: Chargers Have Little to Lose...What's Worst That Can Happen With Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade?
full_text:
Well folks, there comes a point where a team has to decide whether protecting its future is more important than taking a chance on changing its present. For the Los Angeles Chargers, that question could become very real if Marvin Harrison Jr. is genuinely available.
Bleacher Report NFL analyst Alex Kay believes acquiring the former fourth overall pick would be a move worth considering.
Harrison entered the league with enormous expectations. Coming out of Ohio State, he was viewed as one of the safest and most talented wide receiver prospects in years. His time in Arizona has been underwhelming compared to what many expected when he was drafted. That alone could make some teams hesitant to give up meaningful assets for him. However, it also creates the possibility of getting a talented player before his value completely recovers.
For the Chargers, that could be exactly what makes the situation worth exploring.
A disappointing start does not automatically mean a player is destined to remain disappointing obviously. Young receivers can take time to adjust to the NFL, especially when they are placed into a different situation, different scenery, and different schemes.
Harrison would also be walking into a completely different environment if he were moved to an offense built around Justin Herbert.
Instead of defenses being able to focus heavily on the existing weapons, adding someone with Harrison’s size, athletic ability and reputation could force opposing defenses to make difficult decisions.
That does not mean a trade would automatically work. There is a very real possibility that Harrison simply does not become the superstar many expected. Which happens all the time in sports. Giving up significant draft capital for a player who fails to develop would hurt, particularly for a team that still needs to build depth across its roster.
But that is where the situation becomes interesting. The Bolts desperately need a deep threat receiver, as well as a guy who makes plays when nobody else can.
If the asking price is reasonable, the potential reward becomes much harder to ignore.
This is not a case of trading away multiple premium picks for an established superstar. It would be betting on a young player who has already shown enough talent to become one of the league’s best receivers if everything comes together.
There is no guarantee that a change of scenery fixes everything. But there is also no guarantee that sitting back and refusing to take a chance leads to anything better. At some point, teams have to recognize when an opportunity is worth the risk. If Harrison becomes available for a reasonable price, this could be one of those opportunities.

title: One Glaring Statistic Shows How Quickly Chargers Have Digressed
full_text:
It’s been a horrendous four weeks the AFC team that shares SoFi Stadium with the Los Angeles Rams? It’s been a forgettable start to 2026 for the Los Angeles Chargers , who have lost their first four games for the first time since 2017. The head coach that season was Anthony Lynn, who helped the club bounce back with nine victories in their final 12 games to finish 9-7.
Is the latter in the cards for these Bolts? Judging by the team’s performance to date, it seems very remote that this franchise is gearing up for a strong 13-game finish, much less repeat its historic feat of 1992. Of course, never say never is really a big part of the today’s National Football League—which now has every team playing 17 regular-season games.
So how have things gone south so fast? Let’s take a trip back to 2024 and one-time San Francisco 49ers' head coach Jim Harbaugh’s return to the NFL. The Chargers won their first two games and eventually finished 11-6. Quarterback Justin Herbert took a back seat to a physical running game. The young signal-caller connected on 65.9 percent of his passes for 3,870 yards, 23 TD passes and just three interceptions.
Harbaugh’s club turned over the ball a mere nine times—the third-fewest by a team in a single season in NFL history. Then came the playoff disaster at Houston in which Herbert was picked off four times—one of those thefts returned for a score.
This is what it looks like every time Justin Herbert drops back to pass. Congrats to Mike Vrabel and the Patriots. They’re going to be good for a long time to come. pic.twitter.com/pksFNJKeKP
This past season, the Bolts once again finished 11-6 and reached the playoffs. But this was a battered club missing its starting tackles for either part (Joe Alt) or the entire (Rashawn Slater) season.
The offense was understandably stagnant, Herbert was sacked 54 times in 16 regular-season contest, and six more times in the playoff loss at New England. The turnover number jumped from nine to 21, and Herbert also lost a fumble against the Patriots.
*If the #Seahawks don’t intercept this Justin Herbert ball it’s a touchdown #hypothetical pic.twitter.com/QsDpr113ei
And that brings us to 2026. After four weeks, the Chargers have scored 67 points, scored seven touchdowns, and turned over the football 10 times—one more time than in all of the 2024 regular season, and tied for the most in the league.
THE SEAHAWKS DEFENSE FORCES THE GAME-WINNING FUMBLE 😤 Former Charger Uchenna Nwosu gets to Justin Herbert and gets the strip sack 💪 Seattle moves to 3-1 while Los Angeles falls to 0-4. pic.twitter.com/8T8dj0Ilel
It was supposed to be different this season with a new offensive coordinator in Mike McDaniel , a bolstered front line, and a defense that was a Top 5 unit in 2025. And four weeks into the season, these Chargers are the only team in the division with a losing record, and four games behind the Kansas City Chiefs in the AFC West.

title: Jim Harbaugh's Hot Seat Status With Chargers Could Go Nuclear Soon
full_text:
When the Los Angeles Chargers dropped a game to the Buffalo Bills in ugly fashion, we wrote that Jim Harbaugh’s tenure with the franchise probably expired .
Harbaugh and the Chargers then turned around and lost ugly in Seattle to hit 0-4, showing that it was just a matter of time for the hot seat to really fire up and get to that point.
Tack on Harbaugh’s ugly spat with a Chargers reporter this week, and things certainly seem headed that way.
These things take time, clearly. But the implosion appears to be happening slowly right in front of the public.
As such, hot seat analysis from all corners has really started to sour on Harbaugh’s time with the Chargers.
The case for Harbaugh is simple: He’s had plenty of success already and he can point to injuries as a major problem point that derailed this year.
That’s the crux of many arguments for Harbaugh at this point. There’s clearly something wrong with how the Chargers’ front office even goes about adding talent.
Christian D'Andrea of For The Win wrote that the real unforgivable thing is the complete collapse of Justin Herbert.
“Harbaugh may be able to buy some grace by sacrificing McDaniel and pointing to the injuries that have kept his offense in neutral,” D'Andrea wrote. “What he may not be able to survive, however, is Herbert's sudden descent to a bottom-five starting quarterback.”
Sports Illustrated’s Conor Orr added, though, that an older version of Harbaugh might force the Chargers’ hand: “The Chargers will not fire a coach who won 11 games in each of his past two seasons unless vintage, owner-clashing 49ers-era Jim Harbaugh rears his head over the coming months. Given that there is no college head coaching job to escape to, my guess is that the operation will least appear more buttoned-up the closer we get to November and December.”
It’s all fair and doubly concerning: The crux of Harbaugh support right now seems to be that injuries derailed things and he’s, if nothing else, still being a nice guy.
Problem is, at least to some degree, the Chargers front office is just following his vision for the club. And Harbaugh himself has openly admitted that his staff took the wrong approach to the summer work, which might explain why his team looks so unprepared.
It’s safe to suggest that the Chargers would fire Harbaugh long before they move on from Herbert. But it’s a brutal spot to sit, as one of the biggest problems of the Herbert era is the never-ending coaching carousel. Ripping up the program isn’t ideal, either.
But again, if the Chargers keep looking like the worst team in the NFL and the locker room isn’t responding, starting over is pretty much unavoidable.

title: Chargers Owe It To Khalil Mack to Make Trade Calls With Teams Like 49ers, Bills
full_text:
If the Los Angeles Chargers want to do it, a Khalil Mack trade will interest plenty of teams .
Granted,  both the Chargers and Mack would need to want a trade to happen. But at 0-4 with questions around Jim Harbaugh’s tenure starting to become louder, it’s also worth considering if the Chargers won’t start up a fire sale, too.
After all, if this season is lost, why retain an asset like Mack who might not be around next year and part of a possible rebuild, anyway?
And, on a very basic human level, why not do right by Mack and ship him somewhere that gives him a chance to win a title to close what could be his final year as a pro?
Mack contemplated retirement before signing a one-year deal worth $18 million with the Chargers to come back for 2026.
Things haven’t worked out as either party planned. And maybe Mack doesn’t want to be on the move again at the age of 35 now that he’s been with the Chargers since 2022.
But the grass just might be greener. And he certainly has something to offer teams in the hunt. He’s got three sacks and eight quarterback pressures over the four games already. There’s a reason Mack is the very top trade block option in the mind of someone like Bleacher Report’s Kristopher Knox going into Week 5.
In the AFC, the Chargers could call up, say, the Buffalo Bills. That’s a contender at 3-1 and first place in the AFC East surely more than happy to keep stacking advantages. Mack has quite a bit more to offer the Bills than say, Joey Bosa gave them last year.
If the Chargers don’t want to help an AFC team, they could always look to the NFC and call up a team like the San Francisco 49ers.
Funnily enough, those 49ers have a Bosa and injury woes, too. But they’re also 4-0 and trying to stay ahead in a brutal NFC West. For Mack, sticking on the West Coast might just have some appeal, too.
Minimal cap savings aside, a Mack trade wouldn’t just be doing right by him, either. It would also let the Chargers think about the future while getting Tuli Tuipulotu and first-round pick Akheem Mesidor as many reps as possible.
And at this point, Chargers fans would no doubt understand the move and pretty much agree with it, too.

title: Biggest Decision Mike McDaniel Got Wrong Against Seahawks and it Needs to Stop
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-4 and to say their 2026 season is barely on life support would be an understatement. For any chance to make the postseason, the Chargers need to go at minimum 10-3 over the next thirteen games. The team's struggles have been a major source of confusion, specifically for a Jim Harbaugh-led football team.
Procedural penalties, ball security and special teams gaffes have haunted the Chargers at every turn. But, the biggest and most shocking aspect of LA's struggles is that of the offense. The gameplan against the Seahawks did not lean into bread and butter simple offense, it maintained a level of complexity that has yielded rough results.
This past offseason, the NFL world was on the Chargers hype train. The pairing of franchise quarterback Justin Herbert and offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel was viewed as a dream scenario. Upon McDaniel's arrival in Los Angeles, McDaniel and Herbert began tweaking some of his footwork and mechanics to emphasize the quick game. The idea at the time was to be able to get the ball out quickly to reduce the pass rush on Hebert in the same way Tom Brady had limited the Chargers pass rush with Joey Bosa and Melvin Ingram over the years.
The idea to change up Herbert sounded like a good idea at the time and most of the NFL world bought in. The results have been awful and the exact opposite of massive expectations. Herbert may look uncomfortable in the offense and appears to be thinking too much, but the rest of the offense looks to be on similar shaky ground.
The Chargers, through four games, have been penalized a league high 14 times for false starts. The entire offense is struggling with the snap count in the midst of all the other complexities of the offense.
The biggest example of this came when wide receiver Tre' Harris was flagged for a false start because he did not know he was supposed to go in motion. Herbert signaled for the motion and Harris looked at him confused and eventually he started a motion but the ball was snapped resulting in the false start.
Procedural errors cost the Chargers offense yards but most importantly they cost rhythm. The Chargers have been struggling to move the ball with any consistency and seem to shoot themselves in the foot far too often.
Mike McDaniel continues to call incredibly complex designer plays and they rarely appear to work.  The design in itself could work, but the offense is struggling with basic protections and the snap count, expecting them to be able to block up a play with so many moving parts is an unrealistic demand at this point in time.
The design of this jet sweep is just too much. Seattle gets five guys behind the LOS. LB Drake Thomas flies right by Keaton Mitchell untouched. QJ ends up stiff arming him into the earth but the damage is done and he had no where to go. pic.twitter.com/vkEL4F8zf1
McDaniel has been at the helm of elite offenses before but the Chargers are struggling to grasp the complexity of his offense. The mistake of the game and gameplan was just much complexity. A Philly special at the goal line down multiple scores should not be in the arsenal. McDaniel boasted about being able to adjust to players and highlight their strengths, but can he adjust his play calling for the unit to thrive.
Have yet to see any adaptations from him https://t.co/dbOThe44xT
The Chargers may have to start three or four rookies on the offensive line against the Denver Broncos this Sunday. There should be zero expectation that that unit will be able handle the Broncos defensive front and significantly complex protections and trick plays.

title: Rams Injury Report: Aaron Donald Among Three Key Starters Who Could Return vs. Bills
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams will hope to get multiple starters back in Week 5 as they get set to take on the Buffalo Bills. After missing Aaron Donald, Colby Parkinson, and Jaylen Watson against the Philadelphia Eagles last week, the Rams are hopeful that all three will be back for Monday night’s game.
"The expectation is that as long as they progress accordingly then they'll be ready to go," said head coach Sean McVay. "I want to see how Jaylen feels. We'll get a little shoulder harness out there, [see] how he's going to be able to block destruct. Colby is really progressing in a very positive direction. We'll be smart with the kind of reps that he takes. Then like I mentioned to you guys with Aaron, [we'll] see how his back responds. Everything is trended in the right direction.”
On the initial injury report, Donald, Parkinson, and Watson were all listed as limited participants on Monday. Donald was a surprise addition to the injury report last week after head coach Sean McVay said that he had a sore back after the game. The Rams erred on the side of caution by resting Donald last week, and the team was able to get a win without him. All indications are that Donald could play on Monday night .
Additionally, the Rams will hope to get Parkinson back after he was inactive last week with an AC sprain in his shoulder. The Rams will certainly welcome Parkinson back as they look to get back to 13 personnel this week. Without Parkinson, the Rams utilized 11 personnel at their highest rate since Week 5 of last season.
Jaylen Watson also missed last week after dislocating his shoulder in the loss to the Broncos. Getting Watson back before facing a good Bills offense would be a huge boost for the defense. The Rams will look to ramp up Donald, Parkinson, and Watson as the week progresses.
Also on the injury report were linebacker Grant Stuard (hamstring), edge rusher Josaiah Stewart (groin), safety Quentin Lake (hip), linebacker Nate Landman (shoulder), and wide receiver Davante Adams (rest). None of them participated in practice on Thursday.
According to The Athletic’s Nate Atkins, Lake’s injury is minor, and he was heavily iced after Sunday’s game. Landman has been on the injury report the last three weeks and has played. Stewart showed up on the injury report toward the end of last week and managed to play on Sunday. Still, he’ll be one to monitor.
"He's so tough. He pushed through it," said McVay. "He got it when he fell backwards on something so it's a weird deal, but he's doing good. We're just being smart with him."
Not practicing today will be DB Quentin Lake (hip), LB Grant Stuard (hamstring), OLB Josaiah Stewart (groin), ILB Nate Landman (shoulder) and WR Davante Adams (veteran rest day). Lake's injury is minor, Sean McVay said. Lake had it pretty iced up after the game on Sunday.
McVay mentioned that wide receiver Konata Mumpfield had a rotator cuff contusion during his Monday press conference. Mumpfield was a full participant on Thursday.
On the Bills’ side, the Rams will be monitoring the availability of wide receiver DJ Moore, defensive lineman Ed Oliver, and cornerback Dee Alford. All three did not practice on Thursday. Additionally, defensive lineman Landon Jackson and cornerback Christian Benford were limited.
The Rams will certainly hope to be as close to full strength as possible heading into Monday night’s matchup against the Bills. While they managed to overcome several key absences against the Eagles, doing so against the Bills will present a more difficult challenge. With Donald, Parkinson, and Watson trending in the right direction, the Rams could be getting some much-needed reinforcements at an important point in their season.

title: How to Watch Rams vs. Bills in Week 5 (Start Time, TV Channel, What to Watch For)
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams are set to take on the Buffalo Bills in Week 5 on Monday Night Football at SoFi Stadium. After beating the Philadelphia Eagles last week, the Rams are 2-2 and back at .500. Meanwhile, the Bills lost their first game in their new stadium, falling 29-26 to the New England Patriots.
Prior to losing to the Patriots , the Bills looked like an unstoppable force. They beat the Los Angeles Chargers the week before despite turning the ball over five times. Heading into Week 5, the Bills rank fourth overall in total DVOA.
The Rams were staring a 1-3 record in the face before overcoming a 10-point deficit in the fourth quarter. If they’re going to win at home against the Bills in primetime, they’ll need to find a way to be much more consistent.
For the second time this season, the Rams will play at home on Monday Night Football. They played the New York Giants in Week 2, snapping a five-game losing streak on Monday Night Football. The Rams last played the Bills in primetime to open the 2022 season and lost, 31-10.
Fans should expect plenty of penalties in this game. Scott Novak's crew is now responsible for the two games with the highest combined penalty totals this season. Last week, the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Chargers combined for 30 penalties for 280 yards. In Week 2, the Green Bay Packers and New York Jets combined for 27 penalties for 280 yards.
Bills-Rams MNF uniform matchup is set. Appreciate Buffalo going white pants against the royal-heavy Rams.  Best possible primary outcome for this one. pic.twitter.com/ZYOisQaFw5
The Rams and Bills have played some dramatic games in the past. When these two teams met in 2024, the Rams won 44-42 after the Bills nearly erased a 38-21 fourth-quarter deficit. The Rams almost came back from a 28-3 deficit in 2020, but lost 35-32. Back in 2012, Sam Bradford found Brandon Gibson with under a minute left to win 15-12. In the all-time series, the Bills lead 9-6 and have won three of the last four.
Over the past few seasons, Matthew Stafford and Josh Allen have been two of the most prolific quarterbacks in the NFL. They’ve met three times in the regular season, with Allen leading the head-to-head, 2-1. On Monday night, each player has an opportunity to reach a different milestone.
With a win on Monday Night Football, Josh Allen can become the fourth quarterback all-time with at least 100 wins, including the postseason, in his first nine seasons. He can also tie for the third-most regular season wins by a starting quarterback in his first nine seasons. Only Russell Wilson and Patrick Mahomes have more. Additionally, if Matthew Stafford throws a touchdown pass, he can surpass Ben Roethlisberger for the sixth-most touchdown passes, including the postseason, all-time. With three touchdown passes, he can become the first player in NFL history with at least 150 touchdown passes with two franchises.
This season, the Rams and Bills have used three-tight-end sets at the highest rates in the NFL. The Rams lead the NFL in 13 personnel usage at 31 percent. Meanwhile, the Bills are right behind them at 20 percent. Additionally, The Bills also frequently utilize 12 personnel, featuring two tight ends. Tight ends play a huge role in both offenses, making their usage something to watch on Monday night.

title: Rams' Penalty Problems Are Real, but the Numbers Tell a Bigger Story
full_text:
When the Los Angeles Rams lost to the Denver Broncos in Week 3, they were penalized 13 times for 91 yards. It was the most accepted penalties against the Rams in a game since Week 4 of 2020. Last week against the Eagles, the Rams were penalized eight times for 100 yards. The 21 accepted penalties for 191 yards against the Rams are their most over a two-game stretch during Sean McVay's tenure as head coach.
The recent uptick in penalties by the Rams is simply uncharacteristic of a Sean McVay-led team. Throughout the McVay era, the Rams have struggled to score in the red zone at times due to questionable play-calling. This season, the Rams have had to settle for field goals because of penalties.
“The things that really chapped me that I think are a reflection of an undisciplined team are the pre-snap, the procedural things,” said McVay this week. “Those are the things that we can control with focus and concentration. They'll happen from time to time, but we have to minimize those situationally whether that's jumping offsides offensively, things like that, even making decisions where there's no discrepancy on.”
The past 2 weeks, 21 accepted penalties against the Rams measured 191 yards. Both figures are the most in consecutive games in 10 season under Sean McVay, a span of time in which discipline has been a hallmark. I just looked through them all, a few things to note: *Penalties…
In Week 3 against the Broncos, the Rams had to settle for field goals after an offensive pass interference penalty on Davante Adams and a hold on Steve Avila.
Last week, the Rams settled for field goals after a holding penalty on Davis Allen. According to Warren Sharp of Sharp Football Analytics , red-zone holding is up 38 percent, second only to 2019. After taking over at the Eagles’ 38-yard line, a seven-yard run from Williams was called back because of a questionable illegal blindside block.
BLINDSIDE BLOCK…on Puka Nacua?! What happened to the beautiful game of football… pic.twitter.com/RjcsS1MepO
However, this isn’t only happening to the Rams. This season, there have been the most red zone penalties per game by offenses in NFL history according to Sharp. More than 56.55 percent of red zone flags are on offense, which is up from 48 percent. There have also been the most penalties on third and fourth downs in the second half of games in NFL history.
For as frustrating as some of the penalties have been at times, context is important. This season, the relationship between the NFL players, league, and its officials has hit a breaking point. This week, the NFL suspended two officials for their on-field behavior . The 2026 season has seen the most flags in over a decade.
Penalties are certainly up for the Rams, but that’s also the case around the league. Despite the Rams being penalized more, they are still only tied for the 10th-most penalties per game with five other teams, and there are eight teams between 7.5 and 8.0 penalties per game. They have lost 0.15 EPA per play due to penalties, which is the 11th-worst in the NFL. With that said, the Rams still have a net penalty count of -11, which is the fourth-worst.
Penalty Impact so far this year (Somehow another Vikings defense stat) pic.twitter.com/0DByDipxfG
This is a case where multiple things can be true at the same time. Penalties are up around the NFL as a whole. Comparatively speaking, the Rams are also committing more penalties and ranking higher than they have in the past. The Rams have also been on the wrong side of some of the 50-50 calls, most notably the defensive pass interference penalty on Josh Wallace at the end of the game against the Broncos.
Throughout McVay’s tenure, the Rams have generally been one of the more disciplined teams in the NFL. It’s part of what makes the more recent uptick so jarring. Some of the increase can be attributed to the league-wide trend, but the Rams are also to blame. McVay has made it clear that those are mistakes that they need to clean up.
The league-wide trend of more penalties being called certainly adds some context, but it doesn't completely excuse the Rams' lack of discipline over the last two weeks. There are still things that they can control. If the Rams are going to reach their ceiling as a Super Bowl contender, they can't continue allowing self-inflicted mistakes to take points off the board.

title: Kyren Williams Gives the Rams an Answer to Their WR3 Problem
full_text:
When the Los Angeles Rams needed a third wide receiver to step up on Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles, it was running back Kyren Williams who made his presence felt in the passing game. Williams had 10 receptions for 67 yards and became a legitimate receiving threat. Given his success in Week 4 and the offense's continued injuries at tight end, the Rams may need Williams to remain in that role going forward.
If one thing has become increasingly clear with the Rams’ offense, it is how they are lacking a consistent and reliable third wide receiver . Puka Nacua and Davante Adams have combined for 36 catches for 589 yards, while all other wide receivers on the Rams’ roster have combined for 10 catches for 151 yards.
Early in Sean McVay’s tenure with the Rams, the offense consistently featured a running back in the passing game. It certainly helped that the running back at the time was Todd Gurley, but that element has been missing from the Rams’ offense since 2018.
In 2017, Gurley led all Rams players with 64 catches, and his 788 receiving yards trailed only Cooper Kupp. The next season, Gurley was the team’s third receiver with 59 catches for 580 yards. Robert Woods and Brandin Cooks led the wide receivers, while Josh Reynolds was the third option with just 29 receptions for 402 yards.
The Rams entered the season with the idea that they would make 13 personnel their identity on offense. Through the first three weeks, that had been the case. However, with injuries to Terrance Ferguson and Colby Parkinson, the Rams ran the highest percentage of their offense out of 11 personnel since Week 5 of last season.
Despite the increased usage of 11 personnel, Konata Mumpfield, Jordan Whittington, and Tutu Atwell each had just one catch, and none finished with more than 10 receiving yards. Meanwhile, Kyren Williams had 10 catches for 67 yards. Williams became the first Rams player with 10 receptions and 10 carries in a game since Gurley in Week 15 of 2018.
He also became the first player in the NFL this season with 10 receptions and 10 carries in a game. Williams joined Christian McCaffrey and Jahmyr Gibbs as the only players to achieve that feat since 2024. Williams is the first player since Breece Hall in 2023 to have 15 or more rushing attempts for at least 80 yards to go with 10 receptions for at least 65 yards in the same game. That’s something that Gurley only did once in his career in the Rams’ 27-23 win over the Tennessee Titans in 2017.
If the Rams are forced to continue utilizing 11 personnel, they need a third option outside of Nacua and Adams to get involved in the passing game. For the Rams to be successful, they may need to continue throwing the ball to Williams.
While he may not be a standard receiving back, he’s shown that it’s something that he can do successfully. Among running backs with at least 35 routes this season, Williams’ 1.77 yards per route run ranks sixth. He’s also third in receiving yards per game.
Williams is doing all that without having plays designed for him. Only four percent of Williams’ targets have been designed, which is the second-lowest rate in the NFL. However, last week showed what Williams can do when he is a focal point. Against the Eagles, Williams was the first read on 14.5 percent of the team’s targets, which was up from 8.6 percent in the first three weeks.
Williams certainly isn't the same type of player that Gurley was. However, his improvement in the passing game presents an opportunity to bring back an element of the offense that made McVay’s early teams so dangerous. It’s also an area where Blake Corum has struggled. With the Rams struggling to find production from their wide receiver depth, Williams has shown that he can help fill that void.
Williams may not be a traditional receiving back, but he’s proven that he can at least be effective when he gets involved. He already has 21 receptions for 173 yards this season. If he continues at that pace, he’ll finish at 89 receptions for 730 yards. It’s highly unlikely he hits those numbers, but it’s a testament to his early-season success as a pass-catcher.
When the Rams needed a spark on Sunday against the Eagles, they were able to lean on Williams, which also opened things up for Nacua in the passing game. Williams has demonstrated that he can be a reliable option when given opportunities.It's now up to McVay to determine how much of that production can become a consistent part of the offense until the Rams are healthy enough to get back to what they do best.

title: Rams Special Teams Analysis: What's Going Wrong and How to Fix It
full_text:
Through the first four weeks of the 2026 season, the Los Angeles Rams have struggled on special teams . In 2010, the San Diego Chargers went 9-7 and missed the playoffs because of poor special teams play. Much like the Rams this year, they also started the season 2-2.
The Chargers opened that season with a loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, in part because of a 94-yard punt return touchdown by Dexter McCluster. In Week 3, the Chargers gave up a 101-yard kickoff return for a touchdown to the Seattle Seahawks. The Chargers gave up a second kickoff return for a touchdown in the fourth quarter, losing by seven.
That 2010 Chargers team is infamous for having the No. 1 defense and No. 1 offense, but the 32nd-ranked special teams unit. Through four weeks, the Rams have the No. 2 offense and No. 2 defense, but the 32nd-ranked special teams unit.If they don’t fix their special teams, the Rams could be heading down a similarly disappointing path.
According to DVOA, the Rams’ special teams unit ranks 32nd at -14.5 percent. The next four teams ahead of them have a combined record of 0-16. In every game this season, the Rams have had some sort of special teams error. Against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1, the Rams allowed a 45-yard kickoff return to open the second half. It didn’t take long for the 49ers to score a touchdown and take control of the game.
While the Rams beat the New York Giants in Week 2, Ethan Evans opened with a 38-yard punt and Harison Mevis missed a 43-yard field goal. Xavier Smith also bobbled the opening kickoff of the second half and Tanner Ingle took a 15-yard penalty on a kick return.
Against the Denver Broncos, Smith again made poor decisions in the return game. Additionally, Evans shanked a re-kick, and the Rams allowed a 28-yard return to give the Broncos a short field. Neither of the Broncos’ two touchdown drives in the third quarter went more than 52 yards.
Special teams almost cost the Rams last week as well. The Rams allowed a 41-yard punt return to set the Philadelphia Eagles up in the red zone. In the same game, Harrison Mevis missed a 48-yard field goal and had a kickoff go out of bounds.
To the Rams’ credit, they are actively trying to address the issues . Head coach Sean McVay recognizes that changes need to be made. Even though the Rams beat the Eagles on Sunday, McVay addressed the special teams issues.
“We need better,” said McVay on Monday. “As it relates to the return game, you have to do a good job of holding up and doing better on some of the perimeter play. I thought we fielded the ball clean. The conditions were unique, but we have to be able to get some more production out of that. Obviously, I would have loved for us to have made that field goal kick, and then the long punt return is not good. We have to do a better job of casting a net, being able to tackle.”
The Rams cut punt returner Xavier Smith last week and also moved on from Tanner Ingle. Both players had been responsible for key special teams errors in the past. The Rams also signed Maximus Pulley off of the Eagles’ practice squad who is a good special teams player. This week, they signed linebacker Eric Kendricks. Still, the changes are only scratching the surface.
According to DVOA, the Rams’ field goal unit ranks 28th at -4.0 percent. Only the Steelers, 49ers, Dolphins, and Falcons are worse. Their kickoff unit ranks 28th as well at -2.1 percent. Mevis’ longest field goal this season is 48 yards. He’s one of just six kickers without a make over 50 yards. The Rams have lost 0.17 EPA per kick from Mevis, ranking 26th in the NFL.
NFL Kicker Rankings through Week 4 pic.twitter.com/5QLmQMWsLY
It would be one thing if Mevis was missing long field goals, but the Rams don’t appear to trust his leg from range. Mevis is 4-for-6 in his career from beyond 45 yards. The Rams have actively passed up kicking 52-yard field goals and taken delay-of-game penalties to punt. Last week, the Rams went for it on 4th-and-8 instead of allowing Mevis to kick a 53-yard field goal.
This isn’t to say that the Rams should go back to Joshua Karty, but Mevis is just 1-for-3 from 48 yards in his career. From 45+, Karty was 3-for-4. That’s not necessarily an argument for Karty, but rather an illustration of Mevis’ inconsistencies from range. His miss on Sunday against the Eagles was so far left, it didn’t hit the kicking net behind the goal posts.
MEVIS' KICK IS NO GOOD ❌ #NFL #Rams #RamsHouse #Eagles #FlyEaglesFly #LARvsPHI pic.twitter.com/Wbs5Wcu2vP
The lack of confidence in his kicker has forced McVay to become more aggressive, which might be a good thing. At the same time, you have to have a kicker that can make it from range in today’s NFL.
Inside of 45 yards, Mevis has been reliable. However, some are mistaking being reliable for being good when it comes to Mevis. Given Karty’s inconsistencies, Mevis being 46-for-46 on extra points is a good thing.
With that said, 20-of-26 attempts in his career have been inside of 45 yards. He’s 19-for-20 on those attempts. From 45+, Mevis is 4-for-6 with a 66.7 percent make-rate. The NFL average from 45+ is 73.4 percent. In today’s NFL when two first downs can essentially put an offense in potential field goal range, the Rams need a kicker who is consistent inside of 45, but also has the leg to hit from deep.
The Rams don’t necessarily need to replace Mevis, but last year they brought in competition for Karty and they should be looking to do the same now. Tanner Brown was signed by the Rams as a rookie, but didn’t make it through the preseason. He was 29-for-32 in the UFL last year, missing one field goal from inside of 50 yards. Brown also had makes from 60 and 63 yards.
The Rams previously signed Tanner Brown as a UDFA and he didn't make it out of the preseason. Hit bombs from 60 and 63 last year in the UFL. Gotta say he's at least worth a look, right? https://t.co/8R527iZptS
The Rams made a change at punt returner with Alex Bachman last week after cutting Smith. It was a much-needed change, but it’s hard to say that it was the answer. Replacing Smith with Bachman wasn’t a solution, but rather a band-aid.
DVOA currently has the Rams’ kick return unit ranked 32nd at -6.4 percent and their punt return unit ranked 27th at -2.2 percent. Their average starting field position at the 26.8-yard line ranks 29th in the NFL. Rams’ opponents are averaging starting field position about 5.6 yards better than the Rams. That difference ranks 27th.
Best average starting field position: 1. Raiders – 36.5 2. Eagles – 33.9 3. Panthers – 33.8 4. Seahawks – 33.2 5. Bills – 32.8 Worst average starting field position: 28. Titans - 27.5 29. Rams – 26.8 30. Patriots - 26.8 31. Texans – 26.7 32. Chargers – 26.2
We’ll see how this improves without Smith over the next four weeks, but it feels like the Rams still need to do more here. However, the bar remains very low at “simply catch the ball and make good decisions.” Bachman did that last week and likely will remain in that spot until he shows that he can’t be trusted.
If there is another spot that the Rams make a change, it wouldn’t be surprising to see it come at punter. The Rams rank 30th in punting DVOA at -3.4 percent. For every good punt that Evans has, he follows it up with one that puts the defense in a bad spot.
Evans’ seat is, at the very least, getting warm . Special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone called out his inconsistencies last week.
“We need to get more consistency from the punter,” said Ventrone. “Ethan can do a better job being able to elevate the ball and match hang times and distance at a greater rate. We have to do a better job in his position.”
The big return last week against the Eagles was more on the punt coverage unit than it was Evans’ punt. Evans actually did a good job getting the punt along the sideline and his coverage unit was in position to make a play on the returner. Both the punter and coverage unit can be better.

title: Multiple Doctors Believe Rams WR Puka Nacua Is at Risk of Re-Injury
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams just got wide receiver Puka Nacua back last week after missing the previous two games with what the team described as a hip/groin injury.. Nacua looked good in his return with nine catches for 125 yards against the Philadelphia Eagles. However, according to multiple doctors, Nacua could be at risk for re-injury.
On Wednesday, Pro Football Talk’s Mike Florio noted that Nacua has been dealing with a pre-hernia. While it isn’t a hernia right now, it could develop into one.
“The question becomes whether the rest has allowed the weakness/strain in the affected area of the hip/groin to improve sufficiently to prevent a hernia from developing,” said Florio. “If it ever does, there’s only one way to fix it.”
The one way to fix it would be surgery, and the Rams will hope it doesn’t come to that point. A typical recovery from a hernia surgery would be 4-6 weeks and Nacua would almost certainly land on injured reserve if that were to be the case. After resting Nacua for the past two weeks, the Rams are banking on that helping the issue long-term.
However, there is some risk with Nacua, especially with his physical style of play. Toward the end of training camp, Nacua was h eld out due to a psoas injury in his groin. Following the Rams’ Week 1 loss to the 49ers, Nacua felt discomfort during the following week of practice and didn’t return until last week..
Despite the Rams erring on the side of caution with Nacua, some doctors seem to believe it’s only a matter of when, not if, Nacua re-aggravates the injury.
Dr. Jeff Mueller on Twitter noted that there is some re-injury risk.
“My guess with Puka is that this sling suffered enough trauma to require rehab but not to a full extent of requiring sports hernia surgery,” said Mueller. “In that scenario, their hope is that the traumatized tissue scars over/heals enough to where it doesn’t rip any further. However, this does place enough reinjury risk where if he twists sharply and it does rip the tissue more, it could push him into a situation where it causes a true sports hernia.”
Puka Nacua Q: It’s some speculation on our part but we know for sure that Puka has dealt with Groin and Hip Flexor muscle injuries since August with a condition currently labeled as “pre-hernia”. Sports Hernia injuries involve the groin, abdominal and hip flexor musculature.… https://t.co/vYhWttjNjS pic.twitter.com/r40i6k8EkJ
Throughout the offseason, the Rams have erred on the side of caution with several of their star players, Nacua included. If they are able to avoid surgery and a longer absence, that’s obviously ideal.
Still, this is a similar approach that the Rams took with Myles Garrett. The Rams held out Garrett for much of training camp, hoping that the swelling in his knee would go down. Garrett’s knee didn’t respond as the team had hoped and he had one of the worst games of his career in Week 1 against the 49ers because he wasn’t able to feel like himself.Had Garrett simply gotten surgery in the offseason, the team may have been able to avoid that situation altogether.
It appears to be a similar situation here with Nacua. With the Rams being in the middle of the season, they obviously want to avoid the surgery if they can. However, they could be delaying the inevitable.
“This is a matter of when, not if. Best case scenario, he makes it the entire season and ends up having sports hernia repair surgery (likely by Dr. William Meyers) in the off-season,” said Dr. Jesse Morse. “Every time he lifts his leg, pushes his foot down to cut and get off the line, he is stressing this tissue. Every time he reaches out over his head for a ball that is higher than usual, this currently damaged tissue is going to be stressed further.”
Morse noted that if Nacua were to suffer a significant setback, the surgery would be moved up significantly and would take about six weeks to return.
Puka Nacua In my opinion, this is matter of when, not if Best case scenario, he makes it the entire season and ends up having sports hernia repair surgery (likely by Dr. William Meyers) in the off-season. Every time he lifts his leg, pushes his foot down to cut and get off… https://t.co/C6oTmuokV8
Nacua looked good in his return, but his physical style of play will always leave him susceptible to injury. When Nacua spoke to the media last week, he said he felt good. Still, as Florio said, “Nacua has been dealing with the symptoms of the kind of weakness in the structures that can allow a hernia to form. It hasn’t yet, and that may simply be a matter of luck.”
For now, the Rams will hope that the two weeks of rest were enough time for Nacua’s injury to heal. His performance against the Eagles was certainly encouraging, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the issue is behind him. The Rams avoided the worst-case scenario, but the risk of a significant setback may not be going away anytime soon.

title: Rams May Have Made a Mistake Trading Away This Tight End
full_text:
Prior to the regular season during roster cutdowns, the Los Angeles Rams made a surprising trade with the Green Bay Packers. The Rams sent tight end Mark Redman to the Packers for a 2028 seventh-round pick. With Redman likely to be part of roster cuts, it made sense for the Rams to try to get something for him rather than lose him on the waiver wire..
However, with the injuries to Terrance Ferguson and Colby Parkinson in combination with the lack of production from second-round rookie Max Klare, it’s worth asking whether the Rams should have tried to hang on to Redman.
Heading into last week’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles, the Rams entered the game thin at the tight end position. Ferguson was placed on injured reserve and Parkinson was dealing with an AC sprain in his shoulder.
Still, the Rams should have been able to get by without changing too much of their offense given they still had three tight ends on the roster, including a second-round pick in Klare. During the week when McVay was asked whether Klare would get an opportunity to play more, he seemed to imply that would be the case .
“It certainly does,” said head coach Sean McVay. “Obviously, being able to play with multiple tight ends has become a big part of our identity and so it absolutely does.”
By the end of Sunday’s game against the Eagles, the Rams played out of 11 personnel on 88 percent of their offensive snaps. Additionally, Klare played one snap the entire game . Even if Klare is early in his career, if the Rams can’t rely on a second-round pick in that situation, when can they?
Meanwhile, in Green Bay, Redman has become a key part of the Packers continuing to operate out of 13 personnel. With Luke Musgrave on injured reserve, Redman played the second-most snaps at tight end behind Tucker Kraft for the Packers in Week 4 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Redman didn’t just play, but he also looked pretty good and had quite the impact as a blocker.
nice Packers gap run. Mark Redman (#86) bringing it on his block on Dallas Turner. pic.twitter.com/HE1UwR1uNg
Redman hasn’t had too much of an impact in the passing game, but he’s allowed the Packers to continue to operate their offense and stick to their identity. Against the Buccaneers in Week 4, Redman was the 14th-highest-graded tight end via Pro Football Focus. The only Rams tight end to grade higher was Tyler Higbee.
As a blocker, Redman had a 72.3 run-blocking grade, ranking 12th. That would have led all Rams tight ends. On the season, Redman ranks seventh in run-blocking via PFF and is nearly 10 points higher than the Rams’ best blocking tight end in Colby Parkinson.
Oooooh buddy that's the good stuff. pic.twitter.com/R5ozfRXU43
Hindsight is, of course, 20-20. At the time, the Rams didn’t necessarily make the wrong decision by trading Redman. An argument can be made that the trade worked out for both sides. Redman would have struggled to find a role in the Rams’ offense and went to a team where he could contribute.
One of the primary reasons that Klare likely isn’t seeing snaps is his inconsistency as a blocker. That’s typically the biggest transition for tight ends going from college to the NFL. Klare ranked 41st out of 50 tight ends during the preseason as a run blocker.
Still, with the benefit of hindsight, it’s worth wondering if the Rams could have made a stronger effort to keep Redman, especially knowing that Klare may need his entire rookie season to develop.
When the Rams released their initial 53-man roster, they kept seven wide receivers, even though the offense moving to more 13 personnel. There likely wasn’t a need for seven wide receivers on the roster. It’s possible Tutu Atwell could have been kept on the practice squad. Additionally, less than four weeks into the season, the team cut Xavier Smith, despite there already being questions during training camp and the preseason about whether he should have been the punt returner.
It’s fair to say that the Rams didn’t have enough wide receiver depth to warrant keeping seven players at the position.
With that said, keeping six tight ends on the roster certainly would have been a lot. However, if the plan was to simply red-shirt Klare, maybe it should have been more of a consideration. Redman had already been in the offense for a year, spending last year on the practice squad. He also played well in the preseason.
Hello Mark Redman. pic.twitter.com/X2d5jGdokr
Trading Redman wasn’t necessarily a mistake when the Rams made the move. If he was going to be cut, they might as well have gotten something for him. At the same time, with Klare seemingly not ready for a significant role and early injuries at tight end, the Rams could use Redman now.
His ability as a blocker could have helped the Rams continue operating out of 13 personnel rather than changing their identity. Redman’s presence has allowed the Packers to do that while the Rams had to completely shift their offense.

title: Rams Keep Betting on Their Wide Receiver Depth and It Is Not Working
full_text:
One of the glaring issues for the Los Angeles Rams on offense has been the lack of production from a third wide receiver. On Wednesday, the Rams once again passed on the opportunity to add a more experienced player at the position. Since free agency, the Rams could have signed players such as Stefon Diggs, Keenan Allen, and Brandin Cooks and instead opted not to.
When Odell Beckham Jr. was released by the New York Giants last week, it gave them another chance to add a veteran player with experience in the offense and coaching staff. Beckham officially signed to the Minnesota Vikings’ practice squad on Wednesday morning.
Vikings are signing veteran WR Odell Beckham Jr. to their practice squad, as @Schultz_Report reported.
Coming into the season, it was understandable that the Rams may not have felt the need for a third wide receiver in the offense. As the offense looked to shift to more 13 personnel, the value of the third wide receiver diminished and the position wasn’t as needed as it had been in the past.
However, injuries happen in the NFL, and that was the case on Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Rams were without Terrance Ferguson, who was placed on injured reserve, while Colby Parkinson missed the game with an AC sprain.
Without those two players, the Rams were forced to go back to 11 personnel, even if they didn’t necessarily have the players to do it. In Week 4, the Rams operated out of 11 personnel at an 88 percent clip. That’s their highest rate since Week 5 last year. Prior to Week 4, the Rams had operated just 56 percent of their offense out of 11 personnel.
Due to the injuries at the tight end position, the Rams’ usage out of 11 personnel jumped over 30 percent. For much of the game, it looked as if the offense lacked an identity and it made sense. That wasn’t the offense that the Rams planned to be this season. Head coach Sean McVay talked about that struggle to find an identity this week on the Coach McVay Show .
“What’s our identity? Because we’ve had some key figures that are in and out of the lineup, it’s been hard for us to establish.”
The Rams are simply not built to operate consistently out of 11 personnel. DDuring the first three weeks of the season, the offense averaged -0.02 EPA per play out of 11 personnel. That ranked 16th in the NFL. They’ve averaged 0.1 EPA per play out of 13 personnel, which is good enough for the fifth best in the NFL.
That impact was especially seen in the passing game. In 13 personnel, the Rams had a 60 percent passing success rate in the first three weeks of the season. During the first three weeks, they had just a 43.5 percent passing success rate out of 11 personnel. In the first half against the Eagles, the Rams had a 42.1 percent passing success rate out of 11 personnel.
That lack of success is a testament to how the Rams haven’t gotten a lot out of their wide receiver depth. Puka Nacua and Davante Adams have combined for 36 catches for 589 yards and two touchdowns. All other wide receivers combined on the Rams’ roster have 10 catches for 151 yards and one touchdown.
The Rams haven't gotten much out of their WRs not named Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. Puka and Davante: 36 catches, 589 yards, 2 TDs All other WRs combined: 10 catches, 151 yards, 1 TD
While it is true that Ferguson is technically the Rams’ third wide receiver, that becomes an issue when he’s hurt, as he will be over the next three weeks at minimum.
Despite the Rams operating out of 11 personnel at their highest rate in almost a year, they didn’t get any production out of a third wide receiver. Konata Mumpfield, Jordan Whittington, and Tutu Atwell combined for three catches on six targets for 19 yards . None of those players had more than one catch or more than 10 yards.
When the Rams last operated out of 11 personnel on more than 80 percent of their offensive snaps in Week 5 last year, Atwell had two catches for 72 yards and Whittington added two catches for 33 yards as well. There was a lot more balance.
This season, Mumpfield has very clearly been the Rams’ third wide receiver in the pecking order. He’s played 49.5 percent of the team’s offensive snaps. Last week, it was Whittington with more snaps, but for the most part, it has been Mumpfield.
Among wide receivers with at least 50 routes run, Mumpfield’s 42.9 percent targeted success rate ranks 76th. Mumpfield has a -6.6 percent catch rate over expected via NFL Pro, while Whittington’s is -11.4 percent.
When targeting either player, Matthew Stafford is 8-for-17 for 124 yards with one touchdown and an interception. His passer rating when targeting Mumpfield is 65.2 while it’s 74.3 when targeting Whittington. Mumpfield has an EPA per target of -0.11 and Whittington’s is -0.27. There are things to like about Mumpfield, but he hasn’t been good enough at the catch point and remains incredibly inefficient. He’s averaged 1.17 yards per route run, ranking 61st out of 81 qualifying wide receivers.
Again, just because the Rams may not need a third wide receiver as often when the offense is fully healthy doesn’t mean there isn’t a need for a more experienced and reliable third wide receiver in the offense. While no team has operated out of 13 personnel more than the Rams, five other teams have run more than 20 percent of their offense out of 13 personnel and have a reliable third pass catcher at wide receiver.
It’s no longer about these players simply needing an opportunity to prove themselves. As the third wide receivers in the offense, this has been their opportunity and what they’ve done with it. It hasn’t been good enough and it almost cost the Rams on Sunday against the Eagles before Kyren Williams got involved in the passing game.
The Rams don’t need a third wide receiver to become a featured part of the offense. However, they need a player they can rely on to step in when needed. That wasn’t the case when the Rams had to resort to 11 personnel against the Eagles. The Rams are continuing to bet that Mumpfield, Whittington, and Atwell will provide enough, but that hasn’t paid off. There hasn’t been much evidence to suggest that level of confidence is warranted.
Injuries forced the Rams away from their preferred 13 personnel identity against the Eagles, and when they needed their wide receiver depth to step up, nobody did. The Rams escaped Philadelphia with a win, but they may not be as fortunate the next time.

title: The Rams Have a Problem on Offense — And It’s Matthew Stafford
full_text:
Looking at the raw numbers of the Los Angeles Rams’ offense through the first four weeks of the NFL season, it would be easy to come to the conclusion that they are one of the best units in the NFL.
The Rams rank second in total offense with 417 yards per game behind only the Chicago Bears. They also rank second in passing offense with 290.3 yards per game, trailing just the Carolina Panthers.
Those numbers would seemingly tell you that quarterback Matthew Stafford is on his way to repeating as the NFL MVP. However, that has been far from the case. In fact, an argument can be made that Stafford has been one of the weakest links of the Rams’ offense .
The Rams rank just 19th in points per game with 21.3 and their -0.05 offensive EPA per play ranks 16th. On a play-by-play basis, the Rams’ offense is one of the best. They rank sixth in offensive success rate, but it’s a team with a quarterback that can’t get out of his own way to start the season.
To be clear, the Rams’ offense is its best version with Matthew Stafford at quarterback. This isn’t to say that the Rams need to bench Stafford or go to that level of extreme, even if they have a first-round pick on the bench. However, the Rams do need him to be better, especially if they are to reach their goals and be the team that many expected them to be coming into the year.
Stafford has shown the ability to make the high-level throws and bring the team back as he did last week. However, he's lacked consistency and made too many mistakes that have cost the offense in critical moments.
When Stafford turned the ball over on the opening drive on Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles, it marked the first time in his career that he has thrown an interception in the first four games to start a season. In the first four games, Stafford has six touchdowns and six interceptions.
Matthew Stafford has thrown an interception in every game this season. According to ESPN Research, this is his longest streak to open a season in his career.
Heading into Week 5 against the Buffalo Bills, Stafford ranks 17th in ESPN’s QBR. His 80.5 quarterback rating ranks 21st and trails Cam Ward, Aaron Rodgers, Tyson Bagent, Jacoby Brissett, and CJ Stroud. It’s only 0.1 better than Bo Nix.
In the more advanced stats, Stafford’s -0.01 EPA per pass ranks 19th and trails quarterbacks like Deshaun Watson. It simply hasn’t been good enough from Stafford.
Yes, it’s true that not many quarterbacks could have brought the Rams back from 10 points down in the fourth quarter on the road in Philadelphia in the rain. At the same time, there are a lot of other quarterbacks who would not have had the Rams in that position to begin with. The interception at the end of the first half simply cannot happen.
Coming into Sunday’s game, the Eagles hadn’t forced a single turnover on defense. Stafford gave them two and was directly responsible for 10 of Philadelphia’s 20 first-half points.
The Rams’ defense has three interceptions this season. On two of those occasions, Stafford has given the ball right back with an interception. According to Pro Football Focus, he has eight turnover-worthy plays in 2026, which is tied for the fourth most in the NFL.
The Matthew Stafford interception regression is real. Stafford through 8 INTs last year, and is already at 5 picks in 3+ games in 2026. He led the NFL with a +6.8 "net luck" rating during the 2025 season. Was due for more INTs. pic.twitter.com/oQRwZMbWah
In a sense, a regression back to the mean was always going to happen for Stafford after his MVP season. However, his turnover-worthy-play rate of 4.3 percent is the worst since his rookie season with the Detroit Lions back in 2009. Fantasy Points Data actually has his turnover-worthy throw rate even higher at 6.7 percent, behind only Trevor Lawrence.
Stafford has always been a quarterback that is going to take risks and trust his arm a little too much sometimes. That’s been the case on a few of his turnovers this season.
It’s not just the turnovers that have been an issue for Stafford. He has also lacked accuracy on deep targets. Last season, Stafford had a success rate of 46.7 percent with an EPA per pass of 0.74 on deep targets. His success rate ranked fifth and EPA per pass ranked sixth.
This season, Stafford’s EPA per pass of -0.17 ranks 26th and his 28.6 percent success rate ranks 24th. His success rate has dropped 18 percentage points. That’s a significant drop-off. Against the Denver Broncos, he missed Davante Adams a few times on the deep ball. He also slightly overthrew Adams after he had won at the line of scrimmage with a double move.
Again, it hasn’t all been bad for Stafford. There are moments where his arm talent has still been evident. His seven ‘big-time throws’ via PFF rank seventh. On tight-window throws, Stafford’s 0.55 EPA per dropback ranks third behind Patrick Mahomes and Brock Purdy.
Stafford typically improves as the season progresses. Since 2023, Matthew Stafford has averaged 0.08 EPA per dropback in Weeks 1-4. From Weeks 5-18, he’s averaged 0.14 EPA per dropback. That’s roughly a 77 percent jump in efficiency per play after the first month of the season.
If we widen that gap to Weeks 1-6 instead, he averaged 0.06 EPA per dropback compared to 0.16 in Weeks 7-18. Stafford is approximately 2.5 times more efficient per dropback after the first month and a half of the season. This has especially been the case over the last two seasons.
The Rams are officially out of the first month of the season and following Monday night’s game against the Buffalo Bills, the schedule does lighten up slightly. With Puka Nacua already back and Terrance Ferguson eventually returning, the Rams will once again be fully healthy at their skill positions. We have yet to see what the offense truly looks like with both those players on the field.
For the Rams to reach their ceiling, they don’t need Stafford to replicate his MVP-level play from last season. However, he does need to stop being one of the main reasons for the offense’s struggles and inconsistencies. The turnovers need to get fixed. Stafford’s history suggests that better football is coming and he’s still the best option at quarterback for the Rams.
At the end of the day, the Rams will only go as far as Stafford takes them. If the Rams are going to go from an offense that piles up yards to one that consistently puts points on the board, that improvement needs to start with Stafford.
