title: Breaking the Dolphins Monday Roster Move and Injury Updates
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins made a roster move Monday in the aftermath of their Week 4 game against the Minnesota Vikings, though it probably was more a matter of official record than anything else.
The Dolphins announced they had waived running back Carlos Washington Jr., two days after they signed him to the active roster off their practice squad. And the best guess is that Washington will be right back on the practice squad by Wednesday, assuming he doesn't get claimed off waivers.
Washington was signed to back up Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon II for the game against the Minnesota Vikings and the Dolphins couldn't simply elevate him from the practice squad because they needed their two moves to add defensive line depth with both edge Rodney McGraw and interior lineman Mazi Smith.
The Dolphins realistically could have done the move they made with Washington with any of the three players because any of them can be signed off the practice squad anyway if another team wants them badly enough (the only stipulation being that players signed off another team's practice squad have to be kept on the active roster for three weeks).
It just so happens the Dolphins have an opening on the practice squad, the one created when they signed Washington the active roster.
The Dolphins have another running back on the practice squad at this time, trade acquisition Jarquez Hunt, but it says here that Washington being brought back is a very solid bet.
Though he was active against the Vikings, Washington did not get into the game.
Head coach Jeff Hafley offered some injury updates Monday, the best news being that defensive tackle Kenneth Grant will be back at practice Wednesday for the first time in the regular season.
Grant missed the first four games of the regular season after being placed on IR on August 30, but he's now eligible to return to game action.
If Grant can get through the week of practice without any issues, he should be in line to make his 2026 season debut against the Cincinnati Bengals next Sunday and his addition could prove valuable to an interior D-line group — Zach Sieler, Jordan Phillips, Zeek Biggers — coming off its best performance of the season.
The news wasn't quite as encouraging when it comes to wide receiver Caleb Douglas, who missed the past two games because of an ankle injury.
Hafley described Douglas as day-to-day and said "we'll see" in terms of whether Douglas would be able to practice Wednesday.
Keeping in mind that the Dolphins have their bye following this game against Cincinnati, don't be surprised if they err on the side of caution and keep Douglas out one more game, which would give him two more weeks to get back to 100 percent or close to it.
Hafley also put safety Dante Trader Jr. in the day-to-day category after he injured a knee against the Vikings but later returned to the game, and said special teams cornerback Reece Taylor would be week to week with his quad injury.

title: Four Winners And Four Losers From Week 4 Dolphins Loss
full_text:
In their third road contest in four games, the Miami Dolphins had one of their best chances to win this season, but could not get the job done, falling to Minnesota 15-10.
It feels like there was genuine progress made by Miami. After being blown out by Las Vegas and San Francisco, the Dolphins hung around longer than expected against Kansas City and were a TOE away from a possible win against the Vikings.
Bottom line? This "progress" is too slow, and even though the list of winless NFL teams is shrinking, the Dolphins are firmly on that list no team wants to be on. Some players stood out for the Dolphins on both sides of the ball for good and bad reasons, but the same problems persist.
The biggest what-if of the season occurred in the second quarter when Bell caught a 68-yard touchdown to give the Dolphins the lead — except it didn't count because Bell BARELY stepped out of bounds before catching the ball, leading to an illegal touching penalty and wiping the score off the board.
Knowing how the game transpired, it's a brutal mistake for Bell to make. Every play matters more in a game that was this close. But if you were to take away that play, Bell was still a non-factor in this game, targeted three times but not recording a single catch. He was expected to build on a solid performance against Kansas City, but it didn't come close to happening.
One of the biggest negatives of Miami's season up to this point was the lack of a pass rush; opposing quarterbacks' jerseys were way too clean. However, the Dolphins found their groove against the Vikings, and Sieler was the poster boy of the group with three tackles, two tackles for loss, and, most importantly, TWO SACKS.
It's his best overall performance this season, hands down. He set the tone with his first sack, which came on the first play of the game. There was genuine synergy between him and some of the other Dolphins in the trenches, like Chop Robinson and Jordan Phillips.
Don't think this is a sign that Miami's pass rush is "fixed," and that they can continue this moving forward. But they found success against a really solid Minnesota offensive line, and will now take on a historically shaky Cincinnati O-line back in Miami Gardens, so let's see where they go from here.
Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores had his way in terms of getting to Miami's quarterback. Willis had an abysmal 85 passing yards, lost a fumble, and was sacked twice. While he didn't throw an interception, he shucked some questionable throws that could have been picked off.
When he had some solid completions here and there, he couldn't keep it going for back-to-back plays, or there was a penalty that wiped it off the board. In terms of being a dual-threat QB, he wasn't a threat at all in the run game.
I've tried my best to keep Willis off these lists so far this season, but his performance against Minnesota was the breaking point. Miami's offense had opportunities in this game to win, but it genuinely looked like Willis held the offense back at times.
The keys to the run game were given to Gordon following Achane's injury, and he didn't disappoint with 100 yards and a touchdown off nine carries.
His 53-yard pick-up coming out of halftime gave the Dolphins the spark they needed on offense, though it sadly led to a field goal. He could have even done better if one long-distance run hadn't been called back because he was "supposedly" touched at the line of scrimmage after stumbling down, though no TV angle was provided that actually showed that.
Regardless, Gordon was electric in this game and had to put the offense on his back at times. The flashes of speed, agility, and ability to break tackles in prior games culminated in one of his best performances in the NFL, and it was well needed.
In Paul's defense, the officiating crew for this game didn't give the Dolphins any favors, but players eventually need to adjust when they're getting hammered with penalties. Paul did not do that and was hit with three holding penalties. He negated a few quality plays from the offense, including the best run of the game for Willis in the second quarter.
It's a shame, because Paul did look good when blocking for Gordon and company. He had a great game against Kansas City and genuinely looked like he was turning into a quality pass blocker.
However, he regressed against Minnesota and visibly looked frustrated, not just with the officiating, but also with how the O-line struggled — Austin Jackson wasn't any better; it's just the matter of three holding penalties by Paul that put him on this list.
There needs to be a serious discussion about Rodriguez and how he deserves to be in the running for the NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year Award. He's done everything asked of him by Miami and then some, and seems to only be getting better as the weeks pass.
His performance against Minnesota was his best so far—- 18 total tackles (nine of which were solo) on 78 defensive snaps, leading the team in all three categories (tied in snaps). His 18 tackles in a single game are the most by ANY defensive player in the NFL this season in the NFL so far.
Rodriguez always seems to find his way to the football. His ability to wrap up quarterbacks, running backs, and wide receivers is currently unmatched in the NFL, especially considering he's 24 years old. Getting by Rodriguez with the ball in your hand has become a near-impossible task, cementing him as one of the brightest spots on the team this season.
On one hand, this was a decent game for Brooks by the numbers with 13 tackles. However, this slot truly represents everyone who attempted to contain TJ Hockenson, who had one of the best games of his career. Postgame, Brooks claimed ownership of the defense's struggles to keep up with the eighth-year tight end.
With Justin Jefferson not playing, there was hope that Miami's defense could silence Minnesota's passing game, but Hockenson turned out to be the hero that the Vikings needed. He racked up 13 receptions for 119 yards, including some of their biggest plays on offense as the game progressed.
The cherry on top was the final play before the two-minute warning, with Hockenson going down at the 1-yard line to ice the game as Miami had no more timeouts. Jordan Addison and the rest of Minnesota's wide receivers had mediocre performances in comparison; Hockenson was at the right place at the right time to become one of the most unexpected reasons why the Vikings won.
So far, Uche has had a pedestrian season for the Dolphins, but he provided solid snaps for Miami against the Vikings, finishing the day with six tackles and a sack in the second quarter.
He did some of his best work in the second half, including one of the most critical tackles of the game. On 3rd & 8, he stopped Aaron Jones dead in his tracks for a gain of three yards. Minnesota had to settle for a field goal, giving the ball back to Miami's offense, trailing by five points with just under seven minutes to go.
The Dolphins' offense didn't come through, but you can't say the defense didn't give them the opportunity needed to win the game.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 4 Snap Counts Stories: (Overly) Busy Day for the Defense
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 15-10 loss against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, where the biggest news involved two players again being out with injuries — Caleb Douglas and Robert Beal Jr.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Kyle McCord, offensive lineman Andrew Meyer and running back Carlos Washington Jr., who was signed to the 53-man roster off the practice squad Saturday.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies after tight end Will Kacmarek joined Week 3 starters Chris Bell at wide receiver, fullback DJ Herman, guard Kadyn Proctor, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- What stands out here is the ridiculously low number of offensive snaps the Dolphins got, which was 39. That was exactly half the number of plays run by the Minnesota offense.
-- Jaylen Wright got the start at running back with De'Von Achane on IR with a torn ACL, but he quickly gave way to Ollie Gordon II, who ended up with a 22-12 snap advantage and clearly established himself as the current RB1 after rushing for exactly 100 yards.
-- For the first time this season, Kacmarek got more snaps at tight end than Greg Dulcich, with 24 compared to 20.
-- Veteran Jalen Tolbert was active for the second time, but he again barely was a factor on offense as he played only six snaps, two more than special teams specialist Ryan Miller. The Dolphins did use three wide receivers at the same time quite a bit, but this is where we point out that Malik Washington is more like a utility player on offense — a halfback/receiver, if you will — than a pure wide receiver.
-- The Dolphins used a sixth offensive lineman again, though this time it was only one snap for Caedan Wallace.
-- Four players were on the field for all of Miami's 78 defensive snaps: linebackers Jacob Rodriguez and Jordyn Brooks, Taaffe and Johnson.
-- This not surprisingly was a season/career high for the three rookies. The previous high for both Rodriguez and Johnson came in the season opener when both played all 68 snaps against the Las Vegas Raiders. Taaffe's previous high was 52 snaps against Kansas City. It was the second-highest total of Brooks' career, topped only by his 81 snaps for the Seattle Seahawks in a 33-13 victory against the Houston Texans in 2021, his second year in the NFL.
-- The Dolphins opened the game in the nickel and played most of the game with that five-DB alignment. JuJu Brents got 69 snaps at cornerback and Jason Marshall Jr. got 60.
-- Dante Trader Jr. again started at safety alongside Taaffe, but he left the game with a knee injury before returning, and Zayne Anderson wound up playing 29 snaps in Trader's place.
-- On the defensive line, what stood out was Josh Uche, who was very active, getting the most snaps on the edge with 55, five more than Chop Robinson, who also had his moments rushing quarterback Kyler Murray.
-- Practice squad elevations Rodney McGraw and Mazi Smith played 12 and nine defensive snaps, respectively, and each made a play or two, McGraw as a pass rusher and Smith getting penetration on a run that led to a tackle for loss.
-- Eight non-specialists saw action only on special teams — Seydou Traore, Andre Jones Jr., Jackson Woodard, Julius Wood, Jaylin Simpson, Jarrett Kingston, Reece Taylor, and newcomer Shaka Heyward.
-- Speaking of special teams, Traore again led the way with 23 snaps, followed by 18 fo r Miller, Wood and Heyward, who was signed off the Cincinnati Bengals practice squad last week.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to Dolphins-Vikings Matchup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins battled back late, but lost a 15-10 decision against to the Minnesota Vikings. Let’s overreact to the fourth straight loss to begin the Jeff Hafley era.
For the third time in four weeks, Miami was dominated in the third phase. The Dolphins gave up multiple big returns to Myles Price, and muffed three kicks of their own.
In a game that ultimately was decided by one score, having the worst special teams group in the league is going to keep moral victories from translating into material ones. The unit is sloppy, consistently out of place, and hasn’t shown any redeeming qualities outside of a nice Jaylen Wright return in Week 1.
An argument can be made that continuity will help this group over time, but Miami’s offense and defense don’t look nearly as out of place as its kicking game, despite also being made up of plenty of new players. This unit feels substantially worse than the rest of the team, and churning whatever you can of that portion of the roster seems like the best way forward.
The Dolphins' passing game was awful against Minnesota. Malik Willis finished 9-of-17 for 85 yards, and the team went 2-for-9 on third downs. Their biggest play, an out-of-structure touchdown from Malik Willis to Chris Bell, was wiped off the board due to the rookie stepping out of bounds before making the catch.
Outside of Malik Washington making a couple of nice plays in space and finishing with 67 yards, the receiving corps feels razor thin. Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr. missed out on crucial chemistry-building time this offseason, but have been vaulted into vital roles in the absence of Caleb Douglas.
Douglas’ return would not only re-adjust the pecking order, but also add some much-needed size and verticality to an aerial attack that seems insistent on pushing the ball deep down the field a few times a game.
Week over week, Miami is watching its rookies find increased comfortability, and several of them made major impacts on this game.
Jacob Rodriguez was all over the place, logging 18 total tackles, while Kadyn Proctor flashed on some big runs by Ollie Gordon. Michael Taaffe, Chris Johnson, Chris Bell, and Will Kacmarek all also had individual moments that showcased their potential.
Each have missed assignments, and the overwhelming amount of youth on this team is a major factor in Miami’s 0-4 record, but in a season where the team is looking for flashes, they’ve certainly gotten them so far.
Week One’s defensive woes seem like a distant memory compared to the most recent exposure we got against Minnesota. The team grabbed their first four sacks of the season , held Minnesota to zero touchdowns, and held their own on the backend for a majority of the game.
The front four had their best game of the season. Chop Robinson and Josh Uche were impactful, and the interior duo of Zach Sieler and Jordan Phillips appear to have settled in, with both making highlight plays.
The last couple of drives were rough, as Minnesota iced the game on the back of TJ Hockenson, but Jeff Hafley and Sean Duggan have this unit playing hard consistently, and their ascension has kept Miami in their last two games.
For as many individual high-points as there were in this game, there were just as many lows. For instance, following Miami’s lone touchdown drive, they allowed Minnesota to drain over eight minutes of clock, and after rallying to force a field goal, Jaylen Wright struggled to come up with a knuckling kick, knocking Miami’s offense back for their potential comeback drive.
This has been one of the major stories of this season. Penalties inside opposing territory, flags negating game-changing plays, and crucial clock and personnel gaffes late. These moments are to be expected of a young team, but the quantity and timing of them are becoming unacceptable. Whether this is simply the youth or a potential coaching problem is something that needs to be sorted out as soon as possible.

title: Dolphins Week 4 Instant Takeaways: So Close, Yet So Far
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins continue to be a tough out, but they still can't get that elusive first win under head coach Jeff Hafley.
In many ways, the Dolphins let one slip away against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium, dropping a 15-10 decision that moved their record to 0-4.
The Dolphins gave the undefeated Vikings all they could handle, though in fairness Minnesota is a pretty unimpressive 4-0 team on offense, but again mistakes and missed opportunities made the Dolphins come up short.
And that's the plight of a team overloaded with young and unproven players, though some of the culprits on this day were not rookies but rather young veterans with starting experience.
While running back Ollie Gordon II proved a bright spot with his work in the absence of De'Von Achane, the bottom line is the Dolphins once again failed offensively with a fourth consecutive game with fewer than 14 points.
The defense gave the team a chance to win until the end, but then couldn't get the stop needed to give the offense a final opportunity to pull out a late victory.
-- The Dolphins don't have to hear about not having any sacks on the season anymore and they took care of that issue right from the start, courtesy of Zach Sieler. By the time they were done, the Dolphins had four sacks, two by Sieler and one each for Josh Uche and Chop Robinson.
-- Robinson ended with a game-high three QB hits, including back-to-back pressures in the first half and a sack like we haven't seen from him before where it wasn't about his speed and get-off but rather about pushing back right tackle Brian O'Neill into the lap of Kyler Murray.
-- The legend of Jacob Rodriguez continues to grow, this time with a game-high 18 tackles, which is the highest total in the NFL this season. What was lacking from his game this time was a tackle for loss or an impact third-down play. In other words, his performance was good, but maybe it was overblown a bit if you were to believe the folks at FOX and the gushing they were doing.
-- For all the good work of the defense — and it was a good performance, albeit against a mediocre offense missing its best player (Justin Jefferson) — it failed to deliver in the clutch. Needing the ball to try to come back, the Dolphins defense gave up four first downs on each of Minnesota's final drives, the first of which ended in the field goal and the second ending with kneel-downs to end the game.
-- Meanwhile, the Dolphins went three-and-out the only time they had the ball in the fourth quarter, which led to a time of possession advantage for the Vikings in that fourth quarter of 14:00 to 1:00.
-- Covering quality tight ends is not easy for any defense, but the Dolphins must do better than letting T.J. Hockenson completely own the game down the stretch, including the game-sealing third-down reception where he could have scored but instead gave himself up at the 2-yard line to run out the clock.
-- This is a recurring theme, but one we should get used to when we're dealing with so many young players.
-- It also sure looked like the Dolphins couldn't catch a break from the officials the entire game on a day when there seemed to be blown calls or questionable calls all over the place.
-- There were three significant close calls that all went against the Dolphins in this one, the most notable the call that Chris Bell's got a piece of the sideline to nullify his 68-yard touchdown off a brilliant off-structure play by Malik Willis. There also was the replay-assisted decision to rule that the Minnesota player had tipped the ball and therefore the roughing-the-punter penalty that would have given the Dolphins a first down had to be erased. And lastly there was that run where Ollie Gordon II stumbled at the line, got up and raced down the field, only for the officials to rule he was touched before getting up when TV replays didn't clearly show that at all.
-- And we won't talk about the three holding penalties called on left tackle Patrick Paul, all on plays where similar circumstances didn't produce a flag. Let's just say the Dolphins got a flag-happy crew on this day.
-- Willis' final stats again won't look very good for him without telling the real story because he was under duress. But maybe the Dolphins can take some comfort in holding the Vikings to two sacks after they had at least four in each of their first three wins.
-- Back to Gordon, that was some impressive running by the second-year tailback, and it sure looked as though his success came up the middle or over the left side.
-- Malik Washington showed once again why he's the most reliable and dependable wide receiver on the team and his work after the catch was some kind of impressive.
-- We addressed this in our halftime observations, but yes the special teams were rough, but that often happens when you have a talent-defiicient roster and the players on the back end of that roster are those playing in the kicking game.
-- So now the Dolphins are 0-4 for the sixth time in franchise history, the first time since that 2019 season. This 0-4, though, continues to look nothing like the 0-4 of 2019 when they lost by 20 or more points each time.

title: One Thought on All 11 Vikings Offensive Starters One Month Into the 2026 Season
full_text:
The Vikings are a perfect 4-0 a quarter of the way through the NFL season , but it hasn't all been smooth sailing. While the defense and special teams units have pulled their weight and more, the Vikings' offense is still figuring things out.
Things looked a little crisper on offense last week against Miami, but there's still plenty of room to grow moving forward. Now that one month of action has provided a sufficient sample size, here are my thoughts on every Vikings offensive starter four games into the schedule .
The bad news is that Kyler Murray's start with the Vikings hasn't been especially pretty. He's 30th in QBR, 24th in completion percentage, and—we'll save you the time—bottom 10 in most other passing metrics too.
The good news, though, is that each game has been an improvement over the last. Murray has gone from 11 snaps and the ugliest interception human eyes have witnessed, to simply finishing the game against Tampa Bay, to looking somewhat decent against Miami. By Week 12, the Vikings should have a potential MVP at this rate.
Since Jordan Mason's Week 1 injury, Aaron Jones Sr. has been the sole source of the Vikings' offensive production for the most part. Ahead of the season, some writers—including this one—had written Jones off a bit as an aging back who had seen his production drop in three straight seasons.
While those things still remain true, he's actually single-handedly carried the load in the Minnesota backfield this season with 297 yards. He'll get a bit of a break after the bye when Mason returns, but Jones kept this offensive train from completely derailing.
Outside of a scorching hot Week 1 performance with eight catches for 92 yards and two scores, Justin Jefferson has logged just five catches since. He missed the majority of the past two games with injury and slogged through a Chicago monsoon in Week 2, so there's no reason for alarm.
The Vikings' best player should be back in action soon and has been the only bright spot in the receiver room thus far.
Jordan Addison is tracking to fall short of his incredible rookie season numbers for the third straight season, and it's getting hard to get a good read on him. He's got 11 catches for 163 yards this year, and barring a huge outburst the rest of the season, he will again post mediocre numbers for a player many believe to be one of the best WR2's in the NFL.
Obviously, quarterback issues from last year have dragged on into 2026, so Addison's modest production may come with a bit of an asterisk.
Head coach Kevin O'Connell can point to Jennings' work in the run game (h/t Bring Me The Sports ' Will Ragatz) all he wants, but it's hard to look at the big ticket free agent with just two catches and say that things haven't been disappointing.
Again, quarterback play hasn't done him any favors, but Jauan Jennings really needs a few big catches in the coming weeks to show some proof of concept here.
T.J. Hockenson leads all Vikings receivers in most every statistic after a monster 13-catch, 119-yard performance in Week 4. It appears that Murray has found a friend, and that should be welcome news for Hockenson, who took a pay cut and chopped a year off his deal to stay in Minnesota this season. One game does not make a season, though, and we'll see if his connection with Murray is real.
Christian Darrisaw's evaluation never really wavers season-to-season: when he's healthy (he's usually not), he's very good (elite even). The left tackle has yet to play a full season in his six-year career, and after suffering a concussion last week, that may be the case again in 2026.
It's unfortunate for a player who could and should be top-five at his position.
Donovan Jackson was playing some of his best ball before tearing his meniscus last Sunday. He had allowed just two pressures heading into the game, but he will now miss the remainder of the year in what could be a huge loss up front. We'll see what new starter Joe Huber has this week .
After a full summer of worry and panic about the non-center center, Blake Brandel has actually been mostly fine. His snaps have been steady for the most part, and his 76.2 pass-blocking grade with Pro Football Focus ranks fifth among centers. Good enough for me.
Will Fries definitely suffers from 'Kirk Cousins Syndrome': he's been a decent enough player, but his huge contract puts a big magnifying glass on his play. At the time of his signing, Fries was getting paid like a top-10 guard in the NFL. He hasn't been truly awful, but he's probably only played up to the level of maybe a top-30 guard instead, and that's hard to be content with given his deal.
Captain and fan-favorite Brian O'Neill is back with a new extension. He was playing well until Miami's Chop Robinson came to town in Week 4, notching eight pressures and a sack. While that didn't all fall on O'Neill's shoulders, let's hope that game was more of an anomaly than a sign of things to come.

title: The Case for Why Justin Jefferson Should Play vs. the Saints in Week 5
full_text:
The Vikings head to New Orleans this weekend to face the Saints for a Week 5 face-off . The two NFC teams are on opposite paths: the Vikings aim to enter their bye week 5-0, while the Saints hope to avoid a brutal 1-4 start to the season.
It's safe to say the stakes are high for both teams. The Vikings, though, are hoping their X-factor will be available to help them on Sunday: star receiver and St. Rose, LA native Justin Jefferson.
Jefferson, who injured his ankle early in Week 3 against the Buccaneers, was limited in practice to start the week after missing all of Week 4. This progress is certainly a welcome relief for Vikings fans everywhere, but it doesn’t guarantee he'll play this weekend.
Despite any potential concerns out there, here's why I think Jefferson should , and ultimately will, take the field in New Orleans on Sunday.
Let me start by making one thing abundantly clear: Jefferson and the Vikings should not risk putting him on the field if there are any serious concerns about his ankle.
The good news so far is that it seems unlikely. Jefferson hoped to return in the Week 3 game against the Buccaneers, where the injury first occurred, and stood on the sideline with his helmet on after spending time in the blue medical tent. Ultimately, he would head to the locker room for additional testing that determined he had sprained his left ankle.
The team played it safe in Week 4, holding Jefferson out of practices and last Sunday’s game against the Dolphins, but his limited participation in practice to start this week shows he’s making positive strides (h/t: Vikings).
If there were serious concerns about the stability of Jefferson's ankle, he likely wouldn't even be practicing on a limited basis. The 27-year-old wideout stated after practice that the ankle “feels good now” and that he hopes to “rock and roll” on Sunday (h/t: Bring Me The Sports ' Will Ragatz).
Justin Jefferson on his ankle injury against the Bucs: "Like 4 or 5 people tackled me on that play. Big Vita Vea, 300 pounds, he kinda landed on my leg a little bit." "It feels good now. Hopefully, Sunday, being able to rock and roll." pic.twitter.com/eodlc4aiqm
The Vikings' passing game has been less than stellar to start the 2026 season, and Jefferson has played fewer than 20 total snaps with new starting quarterback Kyler Murray after both have left games with injuries.
Jordan Addison was held out of Wednesday’s practice with a hamstring injury, and while he seems like he'll be good to play Sunday, there's no guarantee he’ll be at 100%. Jauan Jennings is next on the depth chart, but he has yet to prove himself reliable this season , with only two receptions for nine yards over three games.
Jefferson’s inclusion in the passing game opens opportunities that simply aren’t there otherwise for him and his fellow wideouts. The Vikings will also face a much tougher slate of opponents in the coming weeks.
After the Saints, they’ll head to their bye before hosting the Colts. Then things get challenging: the Vikings will play the Lions (twice), Bills, Packers, 49ers, Falcons, Panthers and  Patriots between Nov. 1 and Dec. 20.
If the Vikings’ passing offense is going to reach its full potential, Jefferson and Murray will need every possible rep to be at their best before the toughest stretch of the schedule. The Vikings are a very good team , but they need their offense in sync if they want to be true contenders.
If Jefferson is cleared to play on Sunday, I don’t see many things preventing him from suiting up in front of his hometown crowd.

title: 3 Biggest Vikings Concerns Heading Into Week 5 (OL Injuries Among Top Worries)
full_text:
Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season is in full swing , marking another opportunity for the 4-0 Minnesota Vikings to put their undefeated streak on the line. Their next challenge comes Sunday when the New Orleans Saints—who are coming off back-to-back losses—welcome the Vikings to Caesars Superdome, marking the Purple and Gold's final game before their Week 6 bye.
A perfect start to the year has left Minnesota fans with plenty to celebrate, but it would be absurd to think the Vikings are without issues. Head coach Kevin O'Connell and his coaching staff still have a long way to go to unlock the team's full potential , and they can take a step closer to accomplishing that by improving in key areas before it's too late.
That said, here are three of the biggest concerns surrounding the Vikings ahead of Sunday's afternoon contest.
The Vikings' win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 4 came at a price, as the offensive line lost two key contributors. Left guard Donovan Jackson tore his meniscus, likely ending his 2026 campaign , while left tackle Christian Darrisaw is currently in concussion protocol , and time will tell how quickly he clears the five-step process.
Being without any O-line starter would be a challenge, but missing both left-side star blockers could make it harder for the Vikings to move the ball on Sunday. According to Pro Football Focus , Darrisaw has the 14th-best pass-block grade (76.9) among 69 offensive tackles this season and has allowed pressure on 2.3% of offensive snaps compared to 3.8% in 2025.
As for Jackson, he's been among the Vikings' most consistent offensive linemen this season. Although he's been solid at opening run lanes like last year, he's made major improvements in pass protection, with his grade rising from 65.7 to 77.2 after allowing only two pressures across 100 passing downs.
Sunday is almost here, so the Vikings need to have a next-man-up mentality, regardless of how devastating the injury losses are. That said, Joe Huber and Ryan Van Demark will likely start in place of Jackson and Darrisaw, respectively, with Michael Jurgens' potential return adding more help to the interior .
It's safe to say that Aaron Jones Sr. has been one of the hard-working Vikings this season.
Despite this being Year 10 in the league, the veteran running back has been tasked with averaging a career-high 18 carries per game, which includes averaging 20 in the last three outings. It's great to see Jones thrive and occasionally spark the Vikings' inconsistent offense. But it's also fair to say that overworking a 31-year-old RB might not be the best idea for Minnesota's long-term aspirations.
Unfortunately, the team's less-than-ideal backup running back situation has left O'Connell & Co. with no choice but to use Jones as a bell-cow rusher.
With Jordan Mason still on injured reserve, the Vikings have used veteran DeeJay Dallas and rookie Demond Claiborne to support Jones with little success. Claiborne has been one of the most disappointing members of Minnesota's 2026 draft class , averaging just 2.2 yards on six carries. Meanwhile, Dallas has only seen three carries for 10 yards and has been detrimental in pass protection, as evidenced by his putrid 17.8 pass-block grade on PFF .
Former Saints RB Audric Estime was signed to the practice squad last week, but it remains to be seen if he's ready to face his former team. Assuming he isn't, Vikings fans can expect to see a lot of Jones against the Saints' run defense, which allows 147.8 rushing yards per game (30th) and 5.1 yards per carry (30th), at least until Claiborne and Dallas prove to be more than warm bodies.
Remember when Jauan Jennings was signed back in May? The Vikings were optimistic that the former 49ers playmaker could slot in as the No. 3 wide receiver behind Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, potentially giving the Purple and Gold one of the best wideout trios in the NFC, if not the entire league, on paper.
Fast-forward to now, and it's fair to wonder if the Vikings are dealing with some buyer's remorse .
If you haven't noticed Jennings on the field through the first quarter of the season, you likely aren't the only one. The Cowan, TN native looks rather pedestrian with only two catches for nine receiving yards on four targets.
The Vikings' quarterback room has a putrid 16.7 passer rating when targeting him, worse than if the ball were thrown into the ground every play (39.6). His 31.0 run-block grade is another example of his shortcomings , making it hard to feel optimistic about his outlook.
With Jefferson still recovering from an ankle injury and Addison missing Wednesday's practice with a hamstring issue (h/t Vikings), Minnesota might need Jennings to finally wake up this weekend.
The veteran receiver tallied five catches for 89 yards and a touchdown in his last visit to New Orleans in Week 2 of the 2026 season, offering hope that he can replicate that performance on Sunday afternoon.
Otherwise, the Vikings will need to rethink whether and how Jennings fits into their offensive plans going forward.

title: 3 Vikings Coaching Decisions I'd Make If I Were Kevin O'Connell vs. the Saints in Week 5
full_text:
It's Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season, and it brings plenty of potential changes for the Vikings to make in their quest to move to 5-0 ahead of their bye. The Vikings will take their talents down to New Orleans for a matchup with the Saints on Sunday, but they have a few things to take care of first .
After a rash of injuries and several roster moves over the last week, here's how I would handle the game plan if I were in head coach Kevin O'Connell's shoes in the Big Easy this weekend.
It's certainly not flashy, but starting the undrafted free agent from 2025 is probably the best path forward for the Vikings—at least for now. Joe Huber came in for the injured Donovan Jackson last week against Miami and should get the start at left guard this week against New Orleans after a decent performance.
After playing 71 snaps, O'Connell wasn't shy to praise his young lineman in the win.
"Joe’s a good young player that we’ve been really excited about since we first brought him on as an undrafted free agent last year,” said O’Connell. “He’s been able to be versatile to have a game-day role at three spots when called upon. It happened to be left guard yesterday. I thought he had some really good snaps."
Trading for a quality offensive lineman midseason is nearly impossible, and any free agent guard who has even looked at a football in the last year was scooped up by the Packers last week. Luckily, the Vikings have a bye after facing the Saints and can fully evaluate the position then. But if Huber again plays solidly this week, it would be tough to take him out of the lineup in favor of an outside hire.
Much was made about Kyler Murray's odd fit with Minnesota before he even took a snap. Before joining the Vikings, Murray spent 85% of his time in shotgun with the Cardinals , a stark contrast to O'Connell's much tamer 53% rate since becoming the head man in Minnesota (h/t NFL Next Gen Stats and ESPN ).
It shouldn't come as too much of a surprise, then, that Murray's best game so far was when O'Connell opted to operate out of shotgun 54 times in the win over Miami—his most since taking over in 2022.
The Vikings initially hoped to blend O'Connell's under-center preferences with Murray's comfort working out of the gun in some sort of a happy medium. It may already be time, though, that O'Connell just admits his new quarterback is clearly better with what he knows.
With the offense struggling, opportunities for growth and experimentation are dwindling, and O'Connell should probably put aside his ego and recognize that his preferred offense isn't what's best for the team right now.
The Vikings turned heads when they added Odell Beckham Jr. to the practice squad this week.
After getting released by the Giants without registering a catch, the Vikings were quick to make the call to reunite Beckham with his former offensive coordinator from their L.A. Rams days. O'Connell has basically already admitted that Beckham could be elevated for Sunday's game, saying the wideout has familiarity with the scheme.
So, yeah, sure, let's see what the old guy's got left.
Expectations should be low, but it's not like the bottom of the wide receiver depth chart is producing much either. Jauan Jennings, Tai Felton and Myles Price have combined for just three catches through four games, so the bar isn't especially high to clear. If Beckham can get some meaningful production from the WR4 spot, this odd, fun, weird signing will look good in the eyes of many.
If not, well, it drew a few more eyes to the team for a couple of weeks.

title: Vikings Week 5 Mailbag: Murray-O'Connell Fit, OL Help, Odell Beckham Jr.'s Potential Impact & More
full_text:
Welcome to the Week 5 Vikings On SI mailbag!
I once again took to X to see what was on your minds heading into Sunday's showdown with the Saints in the Big Easy.  Questions abound about the 4-0 Vikes, specifically around the offensive side of the ball. Plus, a late addition diving into how the Odell Beckham Jr. signing may impact the team’s current wide receiver room.
To submit your questions, reach out to Jason Harmon on X .
It’s on the table, but his blocking ability may be too important after the loss of tight end Josh Oliver for the season. Jennings has a disappointing stat line of only two receptions for nine yards through three games this season. Will 33-year-old Beckham be a better option to elevate the passing game?
We’ll have to see, but it’s admittedly a long shot given his lack of production in recent seasons.
The Vikings need to sort out the left side of their offensive line, so it’s possible O’Connell still has enough faith in OBJ after their 2021 Super Bowl run with the Rams to flip Jennings for capital. Trading Jennings would lead to a $4.5 million dead cap hit and $5.03 million in total cap savings for the Vikings, per OverTheCap .
There are a number of routes the team can take here. The first is to simply play Joe Huber at left guard and have Ryan Van Denmark fill in at left tackle while Christian Darrisaw is out. The second is to use current center Blake Brandel’s versatility and experience across the line by moving him to the vacant guard spot. This would require the team to fill the center position via trade, free agency, or with Michael Jurgens— who has entered his 21-day open window for practice—coming off the injured reserve.
I can’t imagine new general manager Nolan Teasley paying a premium for temporary help along the offensive line, given how long their laundry list of needs is set to be this offseason, but if he can somehow acquire a long-term starting center that frees Brandel up to play guard, I’d be open to it.
Anyone who knows me would know I’d never pass up an opportunity to discuss Will Reichard. While the “Will the Thrill” memes, edits, and jokes have been abundant, what he is doing is genuinely impressive. He is a perfect 12-for-12 to start the year and has made 31 straight field goals going back to last season. Reichard is also tied for the league lead in scoring, with 42 points scored.
That is more than the 38 total points scored by the entire Vikings’ offense through four games.
At his current pace, he would set the record for field goals made in a season . If the Vikings keep leaning into a simplified offense, Reichard may remain the team's strongest scoring force.
Will Reichard is currently on a 17-game pace of 51 successful field goals and 178.5 total points scored. Both of which would be NFL kicking records. pic.twitter.com/I7a3GlUENS
I would like to see the trends we saw in the second half continue. Get Kyler comfortable in the shotgun formation; start getting him in motion on rollouts and play action, live to fight another down.
My biggest worry is the left side of the offensive line and how an already jumpy OL will react in a loud, hostile environment. Many of the Vikings' offensive woes last week came from procedural penalties, and they simply cannot allow that to happen again this weekend. It’s yet to be seen whether Justin Jefferson will play in his hometown on Sunday, but he is obviously the biggest X-factor in how explosive the passing game could be.
Here’s where things get complicated: Murray and O’Connell looked to have found a decent middle ground in training camp. We saw a ton of shotgun and pistol formations with simple and quick reads. This opened the door to the occasional explosive play, where Murray often hit his weapons deep for touchdowns. Then, it looked like O’Connell reverted to his traditional offensive scheming once the season started.
I worry that there was a similar pattern with J.J. McCarthy in 2025; he looked much better in training camp because there were significant schematic differences between what he was asked to do there and in season. O’Connell eventually shifted the offense towards McCarthy’s skill set after the team was already eliminated from playoff contention. The late-game changes O’Connell made this Sunday give me hope that he won’t wait until it's too late this season.
As for acquiring a quarterback, it is very hard to find a new starter midseason, and the NFL’s QB injury woes make it even more complicated. I can’t see Vegas moving on from Kirk Cousins, given how well their offense has performed to start the year (h/t:NFL).
KIRK COUSINS MAGIC FOR THE TOUCHDOWN! @KCvsLV on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ADaylXSjLZ
If a winless team decides to torch their roster, maybe you make a call.
To be fair, six and a half decades of generational disappointment and football-related pain will do that to you, especially if you’re a fan of multiple Minnesota professional teams. This season has admittedly had a negative vibe around a 4-0 squad, but the reasoning makes sense.
I think it’s entirely possible to acknowledge the excitement of an undefeated start while voicing real concerns about whether the team's winning style is sustainable. On the bright side, the offense can only improve from here.

title: What's Changed (and What Hasn't) About the Vikings' Practice Squad 1 Month Into NFL Season
full_text:
The Vikings have made several adjustments to the team's roster since the initial 53-man roster and practice squad were announced over a month ago. General manager Nolan Teasley and head coach Kevin O'Connell's personnel changes have helped lift the Vikings to a 4-0 record ahead of a Week 5 tilt against the Saints.
One of the most interesting parts of Minnesota's roster moves is how much they've impacted the practice squad. It seems like every week players are being released, signed, promoted or relegated to that unit to keep players available.
Having talent on the practice squad gives the Vikings depth at important positions heading into a week with significant injuries or potentially pushes players who are struggling to be their absolute best to keep their role on game day.
Taking all of the changes from September and into October into account, let's take a look at the original Vikings practice squad compared to the unit as it is today.
Armstead, Briscoe, Byrd, Grandy, Kamara, Leigh, Nelson, Ritzie and Thomas are the nine players who are still on the practice squad from the start of September. Those players are still available to be elevated to the 53-man roster whenever they are needed and can continue to develop in the meantime. Each practice squad member has three elevations per season.
Meanwhile, Gerhardt, Gray, Hailassie, Jones, Phillips, Rudolph and Stewart are the former practice squad players who Minnesota has moved on from. The following three players signed with new teams, while the rest are free agents.
A few players have spent time on the practice squad before being elevated to the 53-man roster. Kyle Van Noy spent the first three weeks of the regular season on the squad before signing to the active roster in Week 4. Minnesota has also used the practice squad to ease the transition for punters Johnny Hekker and Brett Thorson to make sure one of them is available for each game.
Former Saints running back Audric Estime was also recently added, providing some much-needed depth in a backfield that's been lacking since Jordan Mason landed on injured reserve .
Of course, the most notable name on the current practice squad is wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. He shouldn't take long to make his regular-season debut since Jauan Jennings and Tai Felton have essentially been invisible. Perhaps the Vikings will look to add more WRs if they quickly reach the same conclusion that the Giants did.
Overall, the Vikings have been using the practice squad well as a pipeline to the 53-man roster while keeping young talent there to develop.  Teasley should keep his foot on the gas and continue to make moves that keep the practice squad in a position to effectively help the Vikings in moments of need.

title: Why Demond Claiborne Has Already Been the Biggest Letdown of Vikings' 2026 Draft Class
full_text:
Demond Claiborne might have only been a sixth-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, but that didn't stop him from becoming a Vikings fan favorite throughout the summer .
In three preseason games for the Vikings, Claiborne carried the ball 28 times for 73 yards and caught one pass for seven yards. The plan seemed to be to let him continue developing behind Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason and potentially have him become an offensive contributor.
As will happen in the NFL, those plans fell through quickly. Mason suffered a thumb injury that required surgery and was placed on injured reserve. That meant one of Minnesota's running backs would need to step up and assume a bigger role.
Unfortunately, the preseason hype around his potential hasn't translated into regular-season success for Claiborne, who's solidifying himself as the Vikings' most disappointing 2026 draft pick with each passing game.
The Vikings have been trying to find an offensive spark at running back to help out Jones, who has been playing through a knee injury. Instead, the backups haven't been able to rise to the occasion, and it has forced Jones into a bell-cow role .
Meanwhile, Claiborne has played 23 offensive snaps in Minnesota's first four games this season. He has turned that into seven touches for 15 yards while averaging 2.2 yards per rushing attempt. That type of production will not earn him a bigger role, especially when he isn't contributing much as a blocker, either.
The disappointment around Claiborne stems more from the hype that was created around him heading into the season than from the investment that the Vikings made in him. Typically, a sixth-round pick doesn't come with lofty expectations, but that wasn't the case here.
The training camp hype around Claiborne's speed and potential reached astronomical levels. The official Vikings website, bloggers, media sites, and just about anyone who covers Minnesota sports bought into the excitement and got pumped to see what he could bring to the Purple and Gold's backfield.
Instead, the quiet preseason was followed by a struggling regular season performance that is putting the Vikings' RB1 into a rough situation that could have been avoided if Claiborne had shown some of the potential that the rookie running back showed during practices.
The scariest part is that the Vikings were considering parting ways with Jones to save salary cap space this offseason. If he hadn't taken a massive pay cut to stay, Mason's injury would have forced Minnesota into a committee that included Claiborne and DeeJay Dallas.
Thankfully, the 4-0 Vikings were not put in that situation, and they can still lean on Jones. Otherwise, Minnesota's offense could look even more inept than it already does.
Hopefully, Claiborne has had a big enough taste of NFL action to know where he needs to take his game next. If he doesn't, the Vikings might have to turn the page and explore other backup RB options .

title: Coller: Why the Vikings Don't Deserve the 'Fraud' Label Despite Concerns at 4-0
full_text:
The Vikings’ offense has been an endless point of discussion as the analysis world calls them a fraudulent 4-0 team.
If you talk about some of the reasons for the struggling offense, does that make you an apologist? A homer? Does it mean you have to tattoo Viktor Viking’s image on your calf?
When we talk about teams as being “frauds,” it usually means that they have lucked into their success and there’s no chance that it continues. There have been some unsustainable elements of the Vikings’ 4-0 start, like the fact that they have had two long touchdowns against them called back, or that Caleb Williams pulled his hamstring just as he was about to run into the end zone, and then the Vikings blocked a field goal.
Quarterbacks pulling hamstrings and opponents having 60-yard TDs taken off the scoreboard are not really a model for winning.
But there are a lot of things that we can project forward that are sustainable. One of them is the Vikings’ defense smothering opponents’ quarterbacks. Since Flores took over in 2023, the defense has ranked 15th, 12th, sixth and third (2026) in yards per pass attempt allowed and has been in the top 10 in points allowed for three straight seasons.
This year's Vikings could very well be the best version of Flores's defense. Josh Metellus said last week that this offseason, the defense started well ahead of previous years in the install phase because of how many players have been with Flores for multiple years. It shows the players’ confidence in the scheme and chemistry with each other.
It’s also showing in the development of players who flashed before and now are playing with consistency.
A dominant defense alone can put a team in the playoffs. Last year, the Texans were only 13th in points and 18th in yards on offense but went 12-5 behind the No. 2 defense in the NFL. The Denver Broncos came within an injured Bo Nix's ankle of the Super Bowl with the 14th-best offense in points and No. 3 in points allowed. Philadelphia made the postseason as the fifth-ranked defense and 19th-ranked offense in scoring.
Certainly, you would prefer to be the Seahawks, who ranked third in points for and first in points against, but the point is that when folks say that a team is a fraud for winning with defense, well, there are a lot of examples of recent teams doing it. Maybe if this was five years ago, when scoring was going crazy in the NFL, that might not be the case, but this year teams are averaging 332 yards per game, down from 354 in 2020.
The other thing about sustainability is that the Vikings have done some stuff to win games that doesn’t get much praise because it has looked so gnarly. They are No. 7 in offensive turnover percentage. They are 15th in percentage of drives producing points (yes, most of them are field goals). They are 14th in time of possession.
And these things are happening despite the offense struggling mightily.
If we are trying to project forward, the play-it-safe football style that Kevin O’Connell has adopted has been working for a while. The Vikings are winners of their last nine games and almost all of them have looked like this year's first few. No beauty contests in the lot.
Now, nobody believes they can be a serious contender with the 32nd-ranked offense. That’s almost impossible. But there’s a lot that has happened that seems to be getting swept away in the desire to identify the team that’s most likely to fall apart.
Kyler Murray missed nearly two games. Justin Jefferson has missed both the games that Murray played. Christian Darrisaw and Donovan Jackson got hurt. Jordan Mason has been out since Week 1.
That’s a ton of talent that has been sidelined. If the Vikings were 100% healthy and ranked at the bottom of the NFL in passing yards, it would be time to sound the alarms. It’s not really apples to apples to compare them to other teams.
The point isn’t that everything is fine. They have been dreadful to watch on offense so far. Rather, it’s that the four wins weren’t completely random, lucky nonsense. The next part of the schedule will tell us a lot more about this team.
In the second half against Miami, Murray found a groove and hit 16-of-18 passes. If he gets comfortable, the offense gets adapted to him, Mason returns, Jefferson comes back and the O-line patchworks for injuries, the Vikings can find themselves going forward.
The hardest thing to admit when doing analysis is that we really don’t have a big enough sample size yet, especially with a team like this.

title: Vikings' Odell Beckham Jr. Signing Raises More Questions Than Answers
full_text:
Just over a week after the J.J. McCarthy trade, the Vikings had another surprise move in store as Week 5 began. On Wednesday morning, the Vikings added a big name by signing veteran wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. to the practice squad , according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.
BREAKING: Odell Beckham Jr. is signing with the #Vikings , per sources. pic.twitter.com/30XQwSTBvi
The addition comes after an ankle injury to Justin Jefferson and some lackluster play from the rest of the receiver room.
Beckham spent this summer and the first few games of the season with the Giants before getting released in what ended up being a messy separation. He left his second stint with New York without recording a reception and had just nine catches in 2024 with Miami.
After starting his career with three-straight 1000-yard seasons, the 33-year-old Beckham hasn't notched one since 2019, and injuries have largely derailed his promising career. So what's the deal here?
The Vikings' receiving corps has looked shaky behind Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, but does a receiver who hasn't been productive for a few years now really add anything?
Beckham certainly has an impressive resume and even connections with head coach Kevin O'Connell, so let's break down what his signing means and what type of role he could carve out.
First things first. Jefferson's injury has always been considered day-to-day, and there's little reason to think that it's changed in that sense. The ex-Giant's arrival, however, does let the Vikings give Jefferson more time to heal if they want to rest him against the Saints, since the bye week follows immediately.
Still, Beckham's addition likely has more to do with the less-than-impressive performances from the rest of the Vikings' receivers.
The Vikings signed Jauan Jennings earlier this year to be their WR3 in hopes of rounding out what could have been one of the best trios in the league. With just two catches this season, though, it's clear his addition hasn't provided the type of production fans hoped for after Jennings put up over 1,500 yards over the last two seasons with San Francisco.
Behind Jennings, Tai Felton and Myles Price have failed to carve out much of a role either, and the pair have combined for just three catches. For perspective, DeeJay Dallas, a backup running back added at the buzzer, has more yards and catches than Jennings, Price, or Felton. Not great.
Adding Beckham, who does have some familiarity with O'Connell from their time with the Rams, gives the Vikings another option as the fourth or fifth guy. It's doubtful he'll ascend enough to replace Jennings, but O'Connell may look for a more reliable route runner ahead of Felton or Price despite the obvious physical limitations.
Beckham hasn't been able to produce at a high level for several years now, but Minnesota clearly thinks it can squeeze whatever juice he has left out of his game in a reserve role.
Ultimately, signing a veteran with a scheme fit for a veteran minimum feels like a harmless move. There's little reason to expect Beckham to come in and be a difference-maker, but if it means getting a bit more production out of the bottom of the receiver depth chart, it's hard to hate the signing.
This will either be a fun redemption, or Beckham may be looking for another new home by November.

title: Making Sense of the Vikings' Latest Flurry of Roster Moves Heading Into Week 5
full_text:
It's safe to say that the Vikings had a busy Tuesday, making multiple roster moves as the Purple and Gold prepare for a Week 5 showdown against the Saints in New Orleans.
In total, six players were on the move as the Vikings try to manage players coming both on and off injured reserve, among other things. One big loss and the return of a friendly face headlined some of the action, so let's break down a busy day of transactions for Nolan Teasley and company.
The #Vikings have announced the following roster moves - Placed G Donovan Jackson on IR - Signed T Tristan Leigh to the practice squad - Released CB Natrone Brooks, P Johnny Hekker and RB Devin Neal from the practice squad - Waived CB Tyreek Chappell from IR
This one stings, as Donovan Jackson was arguably playing like the Vikings' best offensive lineman through three weeks. Leading up to Sunday's game, Jackson had allowed just two pressures and zero sacks , according to Pro Football Focus . His season is now over with a torn meniscus, and all eyes now turn to backup guard Joe Huber, who took over against Miami when Jackson went down.
Huber has been an ascending player behind the scenes, and while he's not on the level of the first-rounder Jackson, he could be a good enough stopgap for the remainder of 2026. The Vikings could also play around with a few different combinations over the Week 6 bye, but there's no question this team just got worse with Jackson's untimely injury.
After getting signed as an undrafted free agent out of Clemson, Tristan Leigh was waived by the Vikings ahead of the season. He played both left and right tackle during the preseason, and Minnesota apparently saw enough to bring him back to the practice squad for his "Electric Boogaloo" sequel.
The Vikings' practice squad has seen non-stop turnover since the start of the season, and it's hard to say whether Leigh's return will last six months or six days. Still, there's never enough offensive line depth, and he has familiarity with the scheme.
The Vikings released three players from the practice squad:
Hekker's release surely means rookie punter Brett Thorson is on the mend and will be ready to go for New Orleans. That, or Hekker's abysmal display on Sunday, was enough for the Vikings to trust someone else with the all-important duty of holding for Will Reichard. Either way, Hekker's days in purple are over.
Brooks, meanwhile, just learned his coaches' names after spending only five days on the practice squad before getting released again.
In a similar vein, Neal was added to boost an underwhelming running back room, but was also cast aside after just a few days with the team. General manager Nolan Teasley is bouncing running backs around more than a beach ball at a Nickelback concert. After signing and then cutting Jerome Ford, Jaret Patterson and now Neal, it's hard to understand what his plans are with any of these additions. Luckily, Jordan Mason is just one week and then a bye away from his return.
The Vikings made a move with Tyreek—no, not that one—officially waiving Chappell after placing the young corner on injured reserve back in August. The undrafted free agent out of Texas A&M will look to find a new home in 2027.

title: Patriots Coaches Remember 2001 Super Bowl Team Ahead of 25th Anniversary Celebration
full_text:
FOXBORO — Ahead of the New England Patriots ' Week 5 home game against the Las Vegas Raiders, a ceremony for the team's first Super Bowl championship will take place.
Celebrating the 25th anniversary of the now-iconic 2001 team, plus giving Adam Vinatieri his Pro Football Hall of Fame ring at halftime and wearing the Pat Patriot red throwback uniforms, is a love letter to the region as they dip themselves into a pool of nostalgia.
Nobody on this current Patriots team was in the league when that team hoisted the Lombardi Trophy following a 20-17 upset of the St. Louis Rams. Some of them, like Kevin Byard, vaguely remember that team as a young kid, seeing Tom Brady take over for the injured Drew Bledsoe and lead his team through the playoffs.
Andy Borregales grew up admiring Vinatieri and his pressure-packed kicks , but was too young to ever cross paths with him on the football field. Sure, Hunter Henry and Marcus Jones played for Bill Belichick during their Patriots careers, but they were still more than a decade away from entering the NFL.
But they still aren't experts. So far, Mike Vrabel has yet to show any of his old highlights to his current players.
"I was eight years old, so I wasn't fully just like into NFL football just yet," Byard said about his memories of that 2001 season. "I've been a football historian ever since I was young. I was watching NFL Films, NFL Network, stuff like that. So I've definitely been tapped in."
So it's up to the New England coaching staff to sit around and look back on that first championship team. Vrabel, a star linebacker that recorded three sacks and nine pass breakups that season after signing as a free agent, has his photo up right outside the Patriots locker room. Offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels was a first-time NFL coach during that 2001 season, working as a personnel assistant.
Those two have lasting legacies in New England. Vrabel got into the face of Kurt Warner as Rams quarterback — the leader of the "Greatest Show on Turf" — threw a pick-six to Ty Law. McDaniels would eventually become the team's offensive coordinator three different times.
"I'll see those guys on Saturday. I'll see those guys for a quick dinner," Vrabel said Wednesday. "But it's exciting that there are so many guys that want to come back, and it was a special year for everybody involved."
It's making McDaniels feel a bit old as he looks back on his long coaching tenure.
"Boy I was young, and I just think that team embodied all the right things," McDaniels said. "Kind of fought through some early season adversity with the Drew situation and in the injury, and had a lot of new players getting used to each other and familiar with one another, and how to play together. ... 5-5 after 10 games, and then, as happens often in this league, kind of figure out how we had to win.
"...Just super fond memories for me to start my career in the NFL, just watching that happen and being a little fly on the wall and seeing how it operate and how those guys ended up buying into the way we had to win. And then watching them complete the mission down in New Orleans was really cool."
The team is set to have a number of alumni return to Foxboro for the game . On Friday, Matt Chatham, Bobby Hamilton, Marty Moore, Otis Smith and offensive line coach Dante Scarnecchia are taking part in a youth football clinic. The Patriots social team posted an old video of the team celebrating the AFC Divisional game, the Tuck Rule game in the snow against the Raiders, in preparation.
It's becoming a big thing this week at Gillette Stadium.
Other coaches on staff weren't in New England when the Patriots ended up winning the game. Special teams coordinator Jeremy Springer grew up playing quarterback and as a Dallas Cowboys fan, so he wasn't really pulling for the underdog Patriots in that game.
"It was a hell of a game, and I do remember watching it and it was fun to watch," Springer said. "And that kind of started the reign of the wins and me hating the Patriots at the time."
Others, who have extensive coaching backgrounds in New England, appreciate what the Patriots have established in the region. But Doug Marrone has fonder memories of a different era.
"I've always had a great deal of respect," offensive line coach Doug Marrone , who has experience coaching at Coast Guard, Northeastern and Boston College, said — going on to share personal memories about Patriots Hall of Fame lineman John Hannah. "We've studied New England in almost every place where I've been. Respect and acknowledging how hard it is to do what they did, having been in this profession is probably the thing that sticks with me the most."
There was an enduring message for the young McDaniels to learn from that Patriots team, and it's one he wants to carry over into his coaching philosophy 25 years later.
"There's a way to win and everybody can't do it the same way," he said. "I think if you're not too proud to acknowledge what your strengths and weaknesses are, you can figure that out eventually. ... That was a great example of a team that really understand what the phrase complementary football meant."

title: Patriots Get Fantastic News on A.J. Brown's Health
full_text:
FOXBORO — It's been a long few weeks for the New England Patriots without their top wide receiver, but the return of A.J. Brown could be on the immediate horizo n.
Brown, who suffered a high-ankle sprain in the team's Week 1 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, was spotted in the Patriots locker room for the second-straight day on Thursday. Brown walked into the locker room with cleats on with no apparent limp, and had a slight tape job on his right ankle.
The 29-year-old appeared to be in good spirits at his locker, chatting with Drake Maye and Mack Hollins as he untied his cleats . He also took time to chat with some reporters as the rest of his teammates headed out to practice.
That alone, Brown's energy and lack of limp, should be a good sign for Brown as he plans to be activated off of injured reserve. After being placed on IR after the season opener , the Patriots were set to have Brown miss at least four games.
Reports also mentioned that he could end up missing six games, but based on how Brown is looking, his timetable could end up being on the shorter end of that.
A.J. Brown just walked into the locker room with cleats on. Once again, no limp. Had a small tape job on his right ankle.
Brown still has to miss the Patriots' Week 5 battle against the Las Vegas Raiders, and the team is only focused on that game right now.
"He won't be out there today, I can promise you that because he's not eligible," Mike Vrabel said Wednesday. "I can only speak to what I know for today."
The Patriots receivers getting banged up in recent weeks only makes this potential return that much bigger. Mack Hollins, who immediately stepped up after Brown's injury in Seattle, suffered a calf injury in Week 4 and has yet to practice this week.
Once both those guys are healthy, this group can finally attack the season like they did during the kickoff game. Before Brown got hurt, the Patriots looked like they were on their way to beat the Seahawks. Instead, Maye threw three interceptions in the fourth quarter post-injury and left the Patriots in a 0-1 hole.
"Excited to get A.J. back here in a little bit, and hopefully Mack can get back here as soon as possible," Efton Chism III said this week. "We love our room, we love our team."
Chism has stepped up without Brown on the field, a good sign for the depth that this wide receiver possesses. But getting the WR1 back in the fold — where a budding chemistry with Maye was built in traning camp — can help unlock a Patriots offense that's had a bit of trouble at times this season.

title: Patriots Safety Duo Getting More Comfortable Each Week
full_text:
FOXBORO — On Wednesday, both of the New England Patriots ' starting safeties spoke to reporters at their lockers. They spoke about carrying over confidence from game to game, preparing for the Las Vegas Raiders offense they'll be facing on Sunday and clinching the win last week with an interception.
But for Kevin Byard and Craig Woodson, both of them have begun to form a deep bond on the field as they man the last line of the Patriots' defensive backfield. Through three games together, they've combined for 19 tackles, three pass breakups and Woodson's interception put the 29-26 win in Buffalo on ice .
Despite Woodson missing one game with a shoulder injury, he's starting to get more and more comfortable playing alongside the veteran Byard — and vice versa.
"We definitely have chemistry," Woodson told Patriots On SI. "I think for us, we talk all the time and we see a lot of things the same, so I think it makes us play faster."
Woodson shined as a rookie a year ago , and now he's being given an otherworldly mentor in Byard, who led the NFL in interceptions a season ago. Byard, a captain in his first season with New England, has continued to earn the respect of his young counterpart.
And that feeling is mutual. Getting Woodson back only helped a Patriots defense that started the year off strong. That was evident in how the team responded from their Week 3 drubbing in Jacksonville.
"It was awesome," Byard said. "Obviously Craig is another player that we trust on that can go out there and make plays. I think for what we both bring, just being versatile as far as our disguise and different things that we can do. ... It was good to have him back for sure."
The Raiders lean on their tight ends a lot. Both Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer have been big parts of how they've gotten off to a 3-1 start this season, and having bigger bodies on the field could put some additional pressure on the safeties. It's helped Kirk Cousins soldify himself back as a starting quarterback and have the Raiders thickly in the AFC conversaton four weeks in.
"I can't say enough about them," Mike Vrabel said Wednesday. "Really, Brock is a receiver. That's impressive — what he does at his size, the speed, the route craft, and being able to catch at the catch point. He's like a big slot receiver. He has downfield speed, he runs outward breaking routes, he runs routes like a receiver, but then also he's got the ability to double guys up inside.
"I think that Mike has really turned into a complete tight end, and everything that I think people that looked at him coming out of the draft envisioned."
How are both Woodson and Byard embracing that challenging? Head on.
"You kind of have to be good with your keys, read run/pass," Woodson said. "I think we'll get a plan together, get going and stick to that."
"We've done a good job up until this point, but this is going to be probably the biggest challenge up to this point," Byard said.

title: Why Patriots WR Efton Chism Isn't Satisfied With Breakout Performance
full_text:
FOXBORO — Efton Chism III was the talk of New England last weekend. The second-year wide receiver made two impressive catches in the Patriots' 29-26 win against the Buffalo Bills, the second one being a one-handed, game-winning touchdown .
Now Chism, who was on the receiving end of a large media scrum in front of his locker before Wednesday's practice, wants to build on what he put on the field last game in Western New York.
"For me, it’s just reset," Chism said. "The good, the bad, whatever it is, it’s getting back to my work and our work as a team. Try to stack another one."
After A.J. Brown got hurt in the season opener, it opened the door for Mack Hollins to get more snaps. Hollins became the Patriots' top target until a calf injury forced him out of the Week 4 win. That's why Chism was on the field for his touchdown, and why if Hollins isn't able to play against the Las Vegas Raiders this week , the 24-year-old might end up with a larger workload.
"You never know when you're gonna get those opportunites," Chism said. "Excited to get A.J. back here in a little bit, and hopefully Mack can get back here as soon as possible. We love our room, we love our team."
Chism has shown that his hands — whether he's using both of them or just one — are solid and he's starting to build that chemistry with Drake Maye as the year progress. Right now, he's tallying four receptions for 41 yards and that one touchdown in a reserve role. That could easily change in the next few games .
Above Chism on the depth chart is Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Kyle Williams — though it appears Chism has surpassed Williams in terms of snaps played. While Williams ' speed is a nice addition to the offense, there really isn't a part of the offense that easily lends itself to getting the ball into his hands.
We've now seen how Chism can perform under pressure, and it will only allow him to get on the field more. Hollins is working towards getting back on the field for Week 5, though he didn't participate in the Patriots ' first practice.
Chism's teammates have seen his process and if his output in Buffalo didn't impress you, maybe the quotes from his quarterback will.
"Yeah, it's been awesome. Seeing Chiz just come in and be the same guy," Maye said. "He's been doing a lot of the little things that I think were just showing up.
"He comes in every day, enjoys trying to see my side of things, asks questions and tries to get on the same page, and that's what ends up happening. You start seeing the results."
