title: 6 Winners, 5 Losers From the Commanders’ First Four Games
full_text:
The Washington Commanders are four games into the season, which doesn't give us enough time to decide what this team ultimately will be, but it's certainly enough to start figuring out where some of those preseason expectations were right and where they weren't. Washington sits at 1-3 after its loss to the Indianapolis Colts , and a month of actual football has given us more than just wins and losses to judge. Roles have changed, young players have been asked to grow up quickly, and some position groups that were supposed to help carry this team haven't done nearly enough. With that in mind, here are six winners and five losers from the Commanders' first four games.
Sonny Styles Washington clearly had high expectations for Styles when they used the No. 7 pick on him, but there is still a difference between drafting someone that high and immediately asking him to become a major part of an NFL defense. Styles hasn't needed much time . Through four games, he has 20 tackles, a sack, an interception, and a forced fumble, with his best performance coming against Seattle when he finished with five tackles, two passes defended, an interception, and a forced fumble. He has already played every defensive snap in multiple games, which may say more about how Washington views him than any individual statistic does. The rookie treatment is basically over at this point. Styles is being asked to play like someone Washington expects to be around for a long time, and so far he has looked ready for it.
Sonny Styles has been a PROBLEM for some of the NFL’s most dangerous RB’s. Styles has recorded 3 STOPS against both Jonathan Taylor and Saquon Barkley. The Commanders rookie LB is already one of the BEST run-stoppers in the NFL 😳😈 pic.twitter.com/qWDO9mzRLZ
Amik Robertson Robertson was brought in to give Washington another experienced option in a secondary that had plenty of moving parts coming into the season. Four games later, he has done more than simply give the Commanders another option. He has made it difficult to take him off the field. Robertson has 26 tackles through four games and has consistently found himself around the football, including four passes defended and a forced fumble against Seattle before following that with a team-high nine tackles against Indianapolis. The numbers are nice, but the biggest thing with Robertson continues to be how hard he plays regardless of what is happening around him. Washington has had its share of problems in the secondary, but figuring out whether Robertson should be on the field hasn't been one of them. Josh Conerly Jr. Young offensive tackles are going to have rough moments, and Josh Conerly Jr. has certainly had some of his own, but the fact that Washington's right tackle position hasn't become a weekly conversation is probably a pretty good sign. Conerly was handed the job immediately, struggled as a rookie last season, and has taken a step forward in Year 2 , earning a 70.1 pass-blocking grade from PFF through four games while allowing nine pressures over 169 pass-blocking snaps. There is obviously plenty for him to clean up, and nobody should be declaring the position solved after a month, but that's not really the point. Washington's offensive line has already dealt with injuries, different combinations, and plenty of problems elsewhere. Conerly has stepped into one of the hardest positions for a young player to handle and hasn't given the Commanders a reason to start looking for another answer. That's a win. Antonio Williams Williams was one of the better stories coming out of training camp, but we've seen plenty of players have good summers and disappear once the regular season starts. Williams hasn't. He has 12 catches for 124 yards and a touchdown through four games, while his role has grown as Washington has needed more from the receiver room. He played 37% of the offensive snaps in Week 1, 49% in Week 2, and then jumped to 69% against Indianapolis with Terry McLaurin unavailable. That last part matters. Williams isn't just getting developmental snaps anymore because Washington likes what it sees from a young receiver. Injuries have created a need for somebody else to become dependable, and Williams is starting to become one of those guys.
Antonio Williams all routes from his NFL debut 4/64/1 on just 10 routes… GET HIM ON THE FIELD MORE! pic.twitter.com/F9mfhB8yc6
Odafe Oweh Washington didn't add Odafe Oweh just to fill out the edge rotation . It needed somebody capable of creating problems for opposing quarterbacks, and we're starting to see exactly what that looks like. His pressure against Seattle helped create Kain Medrano's pick-six, and against Indianapolis he decided to handle everything himself. Oweh sacked Daniel Jones on the Colts' second offensive play , knocked the ball loose, and recovered it at the Indianapolis 21. It's hard to create a better defensive snap than that. There have been stretches where Washington's pass rush hasn't gotten home enough, but Oweh has consistently looked like one of the players capable of changing a possession when he does. That's exactly what the Commanders needed when they rebuilt the position this offseason. Marcus Mariota Nobody wanted Washington to find out this early whether signing an experienced backup quarterback was worth it, but Jayden Daniels' elbow injury made that question unavoidable. Mariota answered it pretty well. His best performance came against Seattle , when he completed 19 of 31 passes for 183 yards and three touchdowns without turning the ball over in Washington's only win of the season. He also showed the value of having someone with his experience at the line of scrimmage, helping Washington get into better looks when Seattle presented something the offense could take advantage of. Mariota wasn't brought to Washington to be Daniels. They brought him here so the offense wouldn't completely fall apart if Daniels couldn't play . Until Mariota injured his own knee against Indianapolis, that's pretty much what he gave them.
Mike Sainristil's Role This isn't about declaring Sainristil a bad player after four games . It's about where his role was expected to be when the season started compared to where it is now. That change has been pretty dramatic. Sainristil played 98% of Washington's defensive snaps in Week 1 and 82% in Week 2. That dropped to 39% against Seattle, and then just five defensive snaps against Indianapolis. Meanwhile, Robertson and Rasul Douglas have become major parts of Washington's secondary, while Fabian Moreau has also gotten work. Whatever the long-term plan is for Sainristil, his first month went the opposite direction from what almost anyone would've expected when the season started. Running Backs Washington's overall rushing numbers don't look terrible until you start separating the quarterbacks from the running backs. That's where the problem shows up. The Commanders' backs have combined for 331 yards on 96 carries through four games, or about 3.4 yards per attempt. Jacory Croskey-Merritt has 157 yards on 56 carries and hasn't broken a run longer than 11 yards, while against Indianapolis the entire running back room combined for 49 yards on 18 carries. Washington's quarterbacks account for 165 of the team's 496 rushing yards. That isn't exactly the formula the Commanders were looking for, especially during a stretch when Daniels wasn't available and the running game should've been helping whoever was playing quarterback. Instead, Washington has too often needed the quarterback to create rushing production. Tight Ends Washington has enough tight ends to throw a small party, but so far there's been little reason to celebrate what they've done in the passing game. Through four games, the group has combined for 10 catches, 65 yards, and no touchdowns. Chig Okonkwo missing time hasn't helped, but the Commanders still have Ben Sinnott, John Bates, and Colson Yankoff, and none of them have become much of a factor when…

title: Washington Keeps Talking About Fixing Its Penalties. The Numbers Say Otherwise — Commanders Daily
full_text:
While the Washington Commanders aren't the most penalized team in the NFL, they keep finding new ways to shoot themselves in the foot at the worst time. More importantly, the problem the team keeps talking about controlling is actually getting worse over the last two games. Since the start of the season, Washington has 30 accepted penalties for 224 yards, which is the 16th-most in the league (Cleveland has the most with 43). Game-by-Game Penalties - Philadelphia: 6 for 45 - Dallas: 5 for 38 - Seattle: 9 for 57 - Indianapolis: 10 for 84 Offensive coordinator David Blough openly addressed the issue the first moment he got a chance after the Seattle game. "Truthfully, man, it was not really up to our standard as an offense," Blough said. "Too many pre-snap penalties, too many third downs where we couldn't convert. And it starts with me and coaching it and teaching it better." Looking back at his words, I'm realizing his accountability can only go so far if he can't get this under control now, after pinpointing it as an issue, only to have it actually get worse. London gave Washington another example of exactly what Blough was talking about . Late in the third quarter, with the Commanders trailing 20-13, Athan Kaliakmanis hit Antonio Williams for what looked like an 87-yard touchdown. Instead, an illegal shift where Dyami Brown never came to a complete stop wiped it off the board, and Washington went from being an extra point away from tying the game to facing third-and-16 from its own eight-yard line. Kaliakmanis scrambled for eight yards on the next play, and Tress Way came out to punt.
Here’s the play where #Commanders WR Antonio Williams’ 87 yard TD was nullified by two penalties: Illegal shift & Offensive Holding on Dyami Brown pic.twitter.com/LRYOfqokcP
That wasn't the only time Washington hurt itself Sunday, either. Treylon Burks was called for a false start early in the second quarter, the Commanders took a delay of game late in the fourth, and the penalties stretched across all three phases. That's the part that makes this harder to dismiss as one bad afternoon or one position group having problems . When the offense, defense, and special teams all contribute, it becomes something much bigger than cleaning up one guy's mistake. Quinn addressed that this week when talking about how he wants Washington practicing moving forward. "That's what I want to make sure in practice: we're seeing all three phases connected. But let's make sure, man, let's go battle forward, but no fouls that are before the snap. After the snap, those ones, let's handle business between the whistles." That's the distinction Washington has to make now. A hold or pass interference can come from trying to finish a play, but a false start, illegal shift, or delay of game happens before the opponent has really done anything to you. At 1-3, the Commanders already have enough problems without creating extra issues before the ball is even snapped. The Giants game will give them another chance to show this is actually getting fixed, not just talked about. Washington doesn't have to suddenly become the least-penalized team in football, but the number can't keep climbing every week while the same mistakes continue showing up in critical moments. title: Commanders News: Jayden Daniels Nears Return While Washington’s Roster Keeps Changing | Burgundy Roundup

With the team back from London, the focus now turns towards another NFC East matchup with the New York Giants this weekend. Tuesday brought some roster movement, encouraging practice news, and clarity from Commanders head coach Dan Quinn on what needs fixing. The team lost two players poached from the practice squad: the Seattle Seahawks signed running back Robert Henry Jr ., and the Pittsburgh Steelers signed cornerback Terell Smith. Henry had a big preseason game against the Miami Dolphins before fading late in the preseason after a costly fumble hurt his roster chances. He was eventually cut and signed to the practice squad. Smith was more of a developmental cornerback depth piece for Washington. The team now has two practice squad spots to fill.
The Commanders worked out 3 DBs: CB Marcus Allen, CB Antonio Hamilton and S Jack Henderson. Hamilton was with the team last season and through training camp.
With attention now turning toward Wednesday's press conference with Quinn, Jayden Daniels, Sam Cosmi, Rachaad White, and Nick Cross are expected to work their way back toward practice this week, which is great news. Daniels is the obvious headline grabber , with Marcus Mariota currently without a timeline for his return after his second MCL sprain on the same knee in less than three months. Quinn admitted the staff is still "tweaking it" to find the best offensive line combination. Getting Sam Cosmi back should go a long way with that. "We’re still tweaking it to find the right combination for sure," Quinn said. Trey Amos, Deatrich Wise Jr., and Jeremy McNichols are eligible and could begin working their way back, but opening a player's practice window does not mean the player will be immediately activated. That is important for a team that currently has several players on injured reserve and has spent much of the first month dealing with injuries.
Running back Austin Ekeler was set to join the Carolina Panthers ' practice squad in Week 4 when the Washington Commanders called. What's wild is that after being signed back to the roster just a few days earlier, Ekeler not only made the trip across the pond ; he played 17 offensive snaps (27%) against the Indianapolis Colts. That may not sound like much, but Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt led the backs with 29 snaps (45%), Ekeler was next with 17 (27%), and rookie Kaytron Allen played 12 (19%).
Pre-snap penalties are Quinn’s biggest self-inflicted concern “Our performance follows our focus,” he said. And if there’s one place Quinn wants to get right more than anything else, it’s in the pre-snap penalty department. “I am very intent on our self-inflicted fouls that happen pre-snap. I thought the week before we really showed excellent complementary football; the takeaways that turned into points, the field-position battle that we won, and so when we didn’t do that in the last game, you feel that,” he told Kramsky. “And so that’s what I want to make sure in practice: we’re seeing all three phases connected. But let’s make sure, man, let’s go battle forward, but no fouls that are before the snap. After the snap, those ones, let’s handle business between the whistles.”
HC Dan Quinn confirmed that WR Jaylin Lane suffered a season-ending injury in yesterday’s game Wishing you a healthy recovery, @j_lane_2 🙏 pic.twitter.com/cnCdeyTzYJ
After Week 2, we emphasized that after an offseason spent focused on creating them , Washington was heading into the Seattle game with no takeaways. New defensive coordinator Daronte Jones made that a major priority of his offseason program. The unit broke through, getting three against the Seahawks and two in London against Indianapolis. With the takeaway faucet on, the conversation has shifted from whether they're getting them to whether they're turning those extra possessions into points.
Kaliakmanis was called into action and finished the afternoon as the starter when Mariota strained his MCL 12 snaps into the game. The result wasn't what he or the Commanders wanted, as they suffered a 30-13 loss, but he's grateful for the opportunity because of all the lessons he learned in one afternoon. He's already working on some of them so he can be more prepared for his next opportunity.
The coverage kings in Week 4 👑 pic.twitter.com/xcutlCJpxO
We know what's wrong with the Commanders' defense. A lack of top-tier talent in the secondary is undermining coordinator Daronte Jones' efforts to get more creatively aggressive up front.

title: Austin Ekeler's First Game Back Reveals Surprising Truth About Commanders Backfield
full_text:
Running back Austin Ekeler was set to join the Carolina Panthers ' practice squad in Week 4 when the Washington Commanders called. What's wild is that after being signed back to the roster just a few days earlier, Ekeler not only made the trip across the pond ; he played 17 offensive snaps (27%) against the Indianapolis Colts. That may not sound like much, but Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt led the backs with 29 snaps (45%), Ekeler was next with 17 (27%), and rookie Kaytron Allen played 12 (19%). There are two ways to look at this: either Washington already highly trusts a 31-year-old Ekeler coming off an Achilles tendon injury he suffered in Week 2 of the 2025 season, or Allen may not be as far along in the pecking order as we thought. Either way, Bill still got the lion's share of the snaps, even though Ekeler gained more yards on fewer carries and neither back lit things on fire (Ekeler had 4 carries for 29 yards, and one catch for 11; Bill had 9 carries for 15 yards, and two catches for 35 yards). While the initial signing is certainly more about adding another dimension than replacing the current back, the truth is generally in the numbers, which will undoubtedly shift again when White returns. The player this should worry is Allen, who saw Ekeler come in and get officially signed when the team was in the process of making a trip to London , and then get more snaps than him. Obviously, Ekeler wasn't brought in for depth, since the team knows what he can bring when healthy, but it's interesting to see how quickly the younger back rotation shifted. That makes what happened with rookie Robert Henry Jr. even more interesting. Henry flashed during the preseason but was cut and re-signed to Washington's practice squad after a bit of fumblitis, until Seattle signed him away Monday. The Seahawks then decided not to sign veteran Joe Mixon after his physical, potentially opening an opportunity for Henry. Washington, meanwhile, chose to bring back Ekeler and immediately gave him more snaps than Allen.
We've signed RB Robert Henry Jr. Read more » https://t.co/rRC44HuDF0 pic.twitter.com/ciiUr52L9y
The team still appears committed to Croskey-Merritt as its lead back, but Ekeler getting 27% of the snaps right off the street tells me that the coaching staff believes he can help now. I was already expecting him to lead from experience , help in passing-down work and protection, and give the offense a dependable veteran option rather than becoming a volume runner again. We'll have to wait until White gets back before we get a clearer picture of how Washington wants to divide this backfield. title: Three Takeaways from Athan Kaliakmanis' Commanders Debut
full_text:
Jayden Daniels is just two weeks removed from another elbow dislocation. Marcus Mariota sprained his MCL for the second time in the same knee this season. Athan Kaliakmanis is the Washington Commanders' suddenly elevated quarterback, and watchers of the team may as well start analyzing what the third-stringer brings to the team's floundering 1-3 situation .
Aside from earning the distinction of being the first rookie quarterback to check into a 2026 regular-season game, he left a strong impression on anyone curious to see how the backup to the backup would fare in his first taste of NFL action. He arguably outshone his Indianapolis Colts counterpart , Daniel Jones, tossing for 186 yards to the veteran's 143, with a boom-or-bust style sure to elicit strong opinions from the Washington fan base depending on how long they'll have to ride his young arm.
If nothing else, the 23-year-old is hungry for big plays, a feature that shouldn't be taken for granted amongst backups, often more worried about holding onto their tenuous depth chart position than anything else.
The Rutgers product doesn't have to worry much about superior competition, currently standing alone in the position group's room. That willingness to play freely helped him stand alone as the only quarterback in the league to attempt six or more passes of 30-plus yards in a game this season, as well as the first-ever Redskin/Commander/Washington Football Team participant to convert on multiple 40+ yard heaves in his Washington debut.

Kaliakmanis' pre-draft scouting report described exactly the sort of quarterback we saw: someone armed with a strong enough arm to go for the home run play whenever he spotted an open target downfield. He credited his confidence and decisiveness in a prior interview with On SI, though his accuracy on such bold ideas still has some work to do before he's contending for anything resembling a starting spot anywhere.
As bold as he can get in his explosive play hunting, Kaliakmanis was never known for his pinpoint passing. Though he peaked as a 62.2% completion artist as a collegiate senior, he also totaled 27 interceptions and 55 touchdowns in his career thanks to that same aggression before the pros came calling.
He wasn't completely innocent in his messy debut, recording his first NFL pick when he dared to try and make something happen on the run. Like most fresh backups, he'll need some time before he resembles the comfortable decision-maker he knows he can be, a commonality that'll require a healthier context than the one he was suddenly dropped into.
Shifting from Daniels to Mariota on a dime last month never sounded unreasonable to Washington's coaches. Though Mariota is safer and lacks that same big-play upside, both are mobile quarterbacks capable of extending plays with their legs.
Kaliakmanis does not fit that same mold. He's more of your classic hungry gunslinger who's happier to sit back and wait for his most grandiose routes to develop, though he's already proven happy to sprint into space and break out a surprise spin move that sort of-almost worked.

Unfortunately for everyone involved, Washington's offensive line isn't where anyone looking for sustainable cover should hide. They're down their two strongest pass-blockers, Laremy Tunsil and Sam Cosmi, leaving behind a ragtag band of overtasked starters and rotating reserves to keep the offense afloat. That's a tough position for any quarterback to have to navigate — let alone a rookie in his first-ever bit of NFL action.
He'll greatly benefit from Terry McLaurin's return to the starting lineup as the squad's go-to endzone target out deep, as well as a healthy and diverse receiver room to spread the field and give the less-dynamic athlete in Kaliakmanis options.
Even if Daniels is trending toward returning before the bye week, it wouldn't hurt for the coaching staff to remain prepared for alternatives such as their newest signal caller. He's already here and likely to stay as a recent draftee, so they may as well make his life as quarterback as easy as they can.
